questions.stem: A primigravida attends a routine antenatal visit at 30 weeks. Her haemoglobin is 10.9 g/dL, MCV 89 fL and ferritin 40 µg/L. She feels well.
questions.q: What is the most likely explanation for this haemoglobin level?
options: Haemodilution from a larger rise in plasma than red cells
questions.why: Plasma volume rises by about 45% and red cell mass by about 25%, so haemoglobin falls while the MCV and ferritin remain normal. Iron deficiency would lower the MCV and ferritin.

questions.stem: A woman (G2 P1) at 34 weeks develops dizziness and sweating while lying flat for an ultrasound scan. Her blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg and her pulse is 110/min. The symptoms settle within minutes.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Turn her onto her left side
questions.why: After 20 weeks the uterus compresses the aorta and inferior vena cava in the supine position, causing supine hypotension. Left lateral tilt relieves it immediately.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 32 weeks has a soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. She is not breathless and her ECG shows left axis deviation.
questions.q: What is the most likely explanation?
questions.why: An ejection systolic flow murmur and left axis deviation are normal findings in pregnancy. A diastolic murmur would suggest mitral stenosis.

questions.stem: An arterial blood gas taken at 35 weeks for breathlessness shows pH 7.44, pCO₂ 30 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 19 mmol/L and pO₂ 100 mmHg. Oxygen saturation is 99% and the chest is clear.
questions.q: What is the correct interpretation of this blood gas?
questions.why: Progesterone increases ventilation, so the arterial pCO₂ is low (30 mmHg). With renal loss of bicarbonate, this is the normal compensated respiratory alkalosis of pregnancy.

questions.stem: A woman at 28 weeks has a serum creatinine of 92 µmol/L on routine testing. Her blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg and urinalysis shows a trace of protein.
questions.q: Which statement is correct?
options: It reflects muscle growth in pregnancy
It is low because of increased GFR
It is raised for pregnancy and needs renal assessment
questions.why: GFR rises by 50%, so serum creatinine falls below about 75 µmol/L. A value that is normal outside pregnancy is abnormal in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A routine urine dipstick at 26 weeks shows glucose 1+. The woman is well and has no risk factors for diabetes.
questions.q: What is the best next step?
questions.why: Glycosuria is common in pregnancy because of the raised GFR and is not diagnostic; diabetes is confirmed by blood glucose testing.

questions.stem: At 36 weeks a woman's liver function tests show ALP 380 IU/L, ALT 22 IU/L and a normal bilirubin. She has no itching.
questions.q: What is the most likely source of the ALP?
questions.why: Placental ALP rises 2–4 times in normal pregnancy, while ALT and bilirubin remain normal.

questions.stem: At 16 weeks a woman has a total T4 above the normal range, with a normal free T4 and TSH. She has no symptoms.
questions.q: What explains this result?
questions.why: Oestrogen doubles thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), which raises total T4 while free T4 remains normal.

questions.stem: A woman needs laparoscopic removal of a corpus luteum cyst at 7 weeks.
questions.q: Which drug support is needed after surgery?
questions.why: Until 8–10 weeks the corpus luteum is the source of progesterone. If it is removed, progesterone support is needed to prevent miscarriage.

questions.stem: A woman with a booking BMI of 33 asks how much weight she should gain in pregnancy.
questions.q: What is the advised total gain?
questions.why: For a BMI of 30 or more, the advised total weight gain is 5–9 kg.

questions.stem: On the first day after a massive postpartum haemorrhage, the fibrinogen is 2.1 g/L and the platelet count is 140 × 10⁹/L.
questions.q: How should the fibrinogen be interpreted?
questions.why: Fibrinogen at term is 4–6 g/L, so a level of 2 g/L during haemorrhage indicates consumption, and it should be replaced.

questions.stem: Many women develop abnormal glucose tolerance for the first time at 24–28 weeks.
questions.q: Which hormone is mainly responsible?
questions.why: Human placental lactogen (hPL) rises with placental mass and causes insulin resistance in the second half of pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has 7 weeks of amenorrhoea. On bimanual examination the isthmus is so soft that the examining fingers almost meet.
questions.q: What is this sign called?
questions.why: Hegar's sign is a soft, compressible isthmus at 6–10 weeks.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has 10 weeks of amenorrhoea, nausea and a positive urine pregnancy test.
questions.q: Which finding would make the diagnosis of pregnancy certain?
questions.why: Only fetal heart activity, a fetus seen on ultrasound, or fetal parts or movements felt by the examiner are certain signs.

questions.stem: A woman presents with vaginal bleeding at 6 weeks by dates. Serum hCG is 1200 IU/L, and 1560 IU/L when repeated 48 hours later. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and no adnexal mass.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Viable intrauterine pregnancy too early to see
questions.why: In a viable pregnancy hCG rises by at least 63% in 48 hours; a rise of 30% suggests a failing or ectopic pregnancy.

questions.stem: Serum hCG is 3400 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a small amount of free fluid.
questions.q: What is the working diagnosis?
questions.why: Above the discriminatory zone (2000 IU/L on transvaginal ultrasound) an intrauterine sac should be visible.

questions.stem: A woman at 12 weeks has hCG much higher than expected for dates, vomiting and a uterus of 16-week size.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.why: A very high hCG with a uterus that is large for dates and vomiting suggests a molar pregnancy.

questions.stem: The LMP was 10 January 2026 and the cycles are regular at 28 days.
questions.q: What is the expected date of delivery (EDD)?
questions.why: Naegele's rule: 10 January + 7 days − 3 months + 1 year = 17 October 2026 (LMP + 280 days).

questions.stem: The LMP was 1 March 2026 and the cycles are regular at 35 days.
questions.q: What is the corrected EDD?
questions.why: Naegele's rule gives 8 December; a 35-day cycle adds 7 days, giving 15 December.

questions.stem: A certain LMP gives a gestation of 12⁺⁴ weeks, but the crown–rump length on ultrasound corresponds to 11⁺² weeks.
questions.q: How should the pregnancy be dated?
options: Repeat the scan at 20 weeks and decide
questions.why: A difference of more than 5 days (here 9 days) means that the CRL date is used.

questions.stem: A woman books at 34 weeks with no early scan. The scan shows growth at the 3rd centile with normal liquor.
questions.q: What is the correct interpretation of dates?
options: Keep the best clinical dates and assess for growth restriction
questions.why: A late scan cannot date a pregnancy (error ± 3 weeks). A small fetus in late pregnancy is assumed to have growth restriction, not incorrect dates.

questions.stem: A transvaginal scan at 5½ weeks shows a gestational sac in the uterus.
questions.q: Which finding first confirms a true intrauterine pregnancy?
questions.why: A yolk sac distinguishes a true gestational sac from a pseudosac.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman, married for 9 years without children, says she is 7 months pregnant. Her abdomen is enlarged and she reports fetal movements. The hCG test is negative and ultrasound shows an empty uterus.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Pseudocyesis is a firm belief of being pregnant, with symptoms of pregnancy but a negative hCG and an empty uterus.

questions.stem: A woman is 41⁺⁶ weeks by an early dating scan.
questions.q: How is this pregnancy described?
questions.why: Late term is 41⁺⁰ to 41⁺⁶ weeks; post-term begins at 42 weeks.

questions.stem: A healthy 23-year-old plans her first pregnancy.
questions.q: What folic acid dose should she take?
options: 1 mg only after a positive test
0.4 mg daily from before conception to 12 weeks
questions.why: All women take 0.4 mg daily from before conception until 12 weeks to prevent neural tube defects.

questions.stem: A woman on sodium valproate for epilepsy is planning pregnancy.
questions.q: Which folic acid dose is advised?
questions.why: High-risk women (antiepileptic drugs, diabetes, previous neural tube defect, obesity, sickle cell disease) take 5 mg daily.

questions.stem: A booking urine culture grows E. coli > 10⁵/mL. The woman has no symptoms.
questions.q: What is the correct management?
options: Treat with an appropriate antibiotic and recheck
No treatment as she is well
questions.why: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy because 20–30% of cases progress to pyelonephritis.

questions.stem: A woman never vaccinated against tetanus books at 30 weeks.
questions.q: What is the tetanus plan?
options: Td now and a second dose 4 weeks later
questions.why: Two doses of Td are given 4 weeks apart, the second at least 2 weeks before delivery.

questions.stem: A woman with HIV on cotrimoxazole prophylaxis attends at 20 weeks in a malaria-endemic area.
questions.q: Which malaria prevention is appropriate?
options: No SP; insecticide-treated net and prompt testing of fever
questions.why: SP is not given with cotrimoxazole because both are antifolate drugs. She should still use an insecticide-treated net and have any fever tested promptly.

questions.stem: A woman at 18 weeks felt fetal movements 2 weeks ago and lives in a malaria area.
questions.q: When is the first SP dose given?
questions.why: The first dose of SP is given at the first visit after quickening, and the second at least 4 weeks later.

questions.stem: A woman's previous pregnancy was complicated by pre-eclampsia that required delivery at 32 weeks. She is now 10 weeks pregnant.
questions.q: Which drug should start at 12 weeks?
questions.why: Previous pre-eclampsia is a high-risk factor: aspirin 75 mg is given from 12 to 36 weeks.

questions.stem: An RhD-negative woman with no antibodies has vaginal bleeding after a fall at 26 weeks.
questions.q: What is required regarding anti-D?
options: Anti-D only if bleeding is heavy
questions.why: Abdominal trauma is a sensitising event, so anti-D is given within 72 hours.

questions.stem: A low-risk woman at 32 weeks asks for ibuprofen for back pain.
questions.q: What is the best advice?
options: Avoid NSAIDs; use paracetamol and posture advice
questions.why: NSAIDs after 30 weeks carry a risk of premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios.

questions.stem: WHO recommends a minimum number of antenatal contacts in a normal pregnancy.
questions.q: How many contacts are recommended?
questions.why: The WHO model recommends eight contacts.

questions.stem: A woman booked at 11 weeks is found to be HBsAg positive.
questions.q: What should be planned for the baby?
options: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin at birth
Antiviral to the baby for 6 months
questions.why: Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin (HBIG) given to the newborn within 12–24 hours prevent most transmission; breastfeeding is allowed.

questions.stem: A primigravida is examined at 36 weeks. On abdominal palpation a hard, round, ballotable mass is felt in the fundus.
questions.q: What is the next step in antenatal care?
options: Ultrasound to confirm breech and plan ECV
questions.why: Presentation is checked at 36 weeks; a breech presentation is confirmed by ultrasound and ECV is offered.

questions.theme: Signs and tests of pregnancy
questions.lead: For each description choose the matching sign or test.

items.stem: Bluish discolouration of the vagina at 8 weeks.
items.why: Chadwick's sign is caused by venous congestion.

items.stem: First movements felt by the mother at 19 weeks.
items.why: Quickening is felt by the mother and is a presumptive sign.

items.stem: Confirms a true intrauterine pregnancy at 5½ weeks.
items.why: A yolk sac within the sac excludes a pseudosac.

items.stem: hCG level above which an intrauterine sac should be visible on TVS.
items.why: The level is about 2000 IU/L on transvaginal ultrasound.

questions.theme: Antenatal preventive care
questions.lead: For each woman choose the most appropriate preventive measure.

items.stem: A woman with type 1 diabetes who is planning pregnancy.
items.why: Women with diabetes need high-dose folic acid.

items.stem: A woman with chronic hypertension at 12 weeks.
items.why: Chronic hypertension is a major risk factor for pre-eclampsia: aspirin is given from 12 to 36 weeks.

items.stem: A healthy woman at 20 weeks in a high-transmission malaria area who has felt quickening.
items.why: IPTp with SP starts after quickening.

items.stem: RhD-negative woman after an external cephalic version.
items.why: ECV is a sensitising event.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 9 weeks has vomited all day for 5 days and cannot keep fluids down. Her weight fell from 62 to 58 kg, pulse is 112/min and urine ketones are 3+. The uterus feels like 14 weeks in size.
questions.q: Which investigation is most important next?
questions.why: A uterus large for dates with heavy vomiting points to a molar or twin pregnancy, which ultrasound shows at once. TFTs are part of the work-up but will not explain the uterine size.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 10 weeks has vomited everything for 8 days. Bloods: Na⁺ 129, K⁺ 2.8, Cl⁻ 84 mmol/L, bicarbonate 33 mmol/L, urea raised, urine ketones 3+.
questions.q: Which acid–base disturbance is most likely?
questions.why: Vomiting loses HCl and K⁺, so bicarbonate rises with low chloride and potassium. Ketonuria alone does not make an acidosis when the high bicarbonate shows alkalosis.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old at 8 weeks is admitted after 4 days of vomiting. She is dry, pulse 108/min, Na⁺ 131 and K⁺ 3.1 mmol/L. The intern writes a drip chart.
questions.q: Which intravenous fluid is most appropriate?
questions.why: Normal saline with KCl replaces sodium, chloride and potassium. Dextrose before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke, and hypotonic fluids make the low sodium worse.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old at 11 weeks has been on IV 5% dextrose for 3 days for severe vomiting. Today she is confused, cannot walk straight and has horizontal nystagmus. Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, glucose 5.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.why: Confusion, ataxia and nystagmus after dextrose in a starved woman is thiamine (B1) lack; give thiamine IV now. Pyridoxine is added in hyperemesis but does not treat this.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old para 1 at 7 weeks scores 13 on the PUQE score. Urine ketones are 2+ and she manages only small sips of water. She is otherwise well.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Dietary advice and review in one week
Ultrasound and discharge if a single viable fetus
Admit for IV fluids, thiamine and regular antiemetics
questions.why: A PUQE score of 12 or more is severe and she cannot keep up fluids, so she needs admission. Oral treatment at home is for mild disease (score 6 or less).

questions.stem: A 23-year-old at 9 weeks was admitted 48 hours ago with severe vomiting. She has had cyclizine 50 mg 8-hourly IV regularly and is still vomiting every meal. U&E have been corrected.
questions.q: Which drug should be added next?
questions.why: After a first-line drug fails, the next step on the ladder is metoclopramide or domperidone. Ondansetron is third line and steroids come after that.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old at 10 weeks, on IV antiemetics for vomiting, suddenly develops a twisted neck, jaw spasm and eyes rolled upwards on day 3. She is fully alert and her blood pressure is 105/70.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Sudden dystonia with clear consciousness is a known side effect of metoclopramide, so it is limited to 5 days. Wernicke gives confusion, ataxia and eye signs, not spasm.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 9 weeks is admitted with Na⁺ 118 mmol/L after weeks of vomiting. Twenty-four hours later her sodium is 133 mmol/L. On day 3 she has slurred speech, difficulty swallowing and weak limbs.
questions.q: What is the most likely explanation?
questions.why: A rise of 15 mmol/L in 24 hours is far above the limit of 10 mmol/L, causing pontine myelinolysis (dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis). Wernicke does not cause this bulbar picture.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 8 weeks, BMI 31, is admitted with severe vomiting and dehydration. She is put on IV fluids and antiemetics.
questions.q: Which other measure belongs in her admission plan?
options: Strict bed rest until vomiting stops
questions.why: Dehydration and immobility make VTE likely, so every admitted woman gets a VTE assessment with stockings and low-molecular-weight heparin. Bed rest raises the risk and is not advised.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 13 weeks has been in hospital for 2 weeks. She has had cyclizine, then metoclopramide, then ondansetron, with correct fluids and thiamine, but she still vomits and her weight keeps falling.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: When three drug lines fail, steroids are the next step (hydrocortisone 100 mg IV 12-hourly, then prednisolone). TPN and then termination are last resorts after steroids fail.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old G3 at 26 weeks has vomited for 2 days. Temperature is 38.9 °C, pulse 116/min and she has right loin tenderness. Urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Fever, loin pain and a positive dipstick make this pyelonephritis. Vomiting that starts after 12 weeks, with fever or pain, is not hyperemesis.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old at 10 weeks, vomiting for a week, retches hard and brings up fresh blood streaks after a bout of vomiting. Pulse is 96/min, Hb 12.8 g/dL.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the bleeding?
questions.why: Fresh streaks of blood after forceful retching, with a stable Hb, fit a mucosal tear at the oesophagogastric junction. Varices need portal hypertension and bleed heavily.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old para 1 at 24 weeks feels well. Hb is 10.6 g/dL, MCV 88 fL and ferritin 40 µg/L. She takes routine iron and folate.
questions.q: What is the best interpretation?
options: Anaemia of chronic disease: screen for TB
Iron deficiency: double the iron dose
Folate deficiency: start folic acid 5 mg
questions.why: In the second trimester anaemia starts below 10.5 g/dL; normal MCV and ferritin show dilution from plasma rising faster than red cells. No extra treatment is needed.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old primigravida books at 9 weeks. Hb is 10.8 g/dL, MCV 77 fL. She has no symptoms.
questions.q: How is her Hb best classified?
questions.why: In the first trimester the cut-off is 11 g/dL, so 10.8 is mild anaemia (10–10.9). The 10.5 cut-off and physiological dilution apply to the 2nd and third trimesters.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old para 4 at 26 weeks is tired. Hb 8.9 g/dL, MCV 64 fL, ferritin 7 µg/L. She tolerates tablets and has no other illness.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Transfusion of 2 units of packed cells
Ferrous sulphate 200 mg two to three times daily with folic acid
questions.why: Moderate iron deficiency before 34 weeks in a woman who tolerates tablets is treated with oral iron first. Parenteral iron is for intolerance, poor adherence or late presentation.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old at 22 weeks has Hb 9.8 g/dL, MCV 61 fL, red cell count 5.9 × 10¹²/L and ferritin 85 µg/L. She is afebrile. Four weeks of oral iron did not change the Hb.
questions.q: Which investigation is most appropriate next?
questions.why: Very small cells with a normal ferritin and a Mentzer index below 13 (61 ÷ 5.9 about 10) suggest thalassaemia trait; HbA2 above 3.5% confirms it. B12 and folate are for large cells.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old with epilepsy on phenytoin is seen at 28 weeks. Hb 8.6 g/dL, MCV 108 fL, and the film shows hypersegmented neutrophils.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Folic acid 5 mg daily plus iron
questions.why: Large cells with hypersegmented neutrophils in a woman on an anti-epileptic point to folate lack; treat with folic acid 5 mg plus iron. 0.4 mg is the prevention dose for low-risk women.

questions.stem: A para 7 at 37 weeks comes with breathlessness on walking. Hb is 6.2 g/dL, MCV 60 fL. Pulse 104/min, no basal crackles, JVP not raised.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Slow packed-cell transfusion with IV furosemide
questions.why: Hb below 7 after 36 weeks leaves no time for iron to work, so she is transfused with packed cells, one unit over 3–4 hours, with furosemide if overload threatens. Whole blood adds too much volume.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old para 3 at 28 weeks has Hb 6.5 g/dL found at a routine visit. She is well, pulse 92/min, and has no signs of heart failure.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Admit, find the cause, and give oral or IV iron
Hb electrophoresis as an outpatient only
Oral iron and review in 4 weeks
questions.why: Severe anaemia before 36 weeks without failure is admitted, the cause found (malaria, worms, iron lack) and treated with iron; transfusion is for after 36 weeks, failure or Hb below 5.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 35 weeks has Hb 8.4 g/dL and ferritin 6 µg/L. She vomits every iron tablet, including ferrous gluconate.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Iron sucrose 200 mg IV over 30 minutes
Iron dextran without a test dose
questions.why: Intolerance of oral iron and Hb 7–9.9 after about 34 weeks are both indications for parenteral iron; iron sucrose is the safest. Transfusion is not needed at Hb 8.4.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 30 weeks started ferrous sulphate 4 weeks ago. Hb is unchanged at 9.1 g/dL, ferritin 9 µg/L. Her stools are black. She takes the tablet with tea after breakfast.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Take the tablet 1 hour before food with vitamin C, not with tea
questions.why: Tea blocks iron absorption; black stools show she takes the tablets, so fix how she takes them. IV iron is for true intolerance or non-adherence.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old at 24 weeks with Hb 8.8 g/dL and low ferritin starts oral ferrous sulphate. She is seen again after 10 days.
questions.q: Which finding best shows that treatment is working?
options: A rise in the reticulocyte count
questions.why: The first sign of response is a reticulocyte peak at 7–10 days; Hb rises only about 1 g/dL per week. Black stools show she takes the iron, not that it works.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old from Kordofan with known HbSS books at 12 weeks. Hb 8.0 g/dL, ferritin 210 µg/L. She has had two painful crises this year.
questions.q: Which supplement plan is most appropriate?
options: Folic acid 5 mg daily without routine iron
Ferrous sulphate with folic acid 0.4 mg
questions.why: Women with sickle cell disease need folic acid 5 mg for constant haemolysis; iron is given only if ferritin is low, and hers is high. 0.4 mg is the low-risk dose.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 30 weeks with known G6PD deficiency has dysuria and frequency. Urine culture grows E. Coli sensitive to several drugs.
questions.q: Which antibiotic should be avoided?
questions.why: Nitrofurantoin (like sulphonamides and primaquine) causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. The penicillins and cephalosporins are safe.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old is 3 days after an emergency caesarean. Her left calf is painful and 3 cm wider than the right. She is not bleeding; platelets are normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Duplex ultrasound and treat only if positive
Start treatment-dose LMWH, then arrange duplex ultrasound
questions.why: Clinical suspicion of DVT is treated with full-dose low-molecular-weight heparin before the scan unless she is bleeding. D-dimer rises normally in pregnancy and after birth, so it does not help.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 32 weeks has a swollen, tender left leg. Treatment-dose low-molecular-weight heparin was started and the duplex ultrasound is negative, but the leg is still very suspicious.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue LMWH and repeat the duplex on day 4 and day 7
questions.why: A negative scan with high suspicion is managed by keeping low-molecular-weight heparin and repeating the scan; iliac clots may also need MRI venography. Stopping now risks missing a DVT.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old is 5 days after caesarean. She is breathless, pulse 118/min, oxygen saturation 93% on air, and her left leg is swollen. Low-molecular-weight heparin has been started; ECG shows sinus tachycardia.
questions.q: Which investigation is most appropriate next?
options: Compression duplex ultrasound of the legs
questions.why: With leg signs, scan the legs first: a DVT on duplex proves VTE and spares the chest scan. Chest imaging is chosen only if the legs are negative.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old at 30 weeks has sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness, oxygen saturation 94%. There are no leg signs. Chest X-ray is normal. Low-molecular-weight heparin has been started.
questions.q: Which imaging is most appropriate?
questions.why: A normal chest X-ray with no leg signs points to a V/Q scan, which gives a lower breast dose. CTPA is chosen when the X-ray is abnormal.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old on day 6 after birth is breathless with pleuritic pain. ABG shows low oxygen and low CO₂.
questions.q: Which ECG finding is most commonly seen in her likely condition?
questions.why: The commonest ECG finding in PE is sinus tachycardia. S1Q3T3 is the classic textbook sign but uncommon.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old on day 3 after caesarean collapses in the ward. Blood pressure 75/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 36/min, oxygen saturation 82%, JVP raised. Bedside echo shows a dilated right ventricle.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Hypotension with respiratory distress is massive PE: ICU, oxygen, IV UFH (5000 IU then infusion) and thrombolysis or embolectomy. An IVC filter is only for failure or contraindication to anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 10 weeks, booking weight 64 kg, has a DVT of the left femoral vein proven on duplex. Platelets and renal function are normal.
questions.q: Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.why: Low-molecular-weight heparin is the anticoagulant of pregnancy; treatment is 1 mg/kg twice daily by booking weight (50–69 kg = 60 mg bd). Warfarin at 6–12 weeks causes embryopathy; 40 mg daily is only prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old has a DVT diagnosed at 30 weeks and starts treatment-dose low-molecular-weight heparin.
questions.q: For how long should she be anticoagulated?
options: 3 months in total, stopping in pregnancy
Rest of pregnancy and at least 6 weeks after birth (at least 3 months in total)
questions.why: Anticoagulation continues for the rest of pregnancy and at least 6 weeks postpartum, with a total of at least 3 months. The risk is highest after birth, so stopping at delivery is unsafe.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old on treatment-dose enoxaparin for DVT goes into labour. Her last injection was 8 hours ago and she asks for an epidural.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Give protamine and site the epidural
No regional block until 24 hours after the last dose; offer other analgesia
Switch to IV heparin and site the epidural
questions.why: After a treatment dose, wait 24 hours before a block (12 hours after a prophylactic dose). Protamine only partly reverses low-molecular-weight heparin and is not used to allow an epidural.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old para 3 books at 12 weeks. Her BMI is 34. She has no past VTE and no other risk factors.
questions.q: What thromboprophylaxis is most appropriate?
options: LMWH from 28 weeks until 6 weeks after birth
LMWH for the whole pregnancy and 6 weeks after birth
questions.why: Age over 35, BMI over 30 and parity of 3 or more are three risk factors, so low-molecular-weight heparin starts at 28 weeks and continues to 6 weeks postnatal. Four or more factors would mean the whole pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old at 7 weeks had an unprovoked DVT 3 years ago, treated for 6 months. Thrombophilia screen was negative.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan?
options: LMWH for 10 days after birth only
Prophylactic LMWH for the whole pregnancy and 6 weeks after birth
questions.why: A previous unprovoked, oestrogen-related or thrombophilia-related VTE needs low-molecular-weight heparin through the whole pregnancy and 6 weeks after. A VTE provoked by major surgery would count as 3 factors (from 28 weeks).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old is on day 3 after vaginal birth, on treatment-dose low-molecular-weight heparin for a DVT found at 34 weeks. She dislikes injections and wants to breastfeed.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop anticoagulation now that the baby is born
Start warfarin, continue LMWH until INR is 2–3 on two days, and breastfeed
Stop breastfeeding if she takes warfarin
Stop LMWH and start warfarin today
questions.why: Warfarin is safe after birth and in breastfeeding but must overlap with low-molecular-weight heparin until INR is 2–3 on two days (at least 5 days). Warfarin alone at first is not protective.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 26 weeks with a BMI of 33 has a 75 g OGTT. Fasting plasma glucose is 5.8 mmol/L and the 2-hour value is 7.0 mmol/L.
questions.q: What is the correct interpretation?
options: Normal: both values must be abnormal
Impaired fasting glucose: repeat at 32 weeks
questions.why: One abnormal value is enough: fasting 5.6 or more, or 2 hours 7.8 or more, means gestational diabetes. Overt diabetes needs fasting 7.0 or 2 hours 11.1.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old para 3 books at 10 weeks. Her fasting plasma glucose on a lab sample is 7.8 mmol/L. She had no known diabetes before.
questions.q: How should she be classified and managed?
options: Overt diabetes: treat as pre-existing diabetes
Impaired fasting glucose: repeat at 28 weeks
Gestational diabetes: diet and repeat OGTT at 24 weeks
questions.why: A fasting value of 7.0 or more found in pregnancy is overt diabetes and is managed as pre-existing (early anomaly scan, fetal echo, tight control). It is not gestational diabetes.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old had gestational diabetes in her last pregnancy. She is now 10 weeks pregnant and well.
questions.q: When should she first have an OGTT?
options: At 16 weeks, repeated at 24–28 weeks if normal
questions.why: Previous gestational diabetes is the one group tested early, at 16 weeks; a normal result is repeated at 24–28 weeks. Other risk factors are tested at 24–28 weeks.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old at 22 weeks has glucose 1+ on urine dipstick at two visits. She has no risk factors. Her OGTT: fasting 4.6 and 2 hours 6.8 mmol/L.
questions.q: What is the most likely explanation of the glycosuria?
options: Lowered renal threshold for glucose in pregnancy
questions.why: GFR rises in pregnancy and the renal threshold falls, so glycosuria with a normal OGTT is normal. That is why urine glucose is a poor screening test.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 28 weeks (fasting 5.9 mmol/L). After 2 weeks of diet and walking, her fasting glucose is still 5.9 and 1-h post-meal values 8.2–8.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Above target (fasting 5.3 or more, 1 hour 7.8 or more) after 1–2 weeks of diet means adding metformin, the first drug in gestational diabetes. Insulin first is for fasting 7 or more at diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old at 28 weeks has an OGTT: fasting 7.4 mmol/L and 2 hours 10.2 mmol/L. Her BMI is 36.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.why: A fasting value of 7 or more at diagnosis goes straight to insulin. Diet trial first would waste weeks of high glucose for the fetus.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old with type 2 diabetes on gliclazide, enalapril and atorvastatin wants to conceive. Her HbA1c is 8.2%.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop all drugs and conceive now
Stop enalapril and atorvastatin, start folic acid 5 mg, and delay pregnancy until HbA1c is below 6.5%
Continue enalapril for kidney protection and start folic acid 5 mg
Conceive now and continue all drugs with folic acid 0.4 mg
questions.why: Before pregnancy: stop ACE inhibitors and statins, change oral drugs except metformin to insulin, give folic acid 5 mg, and aim for HbA1c below 6.5%. Only above 10% is pregnancy strongly advised against for now.

questions.stem: A newborn of a mother with type 1 diabetes has weak legs, flat buttocks and a short intergluteal cleft. X-ray shows an absent sacrum. The mother's HbA1c at booking was 11%.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Absent sacrum is caudal regression, the most characteristic anomaly of maternal diabetes (the commonest is cardiac). It comes from high glucose in weeks 3–8.

questions.stem: A 4.3 kg baby is born at 38 weeks to a mother with gestational diabetes on insulin. At 2 hours the baby is shaky (jittery) and sweaty and feeds poorly.
questions.q: Which investigation is most urgent?
questions.why: Neonatal hypoglycaemia is the commonest problem: fetal insulin stays high after the cord is cut. Aim for glucose above 2.6 mmol/L; calcium is checked if glucose is normal.

questions.stem: A baby of a mother with poorly controlled pre-existing diabetes is plethoric on day 1. Haematocrit is 70%.
questions.q: What is the main mechanism?
options: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia raises oxygen use, causing hypoxia and more erythropoietin
Maternal insulin crosses the placenta and stimulates the marrow
questions.why: Glucose crosses the placenta but insulin does not; fetal hyperinsulinaemia raises metabolism and oxygen use, and hypoxia drives erythropoietin. Maternal insulin does not cross.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with gestational diabetes on metformin 2 g/day at 32 weeks brings her glucose diary: fasting 4.9–5.1 mmol/L, 1 hour after meals 8.4–8.9 mmol/L. She takes the tablets correctly.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: No change: fasting values are on target
questions.why: The 1-hour target is below 7.8 mmol/L; on maximum metformin the next step on the ladder is insulin (soluble before meals). Metformin's maximum is 2 g/day.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with type 2 diabetes on insulin is 38 weeks. Ultrasound estimated fetal weight is 4.7 kg. Glucose control has been fair.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan?
questions.why: An estimated fetal weight above 4.5 kg in a diabetic carries a high risk of shoulder dystocia, so elective caesarean is offered. Induction suits a normal-sized baby.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old with type 1 diabetes is in established labour at 39 weeks. She normally takes basal-bolus insulin.
questions.q: How should her glucose be managed in labour?
options: IV soluble insulin 0.5–2 U/h plus dextrose, glucose hourly, target 4–7 mmol/L
Usual SC insulin and check glucose after birth
Stop all insulin until after delivery
questions.why: Type 1 needs insulin plus dextrose from established labour, glucose checked hourly, aiming for 4–7 mmol/L. Never give insulin without dextrose, and never stop insulin in type 1.

questions.stem: A woman with type 1 diabetes has just delivered vaginally. Her insulin infusion is still at the labour rate, and her glucose 30 minutes after birth is 3.1 mmol/L.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate step?
options: Give glucagon IM and keep the rate
Double the dextrose and keep the rate
Reduce insulin to the pre-pregnancy dose or lower
questions.why: Once the placenta is out, insulin resistance disappears, so she returns to her pre-pregnancy dose or lower. Stopping insulin entirely in type 1 risks DKA.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with type 1 diabetes at 30 weeks has vomited for a day. She breathes deeply, glucose is 11.5 mmol/L, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, ketones 3+. CTG shows late decelerations.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: IV 0.9% saline and insulin 0.1 U/kg/h, and stabilise her before any decision on delivery
questions.why: DKA occurs at lower glucose in pregnancy. The CTG usually recovers as she is corrected; treat the mother first (saline, insulin, potassium) and decide on delivery later.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old with gestational diabetes on metformin delivered a healthy baby yesterday.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan for her glucose?
options: Stop metformin; no further tests needed
Stop metformin; fasting glucose or OGTT at 6 weeks, then yearly
questions.why: Gestational diabetes resolves after birth, so stop all drugs, but about half develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years: test at 6 weeks and yearly for life.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks has blood pressure 150/100 mmHg on two readings 4 hours apart. Urine PCR is 45 mg/mmol. She has no symptoms; platelets, creatinine and ALT are normal.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: New hypertension after 20 weeks with PCR 30 or more is pre-eclampsia; blood pressure 150/100 mmHg is moderate, and there is no organ sign, so it is not severe.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old para 2 books at 10 weeks. Her blood pressure is 150/95 on two visits; urine protein is negative and she takes no drugs.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Hypertension before 20 weeks is chronic (pre-existing). Gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia start after 20 weeks.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old at 34 weeks, normotensive at booking, now has blood pressure 145/95 mmHg twice. Urine dipstick is negative and PCR 12 mg/mmol. Bloods are normal.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: New hypertension after 20 weeks with no significant proteinuria and no organ damage is gestational hypertension. About 1 in 4 progress to pre-eclampsia, so she needs follow-up.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old at 14 weeks has blood pressure 150/100 mmHg, urine protein 2+ and heavy vaginal spotting. The uterus is the size of 20 weeks and no fetal heart is heard on Doppler.
questions.q: What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.why: Pre-eclampsia features before 20 weeks with a large uterus and no fetal heart point to a molar pregnancy. Ordinary pre-eclampsia does not start before 20 weeks.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old at 33 weeks has blood pressure 145/95 mmHg and protein 1+. She complains of a severe frontal headache and flashing lights since morning. Reflexes are brisk with 3 beats of clonus.
questions.q: How is her condition best classified?
questions.why: Any one organ sign (here severe headache, visual flashes, clonus) makes pre-eclampsia severe whatever the blood pressure. It is not eclampsia until she has a convulsion.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 34 weeks has epigastric pain and vomiting. Blood pressure 145/95 mmHg, protein 2+. Platelets 70 × 10⁹/L, ALT 280 U/L, LDH 900 U/L, glucose 5.0 mmol/L; the film shows fragmented red cells.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Haemolysis, raised liver enzymes and platelets below 100 is HELLP, a severe form whatever the blood pressure. Normal glucose argues against acute fatty liver.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 35 weeks has blood pressure 168/112 mmHg, protein 3+ and headache. She is admitted to HDU and IV labetalol is started.
questions.q: Which regimen is most appropriate to prevent fits?
options: MgSO₄ 4 g IV over 5–15 min, then 1 g/h until 24 h after delivery
MgSO₄ 4 g IV, then 1 g/h for 6 hours
questions.why: Magnesium sulphate prevents and treats eclamptic fits: 4 g loading, then 1 g/h continued for 24 hours after delivery or the last fit. Diazepam is used only if magnesium is not available.

questions.stem: A woman on magnesium sulphate 1 g/h for severe pre-eclampsia for 10 hours now has absent knee jerks. RR is 16/min, oxygen saturation 97% and urine output 35 mL/h.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop the infusion and check the magnesium level
questions.why: Loss of the knee jerk is the first sign of toxicity: stop and check the level. Calcium gluconate is for respiratory depression (RR below 12), which she does not have.

questions.stem: A woman on magnesium sulphate for eclampsia becomes drowsy. Knee jerks are absent and RR is 8/min. Urine output has been 15 mL/h for 3 hours.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment, besides stopping the infusion?
options: 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV slowly, with oxygen
questions.why: Respiratory depression is the second stage of magnesium toxicity, made worse by oliguria (kidneys clear it); the antidote is calcium gluconate. Naloxone reverses opioids, not magnesium.

questions.stem: A primigravida at 37 weeks had an eclamptic convulsion and was loaded with magnesium sulphate 4 g IV. She is on 1 g/h. Two hours later she fits again. Blood pressure 155/100 mmHg.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next drug?
questions.why: A fit on magnesium is treated with an extra 2 g IV. If she still fits, phenytoin, then general anaesthesia.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 33 weeks has blood pressure 170/115 mmHg with a headache. Magnesium sulphate has been started and 500 mL of saline given.
questions.q: Which drug is most appropriate to lower the blood pressure now?
questions.why: Severe blood pressure (160/110 or more) is lowered now with IV hydralazine (or IV labetalol), repeated every 15 min. Methyldopa and twice-daily nifedipine are too slow; ACE inhibitors and diuretics are never used.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old with asthma on inhalers is 30 weeks pregnant. She has pre-eclampsia with blood pressure 155/105 mmHg and no severe features.
questions.q: Which oral drug is most appropriate?
questions.why: Labetalol is first line but blocks β receptors, so it is avoided in asthma; nifedipine is the next line. ACE inhibitors and diuretics are never used in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old with chronic hypertension controlled on enalapril finds she is 8 weeks pregnant. Blood pressure is 135/85.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate change?
questions.why: ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic and are stopped as soon as pregnancy is known; labetalol is first line. Stopping all drugs would let her blood pressure rise.

questions.stem: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia at 32 weeks in HDU had 2 L of saline over 3 hours. She becomes breathless with basal crackles and oxygen saturation 88%. Blood pressure 160/105 mmHg.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Leaky capillaries in pre-eclampsia flood the lungs when drips are run freely; fluids are kept to 80 mL/h. Magnesium toxicity causes slow breathing, not crackles.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with severe pre-eclampsia at 32 weeks is stable on labetalol and magnesium sulphate. Ultrasound: estimated fetal weight below the 5th centile, umbilical artery Doppler shows reversed end-diastolic flow.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Steroids and delivery, usually by caesarean
questions.why: Reversed EDF means the placenta is failing; give steroids (below 34 weeks), keep magnesium sulphate and deliver, usually by caesarean as the fetus will not tolerate labour.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old primigravida with a BMI of 32 books at 11 weeks. Blood pressure 120/75 mmHg; she has no other medical history.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice to lower her risk of pre-eclampsia?
options: Aspirin 75 mg at night from 12 to 36 weeks
questions.why: First pregnancy, age 40 or more and BMI above 30 are moderate risk factors; two or more mean aspirin 75 mg from 12 to 36 weeks. Starting late reduces the benefit.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old primigravida from Gezira at 28 weeks has no fever. Hb is 8.5 g/dL, ferritin 60 µg/L, and the fundal height is 4 cm small for dates. She did not receive IPTp and has no bed net.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause of her anaemia and small fetus?
questions.why: A primigravida in an endemic area with anaemia, a normal ferritin and a small baby, without fever, fits silent placental malaria. Iron deficiency would lower the ferritin.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old at 8 weeks has fever and rigors. RDT is positive for P. Falciparum. She is alert, eating and has no vomiting; Hb 11 g/dL, RBG normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Artemether-lumefantrine 4 tablets twice daily for 3 days
questions.why: Uncomplicated malaria in any trimester, including the first, is treated with AL 20/120 (Sudan protocol 2023). DHA-piperaquine is second line in the 2nd and third trimesters; quinine is for when no ACT is available.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 30 weeks has fever for 3 days and is now confused. The thin film shows 7% parasitised red cells. Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, RBG 90 mg/dL.
questions.q: What is the drug of choice?
options: IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then daily
questions.why: Impaired consciousness and parasitaemia above 5% mean severe malaria; IV artesunate is first line in any trimester. IV quinine is used only if artesunate is not available.

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks on IV quinine for severe malaria becomes restless, sweaty and confused 6 hours into treatment. Her pulse is 112/min and blood pressure 115/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which test should be done first?
questions.why: Quinine releases insulin and the parasites consume glucose, so hypoglycaemia is common in pregnancy; check RBG first. It can mimic worsening cerebral malaria.

questions.stem: A woman at 34 weeks with severe malaria has RBG 32 mg/dL. IV artesunate is running.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV, then a 10% dextrose drip
questions.why: Hypoglycaemia (below 40 mg/dL) is treated with 50% dextrose IV followed by 10% dextrose, checking RBG every 1–2 hours. Artesunate is continued.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old at 34 weeks has a generalised convulsion. Temperature 39.5 °C, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, urine protein negative, RBG 95 mg/dL. The blood film shows ring forms.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Fit, fever and parasites with normal blood pressure and no protein is cerebral malaria until proven otherwise. Eclampsia needs hypertension and proteinuria.

questions.stem: A primigravida at 34 weeks is brought in after a convulsion. Temperature 39 °C, blood pressure 160/110 mmHg, urine protein 2+, RDT positive. You cannot tell which disease caused the convulsion.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: When eclampsia and cerebral malaria cannot be separated, treat both: magnesium sulphate for the fits and IV artesunate for the malaria.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 24 weeks has had fever and rigors for 2 days. The RDT is negative, but she lives in a high-transmission area and malaria is still strongly suspected.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: A negative test with strong suspicion is repeated (thick film to find parasites, thin film for species and %). One negative RDT does not exclude malaria.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old primigravida in a high-transmission area attends ANC at 18 weeks after feeling fetal movements. She is HIV negative and well.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate malaria prevention?
options: SP 3 tablets observed now, a second dose at least 4 weeks later, and a treated bed net
questions.why: IPTp with SP (3 tablets of 500/25 mg, observed) is given after quickening, with a second dose at least 4 weeks later, plus a treated net. SP is not given in the first trimester, and primaquine is avoided.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old at 20 weeks is due her first dose of SP for malaria prevention. Hb is 10.6 g/dL. She has no other risk factors.
questions.q: Which daily dose of folic acid should she take?
questions.why: High-dose folic acid (5 mg) blocks the action of SP, so women on IPTp take 0.4 mg.

questions.stem: A woman at 30 weeks with severe malaria on IV artesunate has blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, cold peripheries and a weak pulse. Hb 9 g/dL, no bleeding.
questions.q: What should be added to fluid resuscitation?
questions.why: Shock in severe malaria (algid malaria) is often gram-negative sepsis; take cultures and give a 3rd-generation cephalosporin. Her Hb does not need transfusion.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old at 22 weeks is on day 3 of artemether-lumefantrine for uncomplicated malaria. She has taken every dose with milk, but she has fever again.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the blood film; if parasites persist, switch drugs
Stop treatment: fever on day 3 is expected
questions.why: Fever again on day 3 needs a repeat film; persisting parasites mean treatment failure and a change of drug. Repeating the same course does not treat failure.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 30 weeks has mild breathlessness and ankle swelling. Pulse 92/min regular, a soft 2/6 ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a third heart sound. Lungs clear, JVP normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure: these findings are normal in pregnancy
questions.why: A soft ejection systolic flow murmur, a third sound and mild breathlessness are normal in pregnancy. Diastolic murmurs, orthopnoea or crackles need investigation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old at 28 weeks had rheumatic fever as a child. She is breathless on mild effort. There is a loud first heart sound and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex.
questions.q: Which investigation is most useful?
questions.why: Echo is the key test: it gives the valve area, ejection fraction and pulmonary pressure. ECG shows rhythm only.

questions.stem: A woman with rheumatic mitral valve disease at 20 weeks is comfortable at rest and doing housework. She gets breathless only when climbing two flights of stairs.
questions.q: Which NYHA class is she?
questions.why: Symptoms on moderate effort (stairs) are class II. Class III is symptoms on mild effort, class IV at rest.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old with an unrepaired VSD is 8 weeks pregnant. She is cyanosed, oxygen saturation 84% at rest, with clubbing and a loud P2.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Explain the high risk of death and offer termination
questions.why: Cyanosis with a loud P2 in a known VSD is Eisenmenger syndrome; maternal death is 40–60%, so pregnancy is contraindicated and termination offered.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with mitral stenosis, NYHA II, is seen at 24 weeks. Hb is 8.2 g/dL, MCV 66 fL. Pulse is 96/min, chest clear.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Anaemia adds load on a diseased heart; remove extra loads (anaemia, infection, hypertension) first. Valvotomy is for severe symptomatic MS.

questions.stem: A woman with mitral stenosis at 30 weeks becomes breathless. Pulse is irregularly irregular at 130/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, lungs clear. ECG shows atrial fibrillation.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Rate control with a beta-blocker or digoxin, plus LMWH
questions.why: AF in MS needs rate control (slower rate = longer filling) and anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin, as the stroke risk is high. Rate control alone ignores clot risk.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve on warfarin finds she is 6 weeks pregnant.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate change?
options: Switch to twice-daily weight-adjusted LMWH until 12 weeks
questions.why: Warfarin causes embryopathy at 6–12 weeks, so low-molecular-weight heparin twice daily by weight is used then; anticoagulation must never stop because valve thrombosis causes death.

questions.stem: A woman with moderate mitral stenosis, NYHA II, is in spontaneous labour at 39 weeks at 4 cm. She is in severe pain with a pulse of 118/min.
questions.q: What is the best analgesia?
questions.why: Early epidural removes pain and the rise in heart rate, which shortens filling time in MS. Low-molecular-weight heparin, if given, is stopped 24 hours before.

questions.stem: A woman with mitral stenosis, NYHA III, reaches full dilatation. After 20 minutes of pushing the head is at +2, direct occipito-anterior, and she is tired and breathless.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Assisted delivery with forceps or ventouse
questions.why: Long pushing strains the heart, so the second stage is shortened with forceps or ventouse. Caesarean is for obstetric reasons only.

questions.stem: A woman with rheumatic heart disease has just delivered the baby. The midwife prepares the drug for the third stage.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate uterotonic?
questions.why: Oxytocin given slowly is safe; ergometrine clamps the veins and causes acute pulmonary oedema, and a rapid oxytocin bolus drops the blood pressure. Carboprost causes bronchospasm and pulmonary hypertension.

questions.stem: A woman with mitral stenosis is 2 hours after delivery. She becomes breathless and coughs pink foamy sputum. Oxygen saturation 88%, crackles at both bases, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Sit up, oxygen, stop IV fluids, furosemide 40 mg IV
Lay flat and give a fluid bolus
questions.why: Autotransfusion after birth gives the highest load on the heart, causing pulmonary oedema; sit her up, give oxygen, stop fluids and give furosemide.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old para 5 is 2 months after a twin delivery. She has had increasing breathlessness and orthopnoea for 3 weeks. She had no heart disease before. Echo: dilated left ventricle, EF 30%, normal valves.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Heart failure from 32 weeks to 6 months after birth with EF below 45% and no other cause is peripartum cardiomyopathy; multiparity and twins are risk factors. Valves are normal, so it is not MS.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with epilepsy has been fit-free for 3 years on sodium valproate. She wants to become pregnant.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Continue valproate and take folic acid 0.4 mg
Switch to a safer drug under the neurologist before conceiving, and start folic acid 5 mg
Stop valproate now and try to conceive
Conceive now and switch drug at 12 weeks
Add carbamazepine to lower the valproate dose
questions.why: Valproate carries about 10% anomaly risk (NTD, heart, cleft, low IQ), so it is changed before conception, never stopped suddenly. Folic acid 5 mg starts 3 months before conception.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old on carbamazepine for epilepsy, fit-free for 4 years, has a positive pregnancy test at 7 weeks.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate step?
options: Continue carbamazepine and start folic acid 5 mg
questions.why: Never stop anti-epileptic drugs suddenly: status epilepticus is more dangerous than the drug. Organogenesis is already under way; continue and give 5 mg folic acid.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old on lamotrigine, fit-free before pregnancy, has two convulsions at 30 weeks. She takes every dose. Blood pressure 115/70 mmHg, urine protein negative.
questions.q: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Lamotrigine levels have fallen from faster clearance
questions.why: Bigger blood volume and faster clearance lower drug levels in pregnancy, lamotrigine most of all; the dose is raised. Normal blood pressure and no protein argue against eclampsia.

questions.stem: A newborn has a cleft lip, small hypoplastic nails and short distal phalanges. The mother takes a single drug for epilepsy.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.why: Cleft, nail and finger hypoplasia with heart defects is fetal hydantoin syndrome from phenytoin. Valproate typically gives neural tube defects.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old on carbamazepine is 12 weeks pregnant and fit-free. Dating scan is normal.
questions.q: Which fetal check is added to her routine care?
options: MRI of the fetal brain at 20 weeks
questions.why: Anti-epileptic drugs raise the risk of heart defects, so fetal echo at 22–24 weeks is added to the anomaly scan (18–20+6 weeks) and growth scans. Karyotype is not affected by the drug.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old known epileptic at 28 weeks has been convulsing for 7 minutes. Blood pressure 115/70 mmHg, urine protein negative, capillary glucose 5.2 mmol/L. Airway is secured and oxygen given.
questions.q: What is the first drug to give?
questions.why: A fit over 5 minutes is status epilepticus; the first-line drug is lorazepam 4 mg IV (or diazepam). Magnesium sulphate is for eclampsia, which normal blood pressure and no protein make unlikely.

questions.stem: A woman with known epilepsy at 36 weeks has a convulsion. Blood pressure is 160/110 and urine protein 2+.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate drug?
questions.why: Hypertension with proteinuria after 20 weeks means eclampsia cannot be excluded, even in a known epileptic; treat with magnesium sulphate.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old with epilepsy is in labour at 39 weeks and asks for pain relief.
questions.q: Which analgesic should be avoided?
questions.why: Norpethidine, the metabolite of pethidine, lowers the convulsion threshold. Early epidural is encouraged because pain, exhaustion and hyperventilation trigger fits.

questions.stem: A woman on carbamazepine throughout pregnancy delivers a healthy baby at 39 weeks.
questions.q: What should the baby receive at birth?
questions.why: Enzyme inducers can cause vitamin K deficiency in the baby, so 1 mg IM is given at birth. Maternal vitamin K from 36 weeks is no longer advised.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old on carbamazepine is 6 weeks postpartum and wants reliable contraception. She does not want more children for 3 years.
questions.q: Which method is most appropriate?
options: Combined pill with a double dose
questions.why: Carbamazepine induces liver enzymes and makes the pill, POP and implant fail; the copper IUD, LNG-IUS or DMPA are reliable.

questions.stem: A woman's lamotrigine dose was doubled at 28 weeks because of convulsions. She is now 6 days after birth and complains of dizziness, double vision and unsteadiness.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate step?
options: Reduce lamotrigine back to her pre-pregnancy dose
CT brain and continue the same dose
questions.why: Clearance falls back after birth, so a dose raised in pregnancy is returned to the old dose within about 10 days to avoid toxicity. Stopping it risks fits.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old on phenobarbitone for epilepsy has just delivered and asks whether she can breastfeed.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Breastfeed only if the drug is stopped
Breastfeed, and watch the baby for drowsiness and poor feeding
Express and discard milk for 2 weeks
questions.why: Breastfeeding is encouraged on anti-epileptic drugs; phenobarbitone can make the baby drowsy, so watch feeding. She should also feed and change diapers on the floor for safety.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old at 33 weeks has itching of the palms and soles, worse at night, for 2 weeks. There is no rash, only scratch marks. Bile acids 28 µmol/L, ALT twice normal, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Itch without a rash, starting on the palms and soles, with raised bile acids is obstetric cholestasis. Polymorphic eruption and pemphigoid both have a rash.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 32 weeks has itchy palms and soles at night with no rash. LFTs and fasting bile acids are normal. Hepatitis serology is negative.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat LFT and bile acids in 1–2 weeks
questions.why: The itch may come weeks before the tests turn abnormal, so repeat them every 1–2 weeks. Do not treat or deliver on itch alone.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old had obstetric cholestasis in her last pregnancy. She asks about the chance of it coming back next time.
questions.q: What is the best estimate of recurrence?
questions.why: Obstetric cholestasis recurs in 45–70% of later pregnancies, so LFTs are checked early next time.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old at 34 weeks has confirmed obstetric cholestasis. She cannot sleep because of the itching.
questions.q: Which drug is most appropriate for the itch?
questions.why: UDCA eases the itch within 1–7 days and improves LFTs. Chlorphenamine only sedates; it helps sleep, not itch.

questions.stem: A woman at 34 weeks with obstetric cholestasis has steatorrhoea and a prolonged PT. She has started UDCA.
questions.q: Which additional drug lowers her main maternal risk?
options: Water-soluble vitamin K 10 mg orally daily
questions.why: Fat malabsorption causes vitamin K deficiency and PPH; water-soluble vitamin K (menadiol) 10 mg daily protects against it.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 34 weeks has obstetric cholestasis. Her highest fasting bile acid level has been 25 µmol/L. She is on UDCA and the fetus is well grown.
questions.q: When should delivery be planned?
questions.why: Mild disease (peak bile acids 10–39 µmol/L) is delivered at 39 weeks; 40–99 at 38 weeks; 100 or more at 35–36 weeks.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old at 33 weeks with obstetric cholestasis has a peak bile acid level of 60 µmol/L. CTG and growth scan are normal.
questions.q: When should delivery be planned?
questions.why: Peak bile acids of 40–99 µmol/L mean moderate disease, delivered at 38 weeks by induction. A normal CTG does not change the plan.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 35 weeks with obstetric cholestasis asks why she cannot simply wait for labour, since her CTGs have all been normal.
questions.q: Which complication is the main reason to plan early delivery?
questions.why: Stillbirth in cholestasis is sudden (bile acids act on the fetal heart) and is not predicted by CTG, so timing is set by the bile acid level. It is not a slow placental failure.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old was treated for obstetric cholestasis and delivered 3 months ago. Her itch went within days, but ALT is still 3 times normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure: this is normal after cholestasis
questions.why: Obstetric cholestasis resolves after delivery; LFTs still abnormal later point to another liver disease (PBC, autoimmune hepatitis, viral).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with obstetric cholestasis in this pregnancy is seen at her postnatal visit and asks for the combined pill.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: The combined pill is the best choice
Use the combined pill after 6 months
Avoid all hormonal methods including the IUCD
Avoid oestrogen; use a progestogen-only method or IUCD
questions.why: Oestrogen pills can bring the itch back in women with past cholestasis, so progestogen-only methods or an IUCD are used.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida at 30 weeks has intense itching that began around the umbilicus and is now spreading to the limbs, with tense blisters on a red base.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Blisters starting around the umbilicus are pemphigoid gestationis. Obstetric cholestasis has no rash at all, only scratch marks.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old at 31 weeks has itching and ALT 3 times normal. Ultrasound of the liver and biliary tree and viral serology are normal.
questions.q: Which test helps exclude primary biliary cholangitis?
questions.why: Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are positive in PBC; anti-smooth muscle antibodies point to autoimmune hepatitis. ALP is made by the placenta and does not help.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida with twins at 35 weeks has vomited for 5 days and is now jaundiced. RBG 40 mg/dL, INR 2.1, ALT 380 U/L, platelets 120 × 10⁹/L, blood pressure 145/90 mmHg, urate high.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Third-trimester vomiting with jaundice, low glucose and high INR is acute fatty liver; twins and first pregnancy are risk factors. HELLP does not cause hypoglycaemia or early high INR.

questions.stem: A woman at 34 weeks has vomiting and RUQ pain. Blood pressure 150/95 mmHg, protein 1+, platelets 90 × 10⁹/L and ALT 300 U/L.
questions.q: Which additional finding would most favour acute fatty liver over HELLP?
questions.why: A failing liver cannot make glucose, so hypoglycaemia is typical of fatty liver, not HELLP. Raised LDH and schistocytes point to haemolysis in HELLP.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 36 weeks admitted with vomiting and jaundice becomes drowsy and sweaty on the ward. Blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, pulse 110/min.
questions.q: Which bedside test is most urgent?
questions.why: Hypoglycaemia in liver failure can kill quietly and causes drowsiness and sweating; check glucose first and every 1–2 hours.

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks with acute fatty liver has had her glucose, clotting and blood pressure corrected in ICU. She is now stable.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Delivery is the definitive treatment and is done once she is stable, whatever the gestation. Waiting lets the liver failure progress.

questions.stem: A woman with acute fatty liver is booked for caesarean. INR is 2.5 and platelets 60 × 10⁹/L despite correction.
questions.q: Which anaesthesia is most appropriate?
questions.why: No spinal or epidural is given if platelets are below 80 or clotting is deranged (risk of spinal haematoma), so general anaesthesia is used.

questions.stem: A woman with acute fatty liver at 34 weeks is going for caesarean. INR is 2.4, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L, platelets 95 × 10⁹/L, and she is bleeding from the cannula sites.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate preparation?
options: IV vitamin K 10 mg, FFP and cryoprecipitate
questions.why: The liver cannot make clotting factors; give IV vitamin K, FFP and cryoprecipitate (plus platelets if needed) before delivery.

questions.stem: A primigravida at 36 weeks with jaundice, vomiting and low glucose also complains of passing large amounts of urine and constant thirst. Glucose is 3.0 mmol/L.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the polyuria?
questions.why: Transient diabetes insipidus is a known feature of acute fatty liver; her glucose is low, so it is not diabetes mellitus.

questions.stem: A woman had acute fatty liver at 35 weeks. Her baby develops hypoglycaemia and later a dilated cardiomyopathy.
questions.q: Which test should the baby have?
questions.why: A fetal LCHAD deficiency is linked to maternal fatty liver; affected babies get hypoglycaemia and cardiomyopathy. The parents should be tested too.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 30 weeks from a village with many recent cases of jaundice after floods has vomiting and deep jaundice. ALT is 2500 U/L, glucose normal, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: ALT above 1000 points to viral hepatitis, and outbreaks from unsafe water are hepatitis E, which can be fulminant in the third trimester.

questions.stem: A primigravida at 35 weeks is ill with vomiting, abdominal pain and jaundice. She is mildly hypertensive.
questions.q: Which set of results fits acute fatty liver of pregnancy best?
options: Bile acids 60, ALT twice normal, all else normal
Glucose normal, INR normal, LDH high, platelets 40
Glucose low, INR high, urate high, ammonia high
questions.why: Fatty liver is liver failure: low glucose, high INR, marked hyperuricaemia, raised ammonia. A normal INR with haemolysis and very low platelets is HELLP.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 9 weeks has vomited all day for a week. She is mildly yellow; ALT is 90 U/L, bilirubin slightly raised, ketones 3+ and Na⁺ 130 mmol/L.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the jaundice?
questions.why: Timing is the first clue: vomiting with ketones and a mildly raised ALT at 9 weeks is hyperemesis. Fatty liver, cholestasis and HELLP occur late in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A woman recovering on day 3 after caesarean for acute fatty liver asks whether her liver will be damaged for life.
questions.q: What is the most accurate advice?
options: Liver failure usually persists for a year
Most women recover within days with no lasting liver damage
She will need lifelong liver tests every 3 months
questions.why: With delivery and supportive care, most women recover fully within days; transplant is rarely needed. It may recur in a later pregnancy, mainly with an LCHAD gene.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 10 weeks has palpitations and weight loss despite good appetite. She has a smooth goitre and exophthalmos. TSH < 0.01 mU/L, free T4 high.
questions.q: Which test best confirms the cause?
questions.why: Goitre and eye signs point to Graves' disease; TRAb confirms it. A radioiodine scan is contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with Graves' disease on carbimazole 20 mg daily has a positive pregnancy test at 6 weeks. She is euthyroid.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate step?
questions.why: In the first trimester carbimazole can cause aplasia cutis and choanal or oesophageal atresia, so PTU is used until about 13 weeks.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old with Graves' disease is 24 weeks pregnant and euthyroid on PTU 200 mg daily.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: After the first trimester carbimazole is preferred to avoid PTU liver failure. Antithyroid drugs are not stopped while disease is active.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old had a thyroidectomy for Graves' disease 3 years ago and takes levothyroxine; she is euthyroid. At 30 weeks the fetal heart rate is 175/min and the scan shows a fetal goitre.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause?
options: Maternal TSH-receptor antibodies crossing the placenta
questions.why: TRAb persist after surgery or radioiodine, cross the placenta and stimulate the fetal thyroid from 12 weeks; that is why TRAb is checked even when the mother is euthyroid.

questions.stem: A healthy 26-year-old at 20 weeks had thyroid tests sent by her GP. Total T4 is above the normal range; free T4 and TSH are normal. She has no symptoms.
questions.q: What is the best interpretation?
options: Normal: oestrogen has doubled thyroid-binding globulin
questions.why: Oestrogen doubles TBG, so total T4 rises in every pregnant woman; free T4 stays normal, which is why free T4 is measured.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 100 µg daily has a positive pregnancy test at 5 weeks. Her last TSH was 1.8 mU/L.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate step?
options: Keep the same dose and recheck at 20 weeks
Increase the dose by 25–30% now and check TSH
questions.why: Need rises early and the fetal brain depends on maternal T4 before 12 weeks; raise the dose by 25–30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed (e.g. 2 extra tablets a week), then check TSH.

questions.stem: A woman at 18 weeks on levothyroxine has a TSH that rose to 4.8 mU/L although her dose was raised correctly. She takes it every morning together with ferrous sulphate.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate step?
options: Take the iron at least 4 hours apart from the levothyroxine
questions.why: Iron binds levothyroxine in the gut and blocks its absorption; separating them by 4 hours fixes the problem without raising the dose.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with poorly controlled Graves' disease has an emergency caesarean. Six hours later: temperature 40 °C, pulse 150/min irregular, agitated and confused.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Propranolol, PTU, then iodine 1 hour after PTU, IV hydrocortisone and cooling
questions.why: Thyroid storm is treated in HDU with fluids, cooling, propranolol, PTU, iodine an hour after PTU, and hydrocortisone, plus treating the trigger. Iodine before PTU can make it worse.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old is 3 months after birth. She has palpitations, anxiety and a small painless goitre. TSH low, free T4 high, TRAb negative, no eye signs.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Painless thyrotoxicosis 1–4 months after birth with negative TRAb is the hyper phase of postpartum thyroiditis (preformed T4 leaking); treat symptoms with a β-blocker, not antithyroid drugs.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old is 6 months after delivery. She is tired, cold and gaining weight. TSH 12 mU/L, free T4 low. Three months ago she had a short spell of palpitations that settled without treatment.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Levothyroxine, then a trial off after about 6 months, and yearly TFTs
questions.why: This is the hypo phase of postpartum thyroiditis; give thyroxine for symptoms, stop at about 6 months to test recovery, and check TFTs yearly (recurrence 70%).

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with Graves' disease takes carbimazole 30 mg daily after delivery and wants to breastfeed.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Breastfeed and check the baby's thyroid function
Breastfeed only if the dose is doubled
questions.why: Breastfeeding is safe; above 15 mg/day of carbimazole (or 150 mg/day of PTU) the baby's TFTs are checked.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old at 18 weeks with Graves' disease has a large goitre and now has stridor and difficulty swallowing. She is on PTU.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Stridor, dysphagia, suspected cancer or allergy to both drugs are indications for surgery, safest in the second trimester. Radioiodine is never used in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old booking at 12 weeks has a positive rapid HIV test on routine opt-out screening. She is well.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start ART only if CD4 is below 350
Confirm with a second, different test
Repeat the same rapid test in 3 months
questions.why: A positive rapid test is confirmed with a second, different test (ELISA with or without Western blot) before the diagnosis is given; then ART starts at once.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old at 16 weeks is newly diagnosed with HIV. CD4 count is 650 cells/mm³ and she is clinically well.
questions.q: When should antiretroviral therapy start, and for how long?
questions.why: ART is started as soon as HIV is diagnosed, at any CD4 and any gestation, and continued for life. Starting late leaves the viral load high at delivery.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 20 weeks with confirmed HIV, normal creatinine, is ready to start treatment.
questions.q: Which regimen is most appropriate?
options: Tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir once daily, for life
questions.why: TLD (300/300/50 mg), one tablet daily and lifelong, is first line. Zidovudine alone cuts transmission only to about 8%.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 18 weeks with HIV has a CD4 count of 280 cells/mm³. She has started TLD.
questions.q: Which additional drug is most appropriate?
questions.why: CD4 of 350 or less (or WHO stage 3–4) needs cotrimoxazole, which protects against PCP, toxoplasma and malaria.

questions.stem: A woman with HIV at 22 weeks takes TLD and cotrimoxazole daily. She lives in a high-malaria area and the clinic nurse says her IPTp dose is due.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Do not give SP; cotrimoxazole already protects against malaria
Give SP and stop cotrimoxazole for a week
questions.why: Two sulfa drugs together cause severe skin reactions, and cotrimoxazole already prevents malaria, so SP is not given. A treated bed net is still used.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with HIV on ART since booking has a viral load below 50 copies/mL at 36 weeks. The fetus is cephalic and she wants a normal birth.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Vaginal birth with oral ART continued; no IV zidovudine
questions.why: With VL below 50 copies/mL, vaginal birth is advised with oral ART continued; IV zidovudine is only for VL of 1000 or more or unknown.

questions.stem: A woman with HIV started ART at 30 weeks. At 36 weeks her viral load is 3500 copies/mL. She is not in labour; membranes intact.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Await labour and give single-dose nevirapine
Vaginal birth with oral ART only
Elective caesarean at 38 weeks with IV zidovudine
questions.why: A VL of 1000 or more at 36 weeks means elective caesarean at 38 weeks, before labour and rupture of membranes, with IV zidovudine and continued oral ART.

questions.stem: An unbooked 22-year-old arrives in active labour at 5 cm. Her HIV status is unknown.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate step?
options: Offer a rapid HIV test now
No test unless she has symptoms
Send ELISA and wait for the result
Test her at the postnatal visit
questions.why: Status unknown in labour: test now with a rapid test so ART, IV zidovudine and infant prophylaxis can start in time.

questions.stem: A woman with HIV (viral load below 50) is in labour at 7 cm with intact membranes. The CTG shows an unclear baseline because the abdominal transducer keeps slipping.
questions.q: Which intervention should be avoided?
options: Active management of the third stage
questions.why: Scalp electrodes, fetal blood sampling and early artificial rupture of membranes expose the fetus to maternal blood and raise transmission. External monitoring is fine.

questions.stem: A woman with HIV on ART for 7 months, viral load below 50 at 36 weeks, delivers a 3.1 kg baby vaginally.
questions.q: Which prophylaxis should the baby receive?
questions.why: A low-risk baby (mother on ART with suppressed VL) gets nevirapine 15 mg daily for 6 weeks. The 12-week dual regimen is for high-risk babies.

questions.stem: An unbooked woman is diagnosed with HIV by a rapid test during labour and delivers 2 hours later. The baby weighs 2.9 kg.
questions.q: Which prophylaxis should the baby receive?
options: Zidovudine + nevirapine for 6 weeks, then nevirapine for 6 more weeks
questions.why: Mother found in labour (or VL of 1000 or more, or ART less than 4 weeks) means a high-risk baby: AZT + NVP for 6 weeks, then NVP for 6 weeks.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old breastfed baby of a mother with HIV has a positive HIV antibody test. The baby is thriving. DNA PCR at 6 weeks was negative.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Maternal antibodies remain in the baby up to 18 months, so an antibody test is not reliable now; DNA PCR is used (and again after weaning).

questions.stem: A woman with HIV on ART in a rural area of Sudan asks how to feed her newborn. Clean water is not reliable and formula is expensive.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Breastfeed, with water and herbs from 1 month
Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months while she takes ART
questions.why: Exclusive breastfeeding on maternal ART is safest where diarrhoea and malnutrition kill more babies than HIV; mixed feeding damages the gut and raises transmission.

questions.theme: Vomiting in early pregnancy (hyperemesis and thyroid)
options: Admit; IV 0.9% saline with KCl, thiamine and antiemetics
