No antithyroid drug; treat the vomiting
questions.lead: For each woman choose the most appropriate next step.

items.stem: A 25-year-old at 7 weeks feels sick each morning and vomits once or twice a day. PUQE score 5, urine ketones negative, weight steady.
items.why: PUQE of 6 or less is mild disease, managed at home with diet advice and reassurance.

items.stem: A 28-year-old at 12 weeks has had cyclizine, metoclopramide and ondansetron with fluids and thiamine for 10 days, and is still losing weight.
items.why: After three drug lines fail, steroids come next; TPN and termination are only for when steroids fail.

items.stem: A 30-year-old at 10 weeks has tremor, weight loss, a goitre and lid retraction with proptosis. TSH < 0.01 mU/L, free T4 high, mild nausea only.
items.why: Goitre and eye signs mean Graves' disease; PTU is the drug in the first trimester (carbimazole is teratogenic now).

items.stem: A 24-year-old admitted at 9 weeks with severe vomiting has a painful swollen left calf, 3 cm wider than the right, on day 4.
items.why: Dehydration and immobility make DVT likely; start treatment-dose low-molecular-weight heparin and then scan.

questions.theme: Anaemia and malaria in pregnancy
questions.lead: For each woman choose the most appropriate treatment or next step.

items.stem: A 23-year-old at 16 weeks has fever and rigors. RDT positive for P. Falciparum. She is alert, eating, Hb 9.6 g/dL, RBG normal.
items.why: Uncomplicated falciparum malaria in any trimester is treated with AL; quinine is used only if no ACT is available.

items.stem: A 26-year-old at 32 weeks has Hb 9.0 g/dL, MCV 68 fL and ferritin 5 µg/L. She tolerates tablets well and has no other illness.
items.why: Iron deficiency in a woman who tolerates tablets, before 34 weeks and with Hb above 9, is treated with oral iron.

items.stem: A para 6 at 38 weeks has Hb 6.4 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, and is short of breath on walking.
items.why: Hb below 7 after 36 weeks needs transfusion, slowly, as there is no time for iron to work.

items.stem: A 27-year-old strict vegan at 26 weeks has Hb 8.8 g/dL, MCV 112 fL, low serum B12 and normal folate.
items.why: Low B12 is replaced with hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM first; folate alone could worsen the nerve damage.

questions.theme: Anticoagulation and thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy
options: Prophylactic LMWH for 10 days after birth
Prophylactic LMWH from 28 weeks to 6 weeks after birth
Prophylactic LMWH for the whole pregnancy and 6 weeks after
questions.lead: For each woman choose the most appropriate plan.

items.stem: A 30-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve has taken warfarin with a good INR from 12 weeks. She is now 36 weeks and well.
items.why: From 36 weeks to birth warfarin is replaced by twice-daily low-molecular-weight heparin, so it can be stopped 24 hours before birth or epidural; warfarin restarts from day 5 after birth.

items.stem: A 37-year-old para 3 with BMI 32 books at 11 weeks with a twin pregnancy. She has no past VTE.
items.why: Age over 35, BMI over 30, parity 3 or more and twins are four risk factors: low-molecular-weight heparin for the whole pregnancy and 6 weeks after.

items.stem: A 29-year-old with BMI 33 has an emergency caesarean in labour. She has no other risk factors.
items.why: Caesarean in labour plus BMI above 30 are two risk factors, so low-molecular-weight heparin for 10 days after birth.

items.stem: A 31-year-old at 32 weeks suddenly becomes breathless and collapses. Blood pressure 70/40 mmHg, oxygen saturation 80%, JVP raised.
items.why: Hypotension with respiratory distress is massive PE: IV UFH and thrombolysis or embolectomy.

questions.theme: Liver disease and itching in pregnancy
questions.lead: For each woman choose the most likely diagnosis.

items.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks has itchy red papules that started inside her abdominal striae, sparing the navel. LFTs and bile acids are normal.
items.why: An itchy rash starting in the striae and sparing the umbilicus is polymorphic eruption; cholestasis has no rash.

items.stem: A 31-year-old at 34 weeks has RUQ pain, blood pressure 160/105 mmHg and protein 2+. Platelets 60 × 10⁹/L, LDH 1100 U/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, INR normal.
items.why: Haemolysis, raised enzymes and low platelets with hypertension is HELLP; normal glucose and INR argue against fatty liver.

items.stem: A 29-year-old at 37 weeks has a routine LFT showing ALP 3 times the non-pregnant range. ALT, bilirubin and bile acids are normal and she has no itch.
items.why: The placenta makes ALP, so an isolated high ALP late in pregnancy is normal.

items.stem: A 33-year-old at 36 weeks has 4 days of vomiting, confusion and jaundice. Glucose 2.4 mmol/L, INR 2.3, urate high, blood pressure 140/90 mmHg.
items.why: Low glucose and high INR in the third trimester mean a failing liver: acute fatty liver.

questions.theme: Fits in pregnancy and the puerperium
questions.lead: For each woman choose the most appropriate immediate drug.

items.stem: A 23-year-old on day 2 after a normal birth has a generalised convulsion. Blood pressure 165/110 mmHg, urine protein 2+, temperature 37 °C.
items.why: Eclampsia can occur after birth; magnesium sulphate loading then maintenance.

items.stem: A 26-year-old with type 1 diabetes at 30 weeks became sweaty and confused, then had a convulsion. Blood pressure 120/75 mmHg, urine protein negative.
items.why: A fit on insulin with sweating is hypoglycaemia until proven otherwise; give dextrose IV.

items.stem: A known epileptic at 26 weeks is still convulsing after two doses of lorazepam 4 mg IV. Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, urine protein negative, glucose normal.
items.why: Status epilepticus not stopped by a benzodiazepine needs second-line IV phenytoin with ECG monitoring.

items.stem: A woman on magnesium sulphate 1 g/h after eclampsia is drowsy, has no knee jerks and respiratory rate 7/min.
items.why: Respiratory depression from magnesium toxicity: stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate.

questions.theme: Timing and mode of delivery in medical disorders
options: Await spontaneous labour, deliver by 40+6 weeks
Elective caesarean at 38 weeks with IV zidovudine
Vaginal birth with oral ART only
Deliver once stable, at any gestation
questions.lead: For each woman choose the most appropriate plan for delivery.

items.stem: A 29-year-old with type 1 diabetes, HbA1c 6.3%, is 37 weeks. Estimated fetal weight 3.8 kg, liquor normal, no other problems.
items.why: Pre-existing diabetes is delivered at 38–39+6 weeks, vaginally by induction, unless there is a complication.

items.stem: A 32-year-old with gestational diabetes controlled on diet alone is 38 weeks. Estimated fetal weight 3.4 kg.
items.why: Well-controlled gestational diabetes can wait for labour, with delivery by 40+6 weeks.

items.stem: A 25-year-old books at 36 weeks and is diagnosed with HIV. She started ART a week ago; the viral load result is not yet available. She is not in labour.
items.why: Viral load unknown (or 1000 or more) means elective caesarean at 38 weeks with IV zidovudine.

items.stem: A 30-year-old at 34 weeks with obstetric cholestasis has a peak bile acid level of 130 µmol/L despite UDCA.
items.why: Bile acids of 100 or more carry a high stillbirth risk; plan delivery at 35–36 weeks.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 at 9 weeks has had light vaginal bleeding since yesterday with mild lower abdominal ache. Her pulse is 82/min and blood pressure 115/70 mmHg. Speculum examination: small amount of blood, os closed. Transvaginal scan shows a live fetus, CRL matching dates.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Bleeding with a closed os and a live fetus is threatened miscarriage; most continue. Inevitable miscarriage needs an open os.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old G4P3 at 11 weeks is brought with heavy bleeding and colicky pain for 3 hours. Her pulse is 124/min and blood pressure 80/50 mmHg. Speculum examination: os open with tissue in the canal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Misoprostol 600 µg orally and review in 2 weeks
Transfuse and repeat the scan in 48 hours
Resuscitate, remove tissue from the os and do surgical evacuation (MVA)
Ergometrine IM and discharge if bleeding settles
questions.why: Heavy bleeding with shock needs resuscitation and surgical evacuation, which is definitive. Medical and expectant options are for stable women.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old G2P1 at 9 weeks by dates noticed her breast tenderness has gone and has brownish spotting. Vitals normal, os closed. Transvaginal ultrasound: CRL 12 mm, no fetal heart activity. She refuses any operation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Misoprostol 400 µg vaginally every 3 hours until passed
Repeat scan in 2 weeks before any treatment
Misoprostol 800 µg vaginally, repeated after 3 hours if needed
questions.why: CRL ≥ 7 mm with no heart confirms a missed miscarriage; the medical regimen under 13 weeks is 800 µg vaginally (or 600 µg sublingually), repeated after 3 hours. 600 µg oral once is the regimen for incomplete miscarriage.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old at 8 weeks by her last period has had one episode of spotting. She is stable. Transvaginal ultrasound: intrauterine gestational sac, mean sac diameter 18 mm, no yolk sac or embryo seen.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose missed miscarriage and offer misoprostol
Give methotrexate for a possible ectopic
questions.why: A missed miscarriage needs a mean sac ≥ 25 mm with no embryo (or CRL ≥ 7 mm with no heart); 18 mm is not diagnostic, so rescan before any intervention. Treating now risks ending a viable pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old presents 2 days after an evacuation at 12 weeks done by an unqualified person. Temperature 39.4 °C, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. Offensive brown discharge, tender uterus, os open.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Take cultures and start IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, then evacuate the uterus
Oral amoxicillin and review in 48 hours
Immediate evacuation before antibiotics are started
questions.why: In septic miscarriage, antibiotics (ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily + metronidazole 500 mg IV 8-hourly) start first, then gentle evacuation. Evacuating before antibiotics risks spreading sepsis and perforating the soft uterus.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old is admitted 3 days after an unsafe abortion with fever, rigors, yellow sclera and dark red urine. Blood pressure 85/50 mmHg. Hb 7 g/dL, creatinine rising.
questions.q: Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.why: Jaundice and haematuria (haemolysis) after septic abortion point to Clostridium. E. Coli is common in septic abortion but does not usually cause this haemolytic picture.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old has had 3 consecutive miscarriages at 8–10 weeks. Lupus anticoagulant was positive on two tests 12 weeks apart. Parental karyotypes and pelvic scan are normal. She is now 6 weeks pregnant.
questions.q: Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Aspirin 75 mg plus enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
questions.why: Antiphospholipid syndrome with recurrent miscarriage is treated with low-dose aspirin plus low-molecular-weight heparin. Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old G4P0 has lost three pregnancies at 21, 19 and 17 weeks. Each time the membranes ruptured and she delivered quickly with little pain. She is now 8 weeks pregnant with a live fetus.
questions.q: What is the best plan?
questions.why: Painless second-trimester losses, each earlier than the last, suggest cervical weakness; history-indicated cerclage is placed at 12–14 weeks. Before 12 weeks many pregnancies still miscarry from other causes.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old P2 has had no periods for 8 months. Since her last delivery she had two curettages for retained products, the second followed by fever. Pregnancy test negative; FSH, prolactin and TSH are normal; no withdrawal bleed after oestrogen–progestogen.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Amenorrhoea after repeated or infected curettage with normal hormones and no withdrawal bleed is Asherman syndrome. Pituitary necrosis (Sheehan) gives low hormones and failed lactation.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old RhD-negative woman at 11 weeks has an manual vacuum aspiration for incomplete miscarriage. Antibody screen is negative.
questions.q: What does she need?
options: Anti-D only if the partner is RhD-positive on testing
Anti-D 500 IU IM with a Kleihauer test
No anti-D: the loss is in the first trimester
questions.why: Before 20 weeks the dose is 250 IU within 72 hours, given for any miscarriage ≥ 10 weeks or after surgical evacuation. 500 IU with Kleihauer is the dose from 20 weeks.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old, 7 weeks since her last period, has left lower abdominal pain and dark spotting. Her pulse is 88/min and blood pressure 118/74 mmHg. Cervical excitation on the left. β-hCG 2600 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus, thin endometrium, small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Early intrauterine pregnancy too small to see
questions.why: With hCG above the discriminatory zone (2000 IU/L on transvaginal ultrasound) an intrauterine sac should be seen; an empty uterus means ectopic until proven otherwise. Complete miscarriage would not give cervical excitation and free fluid with this hCG.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 6 weeks has mild pelvic pain and spotting. She is stable. Transvaginal ultrasound shows neither an intrauterine nor an adnexal sac. β-hCG is 1200 IU/L, and 1250 IU/L after 48 hours.
questions.q: How should this hCG result be interpreted?
options: An abnormal pregnancy, most likely ectopic
questions.why: A viable intrauterine pregnancy raises hCG by at least 63% in 48 hours; a plateau suggests ectopic. A complete miscarriage would show a clear fall.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 7 weeks has mild right iliac fossa pain. Her pulse is 80/min and blood pressure 120/75 mmHg. Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus, 2.8 cm right adnexal mass, no fetal heart, minimal fluid. β-hCG 3200 IU/L. She lives near the hospital and agrees to follow-up.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: Stable, hCG < 5000 IU/L, mass < 3.5 cm, no heartbeat and reliable follow-up fit methotrexate. Expectant care needs hCG < 1000 and falling.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 8 weeks has right iliac fossa pain and is haemodynamically stable. Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus, 4 cm right adnexal mass with an embryo showing heart activity. β-hCG 8000 IU/L. At laparoscopy the left tube looks normal.
questions.q: Which procedure is most appropriate?
questions.why: A live tubal embryo, mass > 3.5 cm and hCG > 5000 need surgery; with a healthy other tube, salpingectomy is preferred. Salpingotomy is chosen when the other tube is damaged and needs hCG follow-up.

questions.stem: A woman treated with methotrexate for a tubal ectopic has β-hCG 4000 IU/L on day 4 and 3700 IU/L on day 7. She is stable with mild pain.
questions.q: How should this be interpreted?
options: Expected rise: repeat hCG in 1 week only
Successful treatment: hCG weekly until negative
Inadequate response: a further dose or surgery is needed
questions.why: Success needs an hCG fall of at least 15% from day 4 to day 7; here it fell only about 7.5%. She is stable, so immediate laparotomy is not indicated.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old collapses at home. She missed her period 7 weeks ago. Her pulse is 130/min and blood pressure 70/40 mmHg, cold and pale. Abdomen distended and tender; she complains of shoulder-tip pain. Urine pregnancy test positive.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Serum β-hCG and repeat in 48 hours
Diagnostic laparoscopy once she is stable
Resuscitate and take her for immediate laparotomy
questions.why: A positive test with shock and haemoperitoneum is a ruptured ectopic: resuscitate and operate now. Waiting for a formal scan or hCG delays surgery in a shocked woman.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old G1 at 14 weeks has vaginal bleeding and severe vomiting. Blood pressure 160/110 mmHg, urine protein 2+, pulse 108/min. Uterus is at 20 weeks size and soft; no fetal heart heard. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a snowstorm pattern with no fetus.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Antihypertensives and wait for spontaneous passage
Suction evacuation, with oxytocin only once emptying has started
questions.why: A complete mole is emptied by suction evacuation. Misoprostol is avoided because contractions push trophoblast into the veins (embolism, spread).

questions.stem: A 23-year-old had suction evacuation of a complete mole 8 weeks ago. Her β-hCG fell at first but has risen on three weekly samples. She now coughs up blood; chest X-ray shows several round shadows.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Rising hCG after a mole with lung metastases (haemoptysis) points to choriocarcinoma, a gestational trophoblastic neoplasia scored by FIGO for chemotherapy. Placental site tumour usually has low hCG.

questions.theme: Bleeding in early pregnancy
questions.lead: For each patient choose the most likely diagnosis. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: A 29-year-old at 10 weeks has heavy bleeding and colicky pain. Os is open; nothing has been passed. Scan shows a fetus with heart activity low in the cavity.
items.why: Heavy bleeding, pain and an open os with nothing passed is inevitable, even with a live fetus. Threatened miscarriage has a closed os.

items.stem: A 33-year-old at 12 weeks by dates says her nausea stopped two weeks ago. She has brown spotting. Uterus is 8 weeks size, os closed.
items.why: Fading symptoms, brown loss and a small uterus with a closed os mean a retained dead fetus.

items.stem: A 26-year-old at 16 weeks has bleeding. Uterus is 16 weeks size. Scan shows a fetus with abnormalities and a thick placenta with cystic spaces; karyotype is 69,XXY.
items.why: Triploidy with an abnormal fetus and cystic placenta is a partial mole; a complete mole has no fetus and is 46,XX.

items.stem: A 24-year-old at 9 weeks bled heavily yesterday and passed tissue. Pain has now settled, os is closed, transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with thin endometrium and hCG has halved in 48 hours.
items.why: Settled pain, closed os, empty uterus and falling hCG mean complete miscarriage; a pregnancy test should be negative at 2–3 weeks.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old G4P3 at 33 weeks has painless bright red vaginal bleeding, about 200 mL, after waking. Her pulse is 92/min and blood pressure 120/75 mmHg. Uterus soft and non-tender, breech presentation, fetal heart rate 140/min.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ultrasound to locate the placenta, avoiding digital vaginal examination
Digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix
questions.why: Painless bleeding, soft uterus and malpresentation suggest praevia: no digital examination until a scan excludes it. She is stable, so immediate caesarean is not needed.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old G3P2 at 31 weeks was admitted with a painless bleed. Scan shows the placenta covering the internal os. Bleeding has stopped, Hb 10.8 g/dL, fetal heart rate normal.
questions.q: What is the best management?
options: Discharge home with advice to return if she bleeds
Keep in hospital, give steroids, keep 6–8 units cross-matched, aim for delivery at 37 weeks
questions.why: When bleeding settles before term, praevia is managed expectantly in hospital with steroids < 34 weeks and blood ready, aiming for 37 weeks. Caesarean at any gestation is for heavy bleeding or instability.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 (previous vaginal birth) had a placenta covering the os at the 20-week scan and again at the 32-week rescan. She has never bled.
questions.q: When should she be delivered?
questions.why: Major praevia without bleeding is delivered by elective caesarean at 37–38 weeks. 36 weeks is the planned timing for placenta accreta spectrum.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida has her anomaly scan at 20 weeks. The placenta is posterior with its lower edge 1.5 cm from the internal os. She has had no bleeding.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: A low placenta at 20 weeks is rescanned at 32 weeks; about 90% move up as the lower segment forms. Planning a caesarean now is premature.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 is 37 weeks. The 32-week scan showed the placental edge 3 cm from the internal os. Head is engaging, she has not bled, CTG normal.
questions.q: What is the best plan for delivery?
options: Caesarean as soon as labour starts
Await labour and allow vaginal birth
Induction of labour now with prostaglandin
questions.why: An edge more than 2 cm from the os allows a trial of vaginal birth. Elective caesarean is not indicated.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old G4P3 with three previous caesarean sections has an anterior placenta covering the internal os at 28 weeks. She is asymptomatic.
questions.q: What is the best next investigation?
options: Colour Doppler ultrasound, with MRI if unclear
questions.why: Praevia over a caesarean scar carries a high risk of placenta accreta spectrum (about 60% with ≥ 3 caesarean section); colour Doppler is used first, then MRI if unclear or posterior. Cystoscopy is not the screening test.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old G5P4 with two previous caesarean sections is 30 weeks. Doppler shows an anterior praevia, lost clear zone, many lacunae and broken bladder line. She reports two episodes of blood in her urine.
questions.q: What is the best delivery plan?
options: Planned caesarean at 39 weeks with manual removal of the placenta
Planned caesarean at 36 weeks with manual removal of the placenta
Planned caesarean at 36 weeks in a specialist centre with consent for hysterectomy, leaving the placenta in place
questions.why: Suspected percreta is delivered at 36 weeks by a team, with 6–8 units ready, uterine incision away from the placenta and hysterectomy with the placenta left in place. Pulling the placenta causes very heavy bleeding.

questions.stem: At an elective caesarean for anterior praevia in a woman with two previous caesarean sections, the baby is delivered through a fundal incision. The placenta does not separate after oxytocin and there is no bleeding yet.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate action?
options: Remove it manually piece by piece
Leave the placenta and proceed to hysterectomy
Firm cord traction while massaging the uterus
Insert a B-Lynch suture and close
questions.why: A placenta that will not separate means accreta spectrum: do not pull it; hysterectomy with the placenta in place. Manual removal opens a bed with no cleavage plane and causes massive haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old RhD-negative G2P1 at 32 weeks had a 150 mL painless bleed that has stopped. Antibody screen is negative.
questions.q: What does she need regarding anti-D?
options: Anti-D 1500 IU IM with a Kleihauer test
Anti-D 500 IU IM within 72 hours plus a Kleihauer test
No anti-D because bleeding was not massive
questions.why: After 20 weeks give 500 IU within 72 hours and use the Kleihauer test to see if more is needed; 1500 IU is given only when a Kleihauer test is not available.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks with blood pressure 160/110 mmHg and proteinuria 3+ has sudden constant abdominal pain and a small dark bleed. Pulse 120/min, blood pressure now 100/70. Uterus hard and tender; fetal heart rate 90/min.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Resuscitate and perform emergency caesarean section
Artificial rupture of membranes and oxytocin
Ultrasound to confirm a retroplacental clot
Magnesium sulphate and observe for 24 hours
questions.why: Abruption with a live, distressed fetus needs emergency caesarean once resuscitation starts. Ultrasound misses most clots; abruption is a clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old G6P5 at 36 weeks has severe abdominal pain and a woody uterus. Scan shows no fetal heart activity. After 2 L of fluid: pulse 96/min, blood pressure 115/75 mmHg; clot test forms a clot at 7 minutes; head is engaged.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Artificial rupture of membranes and oxytocin for vaginal delivery
Wait for spontaneous labour within 2 weeks
questions.why: With a dead fetus and a stable mother, abruption is delivered vaginally by artificial rupture of membranes + oxytocin; labour is usually fast. There is no expectant option in abruption, and caesarean adds risk without fetal benefit.

questions.stem: A woman with a large abruption is bleeding from her cannula sites and the needle punctures. A bedside clot test shows no clot after 10 minutes. Platelets 70 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen very low.
questions.q: Besides red cells, what is the most appropriate treatment?
options: FFP 15 mL/kg and cryoprecipitate while preparing delivery
questions.why: Abruption is the commonest cause of DIC in pregnancy; replace clotting factors with FFP 15 mL/kg and cryoprecipitate, and deliver. Platelets are given when < 50 with bleeding; IM injections are avoided in DIC.

questions.stem: At emergency caesarean for abruption, the uterus looks blue-purple and bruised. After delivery of the placenta it contracts poorly and bleeds.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Pack the uterus and close the abdomen
Leave it: this colour means the uterus is dead
questions.why: Blood in the myometrium (Couvelaire uterus) is not itself an indication for hysterectomy: use uterotonics, massage and compression sutures first. Hysterectomy is the last step.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old G2P1 at 30 weeks was a passenger in a road accident 2 hours ago. She has mild abdominal tenderness and no vaginal bleeding. Vitals normal. Ultrasound: fundal placenta, no clot seen, fetal heart rate 148/min.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge because the scan is normal
Admit for continuous CTG and observation
questions.why: Trauma can cause a concealed abruption that a scan often misses, so she needs continuous CTG monitoring. A normal scan does not exclude abruption.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 at 39 weeks is in labour at 5 cm. Shortly after artificial rupture of membranes there is a small painless bleed and the fetal heart rate drops to 70/min, then becomes sinusoidal. Her pulse is 82, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, uterus soft between contractions.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop oxytocin and observe the CTG
Apt test on the blood before deciding
questions.why: Bleeding at rupture of membranes with fetal distress and a well mother suggests vasa praevia: the blood is fetal, so deliver at once by caesarean in the first stage. Never wait for the Apt test; instrumental delivery needs full dilatation.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old G1 who conceived by IVF has a 20-week scan showing a low-lying placenta and a velamentous cord insertion. Transvaginal colour Doppler shows a fetal vessel running across the internal os.
questions.q: What is the best plan?
options: Admit at 30–32 weeks, give steroids, caesarean at 34–36 weeks before membranes rupture
Induction at 37 weeks with early ARM
questions.why: Known vasa praevia: admit at 30–32 weeks, steroids, and caesarean at 34–36 weeks before rupture of membranes; no artificial rupture of membranes or sweep. Waiting for labour risks fetal death (about 60% if missed).

questions.stem: A 33-year-old G3P2 with one previous lower-segment caesarean is on oxytocin for slow labour. At 8 cm she has sudden severe pain, then the contractions stop. The head, at 0 station, is now at −3. Fetal heart rate 70/min, pulse 128/min, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, little vaginal bleeding.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Tocolysis and repeat examination in 1 hour
questions.why: Scar, sudden pain, stopped contractions and loss of station mean uterine rupture: resuscitate and operate now (decision to delivery < 30 min). The head is no longer in the pelvis, so instrumental delivery is impossible.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old P2 has a laparotomy for uterine rupture in labour. The baby is delivered. There is a clean transverse tear of the lower segment; she is stable after transfusion and wants more children.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate surgical step?
options: Repair the tear and tie both tubes without discussion
Repair the tear and check the bladder
questions.why: A clean tear in a stable woman who wants children is repaired; tubal ligation only with consent. Hysterectomy is for irregular, infected tears or instability.

questions.theme: Bleeding in late pregnancy
questions.lead: For each patient choose the most likely cause. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: A 38-year-old G4P3 with two previous caesarean sections is 34 weeks. Scan shows an anterior low placenta. She reports blood in her urine; there is no vaginal bleeding.
items.why: Praevia over a scar with haematuria suggests villi through the wall into the bladder.

items.stem: A 24-year-old at 34 weeks has spotting after intercourse. Uterus soft, placenta fundal on scan, fetal heart rate normal. Speculum shows a red velvety area around the os that bleeds on touch.
items.why: Post-coital spotting with a normal placental site and a red velvety cervix is ectropion; speculum examination is safe once praevia is excluded.

items.stem: A G7P6 has been in labour for 20 hours with a transverse lie. A ring is felt rising towards the umbilicus. Suddenly the pain eases, contractions stop and fetal parts are felt just under the skin; pulse 140/min.
items.why: Obstructed labour in a multipara with sudden cessation of contractions and easily felt fetal parts is rupture.

items.stem: A 22-year-old at 39 weeks has a small blood-stained mucous discharge with regular tightenings every 5 minutes. Cervix 3 cm, vitals normal, CTG normal.
items.why: Blood-stained mucus with early labour is a show; the loss is small and the mother and fetus are well.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old P1 delivers vaginally. Measured blood loss over the next hour is 900 mL. Her pulse is 96/min and blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, she is alert.
questions.q: How is this bleeding classified?
options: Normal blood loss for a vaginal birth
questions.why: ≥ 500 mL after vaginal birth within 24 hours is primary PPH; 500–1000 mL in a stable woman is minor. Major PPH is > 1000 mL or shock.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old P4 has a normal delivery. Pads and drapes show about 600 mL, but 30 minutes later her pulse is 128 and blood pressure 84/50 mmHg. The uterus is soft and well above the umbilicus.
questions.q: How is this bleeding best classified?
options: Not PPH, as the visible loss is under 1000 mL
questions.why: Shock makes it major PPH whatever the estimate; blood hides as clot in a big soft uterus, and low blood pressure means ≥ 30% of volume is gone. Visible loss is often underestimated.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old P5 delivers twins after 16 hours of oxytocin-augmented labour. The placenta is complete, but she starts bleeding heavily. The uterus is soft and above the umbilicus.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Rub up the uterus and give oxytocin 10 IU slow IV
questions.why: Atony from overdistension and long labour is treated first by massage and oxytocin 10 IU slow IV (then 40 IU in 500 mL over 4 hours). Ergometrine maximum is 1 mg and is not given as a bolus first.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old P1 with pre-eclampsia (blood pressure 165/110 mmHg) bleeds from a soft uterus after delivery. Oxytocin bolus and infusion are running and the uterus remains soft.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next uterotonic?
options: A second 10 IU oxytocin given as a fast IV bolus
questions.why: Ergometrine (and syntometrine, which contains it) is avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia; misoprostol 800 µg is the next step. A fast oxytocin bolus causes hypotension.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old P2 with asthma on inhalers has atonic PPH. Oxytocin, ergometrine and misoprostol have been given and she is still bleeding while theatre is prepared.
questions.q: Which drug should be avoided?
questions.why: Carboprost (PGF₂α) causes bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma. Tranexamic acid is safe and given alongside every step.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old P3 had an atonic PPH 4 hours after delivery. Bleeding is now controlled with uterotonics. Nobody gave tranexamic acid.
questions.q: What should be done about tranexamic acid?
options: Give 1 g IV over 10 minutes now
Do not give it now: there is no benefit after 3 hours
questions.why: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min helps only within 3 hours of birth; given later it gives no benefit and may harm.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old primigravida has a forceps delivery of a 4.1 kg baby. The placenta is complete. She has a steady bright red trickle. The uterus is hard and well contracted at the umbilicus.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Examine the cervix and vagina with a speculum in good light and repair any tear
Manual exploration of the uterus for retained placenta
questions.why: Bleeding with a hard, contracted uterus after an instrumental delivery is trauma until proven otherwise; find and repair the tear. Uterotonics will not stop bleeding from a tear.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old P2 had oxytocin 10 IU IM after birth. Forty minutes later the placenta has not delivered despite controlled cord traction. She is not bleeding; the bladder is empty.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Misoprostol 800 µg and discharge to the ward
Manual removal of the placenta in theatre under anaesthesia with antibiotics
Strong cord traction with fundal pressure
questions.why: After active management, a placenta not out by 30 min is retained; manual removal in theatre with antibiotics. The 60-minute limit applies to physiological management.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old primigravida is shocked immediately after the attendant pulled hard on the cord before the placenta separated. Her pulse is 50/min and blood pressure 70/40 mmHg; little external bleeding. The fundus cannot be felt abdominally and a mass is seen at the introitus.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Peel off the placenta, then replace the uterus
Push the fundus back into place at once, then give oxytocin
questions.why: Shock out of proportion to loss with no fundus felt is uterine inversion; replace it immediately, then give oxytocin. Oxytocin first closes the cervical ring and traps the uterus.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old delivers a macerated stillbirth after an abruption. She bleeds from the uterus, cannula sites and gums. Clot test: no clot at 10 minutes. Platelets 40 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen 1.4 g/L.
questions.q: Along with red cells, which blood products are needed?
options: No products until the uterus is emptied
questions.why: Platelets < 50 with bleeding need platelets, fibrinogen < 2 g/L needs cryoprecipitate, and FFP is given (4 units per 6 units of red cells).

questions.stem: A 26-year-old P1 continues to bleed from a soft uterus after oxytocin, ergometrine and misoprostol. Theatre will be ready in 20 minutes. Her pulse is 118/min and blood pressure 95/60 mmHg; blood is running.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate measure while waiting?
options: Another 10 IU oxytocin as a fast IV bolus
Wait for theatre without further measures
Bimanual compression, then intrauterine balloon tamponade
questions.why: When drugs fail, bimanual compression buys time and a balloon (300–500 mL saline, 12–24 hours) often stops atonic bleeding. Ergometrine maximum is 1 mg in total, already given.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old P1 has a laparotomy for atonic PPH that did not respond to all uterotonics or a balloon. She is stable on transfusion and very much wants more children.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate first procedure?
questions.why: The first surgical step is a B-Lynch suture, which works in about 9 of 10 and keeps the uterus. Hysterectomy is the last step.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old P7 is still bleeding after a B-Lynch suture and uterine artery ligation. Her pulse is 140/min and blood pressure 70/40 mmHg, Bleeding from wound edges, 10 units transfused.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Close the abdomen and give tranexamic acid
questions.why: When a mother keeps getting worse, decide on hysterectomy early: a living mother matters more than her uterus. Transfer of an unstable woman is unsafe.

questions.stem: A midwife in a health centre with a working fridge is managing the third stage of labour of a P2 after a normal birth of a single baby.
questions.q: Which is the recommended uterotonic and route?
options: Oxytocin 10 IU IM within 1 minute of birth
questions.why: Active management of the third stage uses oxytocin 10 IU IM within 1 minute, with delayed cord clamping and controlled cord traction. Misoprostol 600 µg orally is the alternative only when oxytocin is unavailable.

questions.stem: A village midwife without electricity or a fridge attends a home birth. No oxytocin is available.
questions.q: Which drug should she give to prevent PPH after the baby is born?
questions.why: When oxytocin is not available, misoprostol 600 µg orally is used for prevention; it needs no fridge. 800 µg is the treatment dose.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old P3 with moderate mitral stenosis delivers vaginally. The uterus becomes soft and she starts bleeding.
questions.q: Which is the safest first drug regimen?
options: Oxytocin 5 IU slowly IV, then an infusion
questions.why: In heart disease the oxytocin dose is reduced to 5 IU given slowly, since a fast bolus drops blood pressure. Ergometrine is contraindicated in heart disease.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old P2 is seen on day 10 after a vaginal delivery with fresh bleeding, cramping pain, fever 38.6 °C and offensive lochia. The uterus is bulky and tender, os open. Scan shows echogenic material in the cavity.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: IV cephalosporin plus metronidazole, then evacuation of retained tissue
questions.why: Secondary PPH with fever and retained products is treated with IV antibiotics (cephalosporin + metronidazole) and uterotonics, then evacuation. Evacuating an infected uterus first risks perforation.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old had a massive PPH with prolonged shock 8 months ago. She could not breastfeed, has had no periods since, feels tired and cold, and has lost pubic hair.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Failed lactation, amenorrhoea and hypopituitary features after massive PPH are Sheehan syndrome (pituitary necrosis). Asherman gives amenorrhoea but normal lactation and hormones.

questions.theme: Postpartum bleeding
questions.lead: For each patient choose the most likely cause of bleeding. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: After a normal delivery the placenta is checked and a gap is found on the maternal surface. The uterus contracts with massage, then relaxes and bleeding restarts.
items.why: A missing cotyledon stops the uterus contracting well: tissue must be removed.

items.stem: A woman with HELLP syndrome delivers vaginally. The uterus is firm, but blood keeps leaking from her cannula sites and the vaginal blood does not clot.
items.why: Bleeding from puncture sites with a contracted uterus and unclotting blood is a thrombin (clotting) problem.

items.stem: Eight days after a caesarean for prolonged labour, a woman has fever 38.8 °C, offensive lochia and moderate fresh bleeding. The uterus is tender and larger than expected.
items.why: Fever, smelly lochia and a tender bulky uterus in the first weeks is infection: a cause of secondary PPH.

items.stem: A P2 with one previous caesarean has a long labour on oxytocin, then a vaginal birth. She becomes shocked with abdominal pain and haematuria; vaginal bleeding is modest.
items.why: A scar, oxytocin, haematuria and shock out of proportion to the visible loss point to rupture: laparotomy.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 12 weeks has a scan showing twins with one placental mass. The dividing membrane is thin and meets the placenta at a right angle with no wedge of tissue.
questions.q: What is the chorionicity?
questions.why: A thin membrane with a T sign and no chorionic wedge means monochorionic diamniotic. A triangular wedge (lambda sign) would mean dichorionic.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old at 20 weeks after clomiphene treatment has twins: one male and one female, with what looks like a single placental mass.
questions.q: What is the most accurate conclusion?
questions.why: Twins of different sex are dizygotic, and dizygotic twins are always DCDA; the 'single' placenta is two fused placentas.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with monochorionic diamniotic twins is 21 weeks. One sac has a deepest pool of 10 cm and a large bladder; the other twin has almost no liquor, no visible bladder and is fixed against the uterine wall.
questions.q: What is the best management?
options: Selective termination of the smaller twin as first choice
Refer for fetoscopic laser ablation of the placental vessels
questions.why: Poly in one sac and oligo in the other in MC twins is twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome; before 26 weeks fetoscopic laser treats the cause (untreated mortality up to 80%). Delivery at 21 weeks is not viable.

questions.stem: Monochorionic diamniotic twins at 28 weeks have equal amounts of liquor. Middle cerebral artery Doppler shows a high peak velocity in one twin and a low one in the other.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Tiny anastomoses make one twin anaemic (high MCA velocity) and one polycythaemic without liquor difference: TAPS. Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome shows a poly–oligo difference.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with monochorionic diamniotic twins is 30 weeks. Scan shows one twin has died; the other has normal growth, liquor and CTG. She is well.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Do not rush delivery: check clotting, weekly scans of the survivor, aim for 36 weeks
Emergency caesarean to save the survivor
questions.why: In MC twins the survivor is harmed at the moment of the co-twin's death (up to 25% die or have brain injury), so immediate delivery does not help. Check maternal clotting and monitor weekly.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twins has normal growth on 4-weekly scans. Both twins are cephalic.
questions.q: When should delivery be planned?
questions.why: Uncomplicated DCDA twins are delivered at 38 weeks; MCDA at 37 weeks.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old has monochorionic twins with no dividing membrane seen on repeated scans. Growth is normal.
questions.q: What is the best plan for delivery?
questions.why: MCMA twins are delivered by caesarean at 32 weeks because of cord entanglement. 35 weeks is the timing for triplets.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old with dichorionic twins is 37 weeks. Ultrasound: twin 1 cephalic, twin 2 breech; both normally grown. No other complications.
questions.q: What is the recommended mode of delivery?
options: External cephalic version of twin 2 at 37 weeks, then induction
questions.why: When twin 1 is cephalic, vaginal birth is aimed for whatever twin 2's presentation. Caesarean is chosen when twin 1 is non-cephalic.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with dichorionic twins at 37 weeks has twin 1 in breech and twin 2 cephalic on scan.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan?
questions.why: Twin 1 breech is an indication for caesarean, partly to prevent locked twins (chins lock when twin 1 is breech and twin 2 cephalic).

questions.stem: After vaginal delivery of twin 1, the second twin is found to be lying transversely. Membranes are intact, fetal heart rate 140/min and contractions are weak.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Internal podalic version and breech extraction
questions.why: With the sac intact, external version to a longitudinal lie is tried first; internal podalic version is for a transverse twin 2 after the membranes have ruptured.

questions.stem: Twenty-five minutes after twin 1 was born, twin 2 is cephalic at −3 station with ruptured membranes. The cervix is thickening and the fetal heart rate is 80/min.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Twin 2 should be delivered within 20 min; a retained twin 2 with fetal distress and a high head needs caesarean. Instruments need a low head.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old P4 has just delivered healthy twins vaginally and the placentas are complete.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate measure to prevent PPH?
options: Active management of the third stage plus an oxytocin infusion for 2–4 hours
No extra measures after normal active management
questions.why: The overdistended uterus after twins is at high risk of atony, so an oxytocin infusion for 2–4 hours follows active management.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks has an estimated fetal weight on the 8th centile, growing along that centile. Both parents are short. Umbilical artery Doppler and liquor are normal; CTG reactive.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Daily CTG in hospital until delivery
Continue antenatal care and plan delivery at 37–38 weeks
Give steroids and deliver within 48 hours
questions.why: A small baby with normal Doppler and liquor is usually constitutional SGA; do not rush, deliver at 37–38 weeks. Immediate delivery adds prematurity risk without benefit.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old at 22 weeks (dated by an 11-week scan) has a fetus with HC, AC and femur length all below the 3rd centile. HC:AC ratio is normal, Doppler and liquor normal.
questions.q: Which investigations are most useful now?
questions.why: Early, symmetrical restriction with normal Doppler suggests a fetal cause such as chromosomes or infection; karyotype and TORCH look for it. Placental tests fit late, asymmetrical fetal growth restriction.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old with pre-eclampsia is 34 weeks. Ultrasound: AC below the 3rd centile, head circumference on the 40th centile, AFI 4 cm, umbilical artery PI raised.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause of this growth pattern?
questions.why: A small AC with a spared head and low liquor is asymmetrical fetal growth restriction from placental insufficiency: brain sparing, liver glycogen falls and kidney flow drops. Chromosomal causes give symmetrical fetal growth restriction.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 who smokes 10 cigarettes a day is 33 weeks. Symphysis–fundal height is 29 cm and she reports fewer movements.
questions.q: What is the best next investigation?
options: Growth scan with liquor and umbilical artery Doppler
questions.why: An symphysis–fundal height lag > 3 cm or reduced movements needs a growth scan (estimated fetal weight, AC, liquor) plus umbilical artery Doppler. Uterine artery Doppler is a screening test at 20–24 weeks.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 30 weeks has fetal growth restriction (estimated fetal weight < 3rd centile). Umbilical artery Doppler shows absent end-diastolic flow; ductus venosus and CTG are normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Steroids, daily CTG, and deliver by 34 weeks
Weekly Doppler and deliver at 37 weeks
questions.why: Absent EDF with normal DV and CTG: give dexamethasone, monitor daily and deliver by 34 weeks, usually by caesarean. Immediate delivery is for abnormal DV or a pathological CTG.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old at 31 weeks has a fetus with estimated fetal weight below the 3rd centile. She has had steroids and is being scanned twice weekly in a unit with good neonatal care.
questions.q: Which new finding is an indication to deliver now?
options: Absent or reversed a-wave in the ductus venosus
Raised umbilical artery PI with EDF present
questions.why: An abnormal ductus venosus a-wave signals fetal acidaemia, a late near-terminal sign: deliver now if viable. Low MCA PI (brain sparing) is an earlier change.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old at 33 weeks has fetal growth restriction with reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery. CTG shows reduced variability but no decelerations.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Daily CTG and deliver at 37 weeks
Dexamethasone and deliver by caesarean section
questions.why: Reversed EDF means severe placental failure: deliver (about 32 weeks), with steroids first if time, by caesarean. These fetuses cannot tolerate contractions, so induction is unsuitable.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old at 35 weeks has an estimated fetal weight on the 4th centile. Umbilical artery PI is raised but end-diastolic flow is present; MCA PI is low. CTG and liquor are normal.
questions.q: By when should she be delivered?
options: By 37 weeks, with Doppler twice weekly
questions.why: Raised UA PI with EDF present (± low MCA PI) is delivered by 37 weeks with twice-weekly Doppler; induction is possible.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old is 38 weeks with an SGA fetus. Umbilical artery Doppler is normal, liquor normal, CTG reactive, head engaged, cervix favourable.
questions.q: What is the best mode of delivery?
options: Induction of labour with continuous CTG
Vacuum delivery at full dilatation routinely
Caesarean if labour has not started by 39 weeks
questions.why: With normal Doppler and reassuring CTG, induction and vaginal birth with continuous monitoring is suitable. Caesarean is for absent/reversed EDF or an abnormal CTG.

questions.stem: A baby of 1.8 kg is born at 37 weeks to a mother with chronic hypertension. At 6 hours the baby looks plethoric; venous PCV is 70%.
questions.q: What is the mechanism of this finding?
questions.why: In fetal growth restriction, chronic hypoxia drives erythropoietin and causes polycythaemia; PCV is checked routinely in these babies.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 9 weeks had her last baby with severe growth restriction and early-onset pre-eclampsia at 32 weeks.
questions.q: Which measure is most appropriate to reduce the risk this time?
questions.why: Women at high risk of placental disease (previous fetal growth restriction or pre-eclampsia) take low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks. Starting at 28 weeks is too late.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old G3P2 whose first baby was growth-restricted is attending her 22-week visit. Her dating scan was at 10 weeks.
questions.q: Which test best screens for placental growth restriction at this stage?
questions.why: Uterine artery Doppler at 20–24 weeks screens for placental disease. Umbilical artery Doppler is used to monitor a fetus already small; PAPP-A is a first-trimester marker.

questions.theme: Timing of delivery in a small fetus
options: Deliver now, by caesarean if viable
Deliver at about 32 weeks after steroids
Await spontaneous labour up to 41 weeks
Repeat growth scan in 3 weeks before deciding
questions.lead: For each patient choose the most appropriate timing of delivery. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: At 29 weeks the fetus is below the 3rd centile with absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery. Ductus venosus and CTG are normal.
items.why: Absent EDF with normal DV and CTG: steroids, daily CTG, deliver by 34 weeks.

items.stem: At 33 weeks the estimated fetal weight is on the 5th centile; umbilical artery PI is raised with forward end-diastolic flow; CTG normal.
items.why: Raised UA PI with EDF present: Doppler twice weekly and deliver by 37 weeks.

items.stem: At 36 weeks the estimated fetal weight is on the 7th centile, growing along it; umbilical artery Doppler and liquor are normal.
items.why: Small with normal Doppler and liquor is likely constitutional; deliver at 37–38 weeks.

items.stem: At 30 weeks a growth-restricted fetus shows a reversed a-wave in the ductus venosus and decelerations on CTG.
items.why: Abnormal DV or a pathological CTG means acidaemia: deliver now, by caesarean.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old G3P2 at 34 weeks with BMI 38 and a large, tense uterus reports fewer movements for a day. The midwife cannot hear the fetal heart with a Pinard stethoscope or a hand-held Doppler.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Real-time ultrasound to look for heart activity
Abdominal X-ray for signs of fetal death
questions.why: Absent heart sounds on Pinard or hand Doppler are suggestive, not diagnostic (obesity and polyhydramnios give a false result); only real-time ultrasound confirms fetal death. X-ray signs are late and no longer needed.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old in a remote area is found to have a dead fetus at 36 weeks. An old abdominal X-ray shows the fetal skull bones overlapping.
questions.q: About how long has the fetus been dead?
questions.why: Overlapping skull bones (Spalding sign) appear about 7 days after death. Gas in the heart (Robert sign) appears at about 12 hours and the halo sign at about 48 hours.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old chose to wait after a fetal death diagnosed at 32 weeks. Five weeks later she has bleeding gums and bruising. Fibrinogen 0.9 g/L, platelets 80 × 10⁹/L.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Caesarean section before any blood products
Continue expectant management with weekly clotting
Correct the clotting with FFP and cryoprecipitate, then deliver
questions.why: DIC is the most serious complication of a retained dead fetus (about 30% if retained > 3 weeks); correct the coagulopathy and deliver now. Operating before correction risks uncontrolled bleeding.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old with a fetal death confirmed at 33 weeks is well, membranes intact, blood pressure and clotting normal. After counselling she wants to wait for labour to start.
questions.q: What monitoring is needed while waiting?
options: No tests needed if she feels well
questions.why: Expectant care needs clotting checks 2–3 times a week; induce if clotting falls, infection appears or she changes her mind. Most labour within 3 weeks.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old G2P1 (previous vaginal birth) has a fetal death confirmed at 34 weeks. Membranes intact, clotting normal; she requests delivery.
questions.q: Which induction regimen is most appropriate?
options: Mifepristone 200 mg orally, then misoprostol 25 µg vaginally 6-hourly from 36–48 hours later
Artificial rupture of membranes and oxytocin
questions.why: After 28 weeks, mifepristone 200 mg is followed 36–48 hours later by misoprostol 25 µg vaginally 6-hourly (or 25 µg oral 2-hourly). 200 µg doses are for < 27 weeks and would risk rupture at term.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old with two previous caesarean sections has a fetal death at 37 weeks. Cephalic, cervix 1 cm and soft, clotting normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate method of delivery?
options: Foley catheter ripening and oxytocin, or caesarean section
questions.why: With ≥ 2 caesarean sections or a classical scar, routine misoprostol is avoided; use Foley + oxytocin or caesarean. Artificial rupture of membranes is avoided in intrauterine fetal death because of infection.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old is being induced for a fetal death at 35 weeks. After mifepristone and misoprostol the cervix is 5 cm with intact membranes and regular contractions. Clotting is normal.
questions.q: Which step should be avoided?
questions.why: Artificial rupture of membranes is avoided in intrauterine fetal death because of the risk of intrauterine infection and sepsis. Epidural is acceptable when clotting is normal.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old from a rural area of Sudan has a fetal death at 30 weeks. She had fever with rigors and headache last week. Hb 8.2 g/dL, platelets 95 × 10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which investigation is most likely to show the cause?
questions.why: Fever, rigors, anaemia and low platelets in Sudan point to malaria as the cause; a blood film is the test.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old has a fetal death at 37 weeks. The scan shows a large fetus with polyhydramnios; she has had recurrent vulval thrush and thirst.
questions.q: Which investigation is most likely to show the cause?
questions.why: A big baby with polyhydramnios and intrauterine fetal death suggests diabetes; check OGTT and HbA1c.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old delivers her second stillborn baby. She had a DVT last year and two first-trimester miscarriages before that.
questions.q: Which test is most appropriate, and when?
options: Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies during labour
Protein C and S levels on day 1 after delivery
Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies at 6 weeks after delivery
questions.why: Recurrent intrauterine fetal death with thrombosis and miscarriages suggests antiphospholipid syndrome; thrombophilia and antiphospholipid syndrome tests are done at 6 weeks, as pregnancy and the acute event alter results.

questions.stem: On day 3 after a stillbirth at 36 weeks, a 25-year-old has painful, engorged breasts that are leaking milk. She wants the milk to stop.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Cabergoline 1 mg once suppresses lactation; ideally it is given soon after delivery. Metoclopramide raises prolactin and increases milk.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old RhD-negative woman delivers a stillborn baby at 34 weeks. She has no anti-D antibodies.
questions.q: What is the correct anti-D management?
options: Anti-D 1500 IU only if the baby's group is known
Kleihauer test, then anti-D 500 IU IM within 72 hours
No anti-D because the baby is dead
questions.why: After 20 weeks give 500 IU within 72 hours after a Kleihauer test; the dead fetus can still sensitise her. 250 IU is the dose before 20 weeks.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old G3P2 is 32 weeks. Fundal height is 38 cm, AFI 31 cm, estimated fetal weight > 90th centile. Urine shows glucose 2+ on two visits. Anomaly scan was normal.
questions.q: Which investigation is most likely to show the cause?
questions.why: Polyhydramnios with a big baby and glycosuria suggests diabetes (fetal polyuria); check OGTT.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old at 28 weeks has AFI 30 cm. Scan shows two fluid-filled spaces in the fetal upper abdomen.
questions.q: Which further investigation is most important?
questions.why: A double bubble means duodenal atresia, which is strongly linked to Down syndrome; offer fetal karyotype.

questions.stem: A baby is born at 36 weeks to a mother whose AFI was 32 cm. Soon after birth he has much saliva foamy saliva and chokes at the first feed. A nasogastric tube coils back in the upper chest on X-ray.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Drooling, choking and a coiled NG tube are oesophageal atresia, usually with a fistula; the fetus could not swallow liquor, hence polyhydramnios.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old at 30 weeks with idiopathic polyhydramnios has AFI 44 cm. She is breathless at rest and cannot lie flat. Cervix is closed.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Severe (AFI > 40 cm), symptomatic polyhydramnios is relieved by slow amnioreduction; fast drainage risks abruption. Indomethacin is limited to ≤ 72 hours.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old at 30 weeks with symptomatic polyhydramnios was started on indomethacin 25 mg 6-hourly by a junior doctor. On day 6 of treatment the liquor has fallen.
questions.q: What is the most important fetal risk of continuing this drug?
options: Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
questions.why: Indomethacin is used only < 32 weeks and for ≤ 72 hours because it closes the ductus arteriosus and reduces fetal urine (oligohydramnios).

questions.stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 at 39 weeks with AFI 30 cm is in early labour at 4 cm, cephalic, head 3/5 palpable. Membranes are intact; the obstetrician plans to rupture them.
questions.q: What is the best way to do this?
options: Controlled ARM after checking the lie, letting liquor escape slowly
Rapid ARM with a large hook to drain fluid fast
Avoid ARM and wait until full dilatation
questions.why: Sudden decompression in polyhydramnios can cause cord prolapse and abruption, so artificial rupture of membranes is controlled with the lie checked. Caesarean is not needed for polyhydramnios alone.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 30 weeks has had watery vaginal loss for 12 hours. Sterile speculum shows a pool of clear fluid. AFI 3 cm. Temperature 36.9 °C, no contractions, CTG normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix
Erythromycin 250 mg orally 6-hourly for 10 days and dexamethasone 6 mg IM 12-hourly × 4
questions.why: Preterm rupture of membranes < 34 weeks: erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly × 10 days and steroids, watching for infection. Digital examination increases infection and co-amoxiclav is linked to NEC.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 36 weeks has had clear fluid leaking for 6 hours. Speculum confirms a pool; AFI 4 cm; cephalic, CTG normal, no fever.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Erythromycin for 10 days and expectant management to 38 weeks
questions.why: Rupture of membranes at ≥ 34–36 weeks is managed by induction unless caesarean is needed for another reason.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old at 20 weeks has no amniotic fluid on scan. Neither kidney nor the bladder can be seen after waiting 1 hour. Membranes are intact.
questions.q: What is the main cause of death in this baby after birth?
questions.why: Bilateral renal agenesis gives anhydramnios before 22 weeks and lethal pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence); the lungs, not the kidneys, kill first.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 24 weeks has AFI 4 cm. The male fetus has a large, thick-walled bladder with a dilated posterior urethra (keyhole sign) and bilateral hydronephrosis.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: A big bladder with a keyhole sign in a boy is posterior urethral valves blocking urine outflow. Renal agenesis shows no bladder at all.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with chronic hypertension and diabetic kidney disease booked late at 26 weeks. She has taken enalapril since before pregnancy. AFI is 3 cm; growth and Doppler are normal; membranes intact.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the low liquor?
questions.why: ACE inhibitors cause fetal renal failure and oligohydramnios and must be stopped in pregnancy. Normal growth and Doppler argue against placental insufficiency.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 is 42 weeks. AFI 4 cm, growth normal, CTG reactive, cervix Bishop 5.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: Post-term pregnancy with low liquor is induced; the risk of cord compression and stillbirth rises if she waits.

questions.theme: Abnormal amniotic fluid
questions.lead: For each patient choose the most likely cause of the abnormal liquor volume. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: At 31 weeks AFI is 27 cm. Detailed anomaly scan, OGTT and TORCH serology are all normal; the baby's growth is normal.
items.why: Mild polyhydramnios with a normal search for causes is idiopathic, the commonest group.

items.stem: At 22 weeks AFI is 30 cm. The scan shows no cranial vault above the orbits.
items.why: Absent cranial vault is anencephaly; the fetus does not swallow normally, so liquor builds up.

items.stem: At 42 weeks AFI is 4 cm. Growth and umbilical artery Doppler are normal, membranes intact, CTG reactive.
items.why: Liquor falls after term as placental function declines; post-term with oligohydramnios is induced.

items.stem: A woman with a single placenta and two fetuses at 19 weeks has a rapidly enlarging, tense uterus and breathlessness. One sac has a deepest pool of 11 cm, the other almost none.
items.why: Acute polyhydramnios before 20 weeks in monochorionic twins with a poly–oligo pair is twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 39 weeks comes at night with tightenings for 6 hours. They come every 10–20 minutes with no pattern and settled after paracetamol and a rest. The cervix is closed, 3 cm long and posterior, and is the same on repeat examination 2 hours later. CTG is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Admit her and start a partogram
Reassure and send her home with advice on when to return
Give nifedipine to stop the contractions
questions.why: Irregular pains relieved by rest with no cervical change are false (Braxton Hicks) labour, so she can go home. A partogram is opened only in the active phase, from 4 cm.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 at 39+2 weeks has 3 strong contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting 45 seconds. On vaginal examination the cervix is 5 cm dilated and fully effaced, membranes are intact and the head is 3/5 palpable. Fetal heart rate is 140/min.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start a partogram, plotting the dilatation on the alert line
Rupture the membranes to speed up labour
Start oxytocin to keep 5 contractions in 10 minutes
Repeat the vaginal examination every hour
Transfer to theatre for caesarean section
questions.why: She is in the active phase of the first stage (from 4 cm), so the partogram is started on the alert line. Routine artificial rupture of membranes or oxytocin is not used in normal labour.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old para 1 with an uneventful pregnancy is in spontaneous labour at 40 weeks. Cervix is 6 cm, liquor is clear and the admission fetal heart rate is 135/min with normal maternal observations.
questions.q: How should the fetal heart be monitored in the first stage?
options: A 20-minute admission CTG and no further monitoring
Intermittent auscultation for 1 minute after a contraction every 15–30 minutes
questions.why: Low-risk women need intermittent auscultation every 15–30 min in the first stage. Every 5 min is the second-stage interval, and continuous CTG is for high-risk labour.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old para 3, no epidural, has been fully dilated for 70 minutes and pushing well. The head is 0/5 palpable at +2 station, occipito-anterior position, with no caput or moulding. Contractions are 4 in 10 minutes and fetal heart rate is 140/min.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Assess for an assisted (instrumental) vaginal delivery
Start oxytocin and reassess in 2 hours
Apply fundal pressure with each contraction
questions.why: The second stage limit for a multipara without epidural is 1 hour, so this is delay: with the head low and occipito-anterior, instrumental delivery is the answer. Another hour of pushing would be acceptable only for a primigravida or with an epidural.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old para 2 received oxytocin 10 IU IM within a minute of the birth of her baby. Forty minutes later the placenta has not delivered despite controlled cord traction and an emptied bladder. Blood loss is 200 mL and she is stable.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Wait a further 30 minutes for spontaneous delivery
Pull firmly on the cord without counter-pressure
Manual removal of the placenta under anaesthesia
Give ergometrine 0.5 mg IV and wait
questions.why: With active management, a placenta still in after 30 min is retained and needs manual removal. Waiting 60 min applies only to physiological management.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida with pre-eclampsia (blood pressure 160/10 mmHg5 mmHg on treatment) has just delivered a live baby vaginally. A single fetus was confirmed on scan.
questions.q: Which uterotonic should be given for the third stage?
questions.why: Oxytocin 10 IU IM is the active management of the third stage drug for every woman. Ergometrine-containing drugs are given only if blood pressure is normal, because they raise blood pressure sharply.

questions.stem: A midwife conducts a birth in a rural health centre. The refrigerator broke a week ago and there is no oxytocin. The baby is born healthy and no further fetus is felt on abdominal palpation.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate drug for the third stage?
questions.why: If oxytocin is not available, misoprostol 600 µg orally is used for active management of the third stage. 25 µg is the dose used to induce labour with a live term fetus.

questions.stem: During the second stage of a 26-year-old primigravida, the head delivers. On feeling the neck, the cord is wrapped tightly twice and cannot be slipped over the head or shoulders. Fetal heart rate before delivery of the head was normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Clamp the cord in two places and cut between the clamps
Push the head back and perform caesarean section
Wait for the next contraction with the cord in place
Apply strong downward traction on the head
Perform an episiotomy and wait for restitution
questions.why: A tight cord that cannot be loosened is double-clamped and cut before the shoulders are delivered. Waiting with a tight cord risks fetal hypoxia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old para 4, unbooked with no scan, delivers a 2.3 kg baby. After the birth, the midwife notes the uterus is still about 32 weeks in size and firm, with little bleeding. Oxytocin is drawn up.
questions.q: What should be done before giving the oxytocin?
options: Palpate the abdomen (or scan) to exclude another fetus
questions.why: A large uterus after a small baby suggests an undiagnosed twin; giving a uterotonic would trap the second twin. Exclude a second fetus before any uterotonic.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old primigravida has clinical pelvimetry at 38 weeks. The pelvic inlet feels heart-shaped, the ischial spines are prominent and the subpubic arch admits only one finger.
questions.q: Which labour problem is she most at risk of?
options: Delay at the inlet with the head engaging transverse
Face to pubis delivery with an easy second stage
Occipito-posterior position with deep transverse arrest
questions.why: These features describe an android pelvis, which leads to occipito-posterior position and deep transverse arrest. Transverse engagement with delay at the inlet fits the flat platypelloid pelvis.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old para 3 was given pethidine 100 mg IM in early labour; labour then progressed very fast and she delivered 70 minutes later. The baby is floppy with poor breathing effort. After drying and inflation breaths the heart rate is 120/min but there is still no regular breathing.
questions.q: Which drug is most likely to help the baby?
questions.why: Pethidine close to birth causes neonatal respiratory depression, reversed by naloxone. Adrenaline is for a heart rate that stays low despite ventilation and compressions.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old primigravida delivers at home. The attendant pulls hard on the cord before any contraction. There is a sudden gush of blood, she becomes pale and sweaty with blood pressure 70/4 mmHg0 mmHg, and the fundus cannot be felt abdominally. A smooth mass is seen at the introitus with the placenta attached.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Shock out of proportion to blood loss, an absent fundus and a mass at the vulva after cord traction mean uterine inversion. In atonic PPH the soft uterus is still palpable abdominally.

questions.stem: After a normal birth, the midwife examines the placenta. The cotyledons look complete, but two vessels run from the placental edge across the membranes and end at a round hole in the membranes. Bleeding is 300 mL and continuing slowly.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure, as the placenta is complete
Give ergometrine and discharge after 4 hours
Explore the uterus and remove the retained lobe under anaesthesia
questions.why: Vessels running to a gap in the membranes mean a succenturiate lobe has been left behind; it must be removed to prevent PPH and infection. A complete-looking main placenta does not exclude this.

questions.stem: A baby born by ventouse to a primigravida is checked on day 2. There is a soft, fluctuant swelling over the right parietal bone that does not cross the suture lines and has grown since birth. The baby is otherwise well.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: A swelling limited by sutures that grows after birth is subperiosteal: a cephalhaematoma. Caput crosses sutures, is present at birth and goes in days.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks was 4 cm dilated at 08:00. At 12:00 the cervix is 5 cm, membranes intact, head 3/5 with no moulding, and the partogram shows 2 contractions in 10 minutes in dotted boxes. Fetal heart rate is 140/min, normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Artificial rupture of membranes, oxytocin if needed, and reassess in 2 hours
Give pethidine and let her sleep
questions.why: Less than 2 cm in 4 hours with weak contractions in a primigravida is slow progress from poor power, treated by artificial rupture of membranes then oxytocin with review in 2 hours. Caesarean is for obstruction or failure after augmentation.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old para 6 has been in labour for 16 hours. The cervix has stayed at 6 cm for 4 hours despite strong contractions, 4 in 10 minutes each over 40 seconds. The head is 4/5 palpable with +3 moulding and a large caput, the cervix is swollen and the urine is blood-stained. She is dry with ketonuria.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Oxytocin augmentation and reassess in 2 hours
Artificial rupture of membranes and wait
IV fluids, antibiotics and catheter, then caesarean section
questions.why: Good contractions with no descent, +3 moulding and haematuria mean obstructed labour: resuscitate then caesarean. Oxytocin in a multipara with obstruction risks uterine rupture.

questions.stem: A primigravida is being followed with a partogram in a health centre with no theatre. She was plotted at 4 cm at 06:00. At 10:00 the cervix is 6 cm, so the plot lies just to the right of the alert line. Mother and fetus are well.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue routine care until the action line is reached
Start oxytocin in the health centre
Perform artificial rupture of membranes and keep her
Repeat the vaginal examination in 8 hours
questions.why: Crossing the alert line in a centre without theatre means refer, so she reaches hospital before the action line. Oxytocin should not be started where caesarean is not available.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old para 2 in labour at 38 weeks has a partogram showing liquor letter 'B' at the last examination. Her pulse has risen from 84 to 118/min over 2 hours and the uterus is tense and tender between contractions. Fetal heart rate is 165/min.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Blood-stained liquor with maternal tachycardia and a tense, tender uterus points to abruption. Vasa praevia causes fetal compromise with painless bleeding at rupture of membranes and no maternal tachycardia or uterine tenderness.

questions.stem: During a vaginal examination in active labour, the doctor feels the parietal bones overlapping each other at the sagittal suture. With gentle finger pressure the overlap can be pushed back.
questions.q: How should this be recorded on the partogram?
questions.why: Overlapping bones that can be reduced are moulding +2. +1 is bones touching, +3 is overlap that cannot be reduced; 'C' is a liquor letter (clear).

questions.stem: On a partogram, the contraction row at 14:00 shows 4 boxes filled in completely (solid shading) for that half-hour.
questions.q: What does this entry mean?
options: 4 contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting 20–40 seconds
4 contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting more than 40 seconds
4 contractions in 30 minutes, each lasting less than 20 seconds
A contraction every 4 minutes lasting less than 20 seconds
A single contraction lasting more than 4 minutes
questions.why: The number of boxes is the frequency in 10 min and solid shading means each lasts over 40 s. Lines (hatching) would mean 20–40 s.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old primigravida is 8 cm dilated with clear liquor. The CTG shows a baseline of 135/min, variability 10 bpm and accelerations. With each contraction the fetal heart rate falls by 25 bpm, starting with the contraction, lowest at its peak and back to baseline as it ends.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.why: Decelerations that mirror contractions are early decelerations from head compression; with a normal baseline and variability the CTG is normal. Scalp sampling is for a pathological CTG.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with pre-eclampsia is on oxytocin at 5 cm. For the last hour the CTG shows baseline 150/min, variability 4 bpm, no accelerations, and a fall of 30 bpm starting 20 seconds after the peak of each contraction, recovering after it ends.
questions.q: How should this CTG be classified?
options: Cannot be classified without scalp pH
questions.why: Repeated late decelerations and variability < 5 bpm for > 50 min are each pathological features. Suspicious would need only one suspicious feature, such as variability < 5 for 30–50 min.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida at 39 weeks has had ruptured membranes for 30 hours. Her temperature is 38.6 °C and pulse 110/min. The CTG shows a baseline of 175/min, variability 10 bpm, no decelerations.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the CTG change?
questions.why: Fetal tachycardia with maternal fever after prolonged rupture of membranes points to chorioamnionitis. Cord compression gives variable decelerations, not a raised baseline.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old in early labour at 39 weeks has an admission CTG with a baseline of 140/min and no decelerations. For 30 minutes the variability is 3 bpm and there are no accelerations; then she drinks juice, variability returns to 10 bpm and accelerations appear. No drugs were given.
questions.q: What is the most likely explanation of the first 30 minutes?
questions.why: Low variability for up to about 40 min that recovers with accelerations is a fetal sleep cycle. Hypoxia does not correct itself with return of accelerations.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old RhD-negative woman with known anti-D antibodies (high titre) is admitted at 34 weeks with reduced fetal movements. The CTG shows a smooth, regular, wave-like pattern of 3 cycles per minute with no variability and no accelerations.
questions.q: What does this pattern most likely indicate?
questions.why: A sinusoidal trace is pathological and is classically due to severe fetal anaemia, as in Rh isoimmunisation. Fetal sleep gives low variability, not regular sine waves.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old primigravida at 6 cm has an epidural top-up. Ten minutes later her blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg and the fetal heart rate falls to 90/min, staying low for 4 minutes. She is lying on her back. Contractions are 3 in 10 minutes and there is no bleeding.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Turn her to the left side and give an IV fluid bolus
