questions.why: A prolonged deceleration after epidural hypotension is treated by intrauterine resuscitation: left lateral and IV fluids. The fetal heart rate usually recovers; caesarean is needed only if it does not.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida at 6 cm has a suspicious CTG for an hour. Fetal scalp blood sampling gives a pH of 7.22. The CTG is unchanged.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: A pH of 7.21–7.24 is borderline and the sample is repeated in 30 min. Delivery is indicated at 7.20 or below.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old para 2 has been fully dilated for 40 minutes. The head is 0/5 palpable at +2 station in the occipito-anterior position with no caput. The fetal heart rate falls to 85/min for 4 minutes and does not recover between pushes.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: Fetal distress in the second stage with a low occipito-anterior head is delivered by ventouse or forceps, which is faster than caesarean. Caesarean is the route for fetal distress in the first stage.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old primigravida had labour at home for 2 days and delivered a stillborn baby in hospital. Ten days later she complains of constant leaking of urine from the vagina, day and night, with no urge.
questions.q: Which measure immediately after delivery would most likely have prevented this?
options: Continuous bladder drainage by catheter for 14 days
questions.why: Constant leaking after prolonged obstructed labour is a vesicovaginal fistula from pressure necrosis; a catheter for 14 days after obstruction helps prevent it. Pelvic floor exercises treat stress incontinence, not fistula.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old para 7 laboured at home for 20 hours before arrival. There is a ridge across the abdomen that has risen toward the umbilicus, the lower uterus is tender, a catheter drains blood-stained urine and the fetal heart rate is 100/min.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Full bladder above a normal uterus
Obstructed labour with a pathological retraction ring
Physiological retraction ring of normal labour
questions.why: A rising Bandl's ring with haematuria and fetal distress is obstructed labour with impending rupture, needing caesarean now. The physiological ring is not palpable as a rising ridge and does not come with haematuria.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old G2P1 at 31 weeks has had tightenings for 3 hours. She is afebrile, the uterus is soft between tightenings and the membranes are intact. The cervix is closed, transvaginal cervical length is 28 mm and fetal fibronectin is negative. CTG is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: A negative fFN with cervix > 15 mm means birth in the next 7–14 days is unlikely, so drugs are avoided. Steroids and tocolysis are for likely preterm birth.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks has regular painful contractions every 5 minutes. The cervix is 2 cm dilated and 80% effaced, membranes intact, temperature 36.8 °C and CTG normal. There is a neonatal unit in the hospital.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection and nifedipine
questions.why: At 24–34 weeks, steroids plus tocolysis for 48 hours is the plan. Two tocolytics are never combined, and magnesium sulphate neuroprotection is for < 32 weeks.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 30 weeks in threatened preterm labour is given steroids. The registrar asks you to start nifedipine.
questions.q: What is the correct nifedipine regimen?
options: 30 mg sublingually, then 20 mg 8-hourly for 7 days
30 mg orally, then 20 mg 8-hourly for 48 hours
questions.why: Nifedipine is given 30 mg orally, then 20 mg 8-hourly for 48 hours. Sublingual use causes sudden hypotension and is never used.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old at 30 weeks with known severe mitral stenosis presents in preterm labour with the cervix 2 cm. She has received the first dose of steroids.
questions.q: Which tocolytic is most appropriate?
questions.why: β-agonists cause tachycardia and pulmonary oedema and are avoided in heart disease, so nifedipine is used. Two tocolytics are never combined.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 29 weeks in preterm labour received her first dose of betamethasone 6 hours ago. The cervix is now 7 cm and birth is expected within a few hours. A paediatrician is called.
questions.q: Which additional drug is most appropriate now?
options: Magnesium sulphate 4 g IV over 20 minutes, then 1 g/h
A second dose of betamethasone immediately
questions.why: Below 32 weeks with birth expected within 24 hours, magnesium sulphate protects the fetal brain and reduces cerebral palsy by about a third. Tocolysis is contraindicated in advanced labour.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 30 weeks is receiving magnesium sulphate before an expected preterm birth. Two hours later she is drowsy, her respiratory rate is 9/min and the patellar reflexes are absent.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Halve the infusion rate and recheck in an hour
Stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate 10%, 10 mL IV
Give a further 2 g bolus of magnesium sulphate
questions.why: Lost reflexes and slow breathing are magnesium toxicity: stop magnesium sulphate and give calcium gluconate 10%, 10 mL IV. Halving the rate is not enough once breathing is depressed.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old at 30 weeks has regular contractions with the cervix 3 cm and intact membranes. Her temperature is 38.5 °C, pulse 112/min, the uterus is tender between contractions and the fetal heart rate is 175/min. Urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Nifedipine and steroids, then reassess after 48 hours
Atosiban infusion until the fever settles
questions.why: Fever, a tender uterus and fetal tachycardia suggest intrauterine infection, which contraindicates tocolysis: give IV antibiotics and deliver. Delaying birth leaves the infected uterus in place.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with type 1 diabetes at 32 weeks has threatened preterm labour and receives dexamethasone 6 mg IM. The next morning her capillary glucose readings are 14–16 mmol/L. She is well and not ketotic.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: No action; glucose will settle in 6 weeks
Repeat the steroid course to complete treatment
Increase her insulin dose with close glucose monitoring
questions.why: Steroids cause maternal hyperglycaemia, so insulin is increased and the course is completed. Stopping steroids loses the fetal lung benefit.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old with epilepsy on carbamazepine presents at 30 weeks in threatened preterm labour. Steroids are planned.
questions.q: How should the dexamethasone be given?
options: The usual dose of 6 mg IM 12-hourly × 4
Half the dose because of seizure risk
questions.why: Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that speeds steroid breakdown, so the dexamethasone dose is doubled. The standard dose would give too little effect.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old at 27 weeks with preterm labour is started on indomethacin because nifedipine is unavailable. The course is planned for no longer than 48 hours.
questions.q: Which fetal complication is the main concern with this drug?
options: Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
questions.why: Indomethacin, a prostaglandin inhibitor, can close the ductus early and reduce liquor, so it is used < 32 weeks for ≤ 48 hours. Neonatal hypoglycaemia is a β-agonist effect.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old had a spontaneous birth at 30 weeks in her last pregnancy. She is now 20 weeks, has no symptoms, and transvaginal scan shows a cervical length of 18 mm with a closed os.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly until 34 weeks
questions.why: A previous preterm birth with a cervix < 25 mm calls for vaginal progesterone (or cerclage). Steroids are given only when birth is expected, from 24 weeks.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old G4P0 has had three losses at 18–20 weeks. Each time she came with painless opening of the cervix and the membranes bulging, with little pain. She is now 8 weeks pregnant with a live fetus.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management in this pregnancy?
options: Serial scans only, with no intervention
questions.why: Three painless mid-trimester losses justify a history-indicated cerclage at 12–14 weeks. A stitch at 24 weeks is too late to prevent the usual loss.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old had a McDonald suture placed at 13 weeks. At 30 weeks she presents with regular painful contractions every 4 minutes, and the cervix is changing on speculum examination despite the stitch.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Give nifedipine and leave the suture in
Perform caesarean section with the suture in place
questions.why: A cerclage is removed at once when labour starts, to avoid the cervix tearing or the uterus rupturing. Leaving it to 37 weeks applies only when there is no labour.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old at 33 weeks is in established preterm labour, cervix 6 cm, membranes intact. No vaginal swab has been taken in this pregnancy and she has no allergy.
questions.q: Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate in labour?
options: No antibiotic, as the membranes are intact
Benzylpenicillin 3 g IV, then 1.8 g 4-hourly until birth
Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
questions.why: Group B streptococcus status unknown in preterm labour needs intrapartum benzylpenicillin. Erythromycin is the preterm prelabour rupture of membranes regimen and co-amoxiclav raises NEC.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 32 weeks in spontaneous preterm labour has been fully dilated for 1 hour with an epidural. The head is at +2 station, occipito-anterior, and her pushing is weak. CTG is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate method of delivery?
questions.why: Below 34 weeks ventouse is avoided because the soft skull bleeds (cephalhaematoma, subgaleal, brain bleeds); forceps are used. Caesarean is not needed with a low occipito-anterior head.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 16 weeks, whose last baby was born at 32 weeks, reports a thin grey vaginal discharge with a fishy smell. The vaginal pH is 5.0 and clue cells are seen on microscopy.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
questions.why: This is bacterial vaginosis, a treatable cause of preterm birth: metronidazole 500 mg BD for 7 days (or clindamycin). Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 at 32 weeks reports a sudden gush of clear fluid 2 hours ago, then a trickle that wets her clothes on standing. She has no pains. Pulse, temperature and fetal heart rate are normal.
questions.q: Which examination should be done first?
questions.why: A sterile speculum shows pooling and allows swabs without carrying bacteria up. Digital vaginal examination is avoided unless she is in labour, as it shortens the time to infection.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 34 weeks reports wetness for a day. Speculum shows a little blood-stained discharge but no pooling, even on coughing, and no fern pattern on the slide. The nitrazine stick turned blue. Ultrasound shows a normal liquor volume.
questions.q: What is the best interpretation?
options: High leak of membranes needing erythromycin
Membranes probably intact; nitrazine is falsely positive from blood
questions.why: Blood, semen and BV make nitrazine falsely positive; no pooling, no ferning and normal liquor favour intact membranes. Nitrazine alone does not confirm rupture.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old para 5 at 35 weeks complains of wet underwear, mainly when she coughs or lifts her children. Speculum shows no pool in the posterior fornix, the fluid smells of urine and nitrazine paper stays yellow. Liquor volume is normal on scan.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Leakage only on coughing, acidic fluid smelling of urine and no pooling mean stress incontinence. A fistula leaks constantly, not with coughing only.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 30 weeks has confirmed rupture of membranes with clear liquor and no contractions. She is afebrile, pulse 82/min, uterus non-tender and CTG normal. Steroids have been started.
questions.q: Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
options: No antibiotic unless she develops fever
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily until delivery
questions.why: Erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days delays labour and reduces infection in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. Triple IV antibiotics are for established chorioamnionitis.

questions.stem: An intern prescribes co-amoxiclav for a 23-year-old with ruptured membranes at 29 weeks because erythromycin is out of stock in the ward.
questions.q: Which neonatal complication is increased by this choice?
questions.why: Co-amoxiclav in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes raises necrotising enterocolitis in the baby, so erythromycin is the drug. RDS is reduced by steroids, not affected by the antibiotic choice.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old at 30 weeks was admitted 2 days ago with ruptured membranes and has had erythromycin and both doses of betamethasone. She now has regular contractions every 4 minutes. She is afebrile and the CTG is normal. Group B streptococcus status is unknown.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Magnesium sulphate and IV benzylpenicillin, and allow labour
questions.why: Tocolysis has no role in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. In labour < 32 weeks give magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection and penicillin for group B streptococcus (preterm, unknown status).

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 31 weeks has been on the ward for 5 days with ruptured membranes. Today her temperature is 38.2 °C, pulse 112/min, the uterus is tender and the liquor is offensive. Fetal heart rate is 170/min. She had her last steroid dose 3 days ago.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: IV ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole, and deliver
Repeat the steroid course and deliver after 48 hours
Caesarean section for infection, without antibiotics
questions.why: This is chorioamnionitis: triple IV antibiotics and delivery at any gestation. Caesarean is only for obstetric reasons; infection itself is not an indication, and antibiotics are not withheld.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old at 29 weeks has ruptured membranes and is on erythromycin. The ward plan is to check her every 4 hours.
questions.q: Which finding is most often the first sign of intrauterine infection?
questions.why: A rising fetal heart rate (> 160/min) on CTG is often the earliest sign of chorioamnionitis, before maternal fever. That is why daily CTG is part of preterm prelabour rupture of membranes care.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 33 weeks has had ruptured membranes for 1 week. She remains well with normal temperature, pulse, CRP and CTG, and the fetus is cephalic and growing normally.
questions.q: When should delivery be planned?
questions.why: With no infection, distress or abruption, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes is delivered at 37 weeks. Earlier delivery is for complications.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 39 weeks had a gush of clear fluid 18 hours ago with no contractions. She is afebrile, the CTG is normal, the head is 2/5 palpable and the group B streptococcus swab taken at 36 weeks was negative.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Offer a choice of induction now or waiting up to 24 hours
Wait for labour for up to 72 hours
questions.why: About 75% labour within 24 hours, so at 18 hours she can choose induction now or wait to 24 hours with observations. Steroids are not given at term.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old para 1 at 40 weeks had clear liquor draining for 26 hours with no contractions. She is afebrile, CTG is normal and the cervix is soft and 3 cm dilated. Group B streptococcus status is unknown.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Dinoprostone 3 mg and repeat in 6 hours
questions.why: No labour by 24 hours means induce, and with a favourable cervix oxytocin is used; rupture of membranes > 24 hours needs group B streptococcus prophylaxis. Prostaglandin is used only if the cervix is unfavourable.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old primigravida at 38+5 weeks presents 3 hours after rupture of membranes with no contractions. The pad shows thick green liquor. She is afebrile and the CTG is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Wait up to 24 hours for spontaneous labour
Send home and review in the morning
questions.why: Meconium is a reason to induce now without the 24 hours wait. Caesarean is not needed while the CTG is normal.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has rupture of membranes confirmed at 21 weeks. Over the next weeks the scan shows almost no liquor around the fetus. She wishes to continue the pregnancy.
questions.q: Which neonatal complication is she most at risk of, specific to this timing?
questions.why: Rupture before about 24 weeks with no liquor stops lung growth, causing pulmonary hypoplasia. Retinopathy and NEC follow prematurity at any gestation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old at 33 weeks with ruptured membranes and a breech presentation is on the antenatal ward. During a routine CTG the fetal heart rate suddenly drops to 70/min and stays low for 3 minutes. She has no pain or bleeding.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Vaginal examination to look for the cord
questions.why: Sudden bradycardia with rupture of membranes and a breech suggests cord prolapse, so feel for the cord at once; if present, caesarean now. Scalp sampling is not possible or useful here.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old primigravida with sure dates, regular cycles and a 12-week scan matching her LMP is now 41+3 weeks. The pregnancy has been low risk, CTG is normal and the deepest pool is 4 cm.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: Low-risk women with sure dates are offered induction at 41+3 weeks, which reduces stillbirth without raising caesarean sections. Waiting to 42 weeks raises perinatal death.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with irregular cycles is 42+1 weeks by her LMP. Her booking scan at 10 weeks measured a crown–rump length that gives a gestation 11 days less than her LMP dates.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate step?
options: Use the LMP: she is post-term and needs induction today
Take the average of the two dates
Repeat the scan today to re-date the pregnancy
Use the scan date: she is 40+4 weeks
questions.why: When an early CRL scan and the LMP differ by more than 5 days, the scan date is used. A late scan must never be used to re-date.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old para 2 booked late at 32 weeks. She is sure of her LMP, has regular 28-day cycles and was not on contraception. Her only scan, at 32 weeks, gave a gestation 3 weeks less than her LMP dates. By LMP she is now 41+4 weeks.
questions.q: Which date should be used to plan her care?
options: The average of LMP and scan dates
questions.why: A third-trimester scan has an error of with or without 3 weeks and cannot re-date a pregnancy; a sure LMP with regular cycles is used. So she is 41+4 and should be offered induction.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old at 41+4 weeks declined induction 1 day ago. Today she says the baby is moving well. CTG is normal but the scan shows a deepest pool of 1.5 cm.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: Low liquor (deepest pool < 2 cm) in a post-date pregnancy is an induce-now trigger even with a normal CTG. Continued monitoring is only for women with normal findings who decline induction of labour.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old at 41+3 weeks with a low-risk pregnancy declines induction after counselling. She asks how the baby will be checked.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate monitoring plan?
options: CTG and deepest-pool scan twice a week
questions.why: If induction is declined, CTG plus deepest pool twice a week with kick counts is advised, and Doppler if the baby is small. Weekly CTG is too infrequent.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old at 40+5 weeks asks for a membrane sweep to avoid formal induction. Her 32-week scan reported the placenta 1.5 cm from the internal os and it has not been rescanned.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate response?
options: Perform the sweep; low placenta is irrelevant at term
Do not sweep; arrange a scan for placental site first
Perform the sweep and give oxytocin
Perform ARM at the same examination
questions.why: A sweep or any digital examination is avoided with a possible low placenta until the site is known. Prostaglandin and artificial rupture of membranes carry the same risk.

questions.stem: A baby is born at 42+3 weeks weighing 3.0 kg. He is long and thin with a scaphoid abdomen and little fat, peeling skin on the palms and soles, long nails, no vernix, and green-stained skin and cord. He looks alert and anxious.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: These are the signs of postmaturity (placental insufficiency) seen in about 20% of post-term babies. The same features at 37 weeks would point to growth restriction instead.

questions.stem: A baby born at 42+2 weeks weighing 4.3 kg is 3 hours old. The midwife finds him shaky (jittery) and feeding poorly. Temperature is 36.6 °C and he is pink and well perfused.
questions.q: Which investigation should be done first?
questions.why: Post-term and big babies are prone to hypoglycaemia, which causes jitteriness and is quick to check and treat. Calcium is a later consideration.

questions.stem: At 42 weeks a baby is born through thick meconium-stained liquor. At birth he cries at once, has good tone and a heart rate of 150/min.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Suction of the mouth and nose on the perineum
Tracheal intubation and suction below the cords
Routine care: dry, keep warm and skin-to-skin
questions.why: A vigorous baby needs only routine care; suction on the perineum or of the trachea is not done. Resuscitation is for a floppy baby.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old para 1 at 42 weeks has labour induced. At 4 cm, artificial rupture of membranes shows thick meconium. The CTG then shows late decelerations with every contraction and reduced variability for 60 minutes.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: Meconium with a pathological CTG in the first stage needs caesarean. Ventouse is not possible at 4 cm.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old unbooked primigravida is 43 weeks by sure dates. Scan shows a fetus with no cranial vault above the orbits and normal liquor volume.
questions.q: Deficiency of which fetal hormone best explains why labour has not started?
questions.why: The fetal hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis triggers labour; with anencephaly (and adrenal hypoplasia) fetal cortisol is low and pregnancy is prolonged. Fetal oxytocin is not the trigger.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old who delivered at 42+2 weeks in her first pregnancy is now 8 weeks pregnant. She asks how likely it is to happen again.
questions.q: What is the approximate risk of another post-term pregnancy?
questions.why: After one post-term pregnancy the recurrence is about 30% (40% after two). 5–10% is the background rate.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old para 3 at 42 weeks with an estimated fetal weight of 4.4 kg is delivering. The head is born but the face turns red, the chin presses back against the perineum and the shoulders do not follow with the next contraction and gentle traction.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: The 'turtle sign' with failure of the shoulders after the head is shoulder dystocia, a risk of the big post-term baby. Deep transverse arrest happens before the head is born.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida at 41+3 weeks with sure dates is admitted for induction. The fetus is alive, cephalic and the CTG normal. Vaginal examination: cervix 2 cm dilated, 2.5 cm long, medium consistency, mid-position, station −2. She has no uterine scar.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate method of induction?
options: Artificial rupture of membranes and oxytocin
Dinoprostone 3 mg tablet in the posterior fornix
questions.why: Modified Bishop = 1+1+1+1+1 = 5, unfavourable, so the cervix is ripened first with dinoprostone for a live fetus. Artificial rupture of membranes + oxytocin is for a score of 8 or more.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old para 2 at 41+4 weeks is examined before induction. The cervix is 4 cm dilated, 0.5 cm long, soft and anterior, with the head at station 0.
questions.q: What is her modified Bishop score and its meaning?
questions.why: Dilatation 3–4 cm = 2, length < 1 cm = 3, station 0 = 2, soft = 2, anterior = 2: total 11, favourable (≥ 8), so artificial rupture of membranes + oxytocin. The maximum score is 13.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old had one lower-segment caesarean for breech 3 years ago. She is now 41+3 weeks, wants a vaginal birth, and the hospital has a theatre on site. The cervix is closed, 3 cm long and firm (Bishop 3). The baby is cephalic.
questions.q: What is the method of choice to ripen the cervix?
options: Foley balloon catheter, then ARM and oxytocin
questions.why: A Foley balloon causes no hyperstimulation and is the choice with a previous scar. Misoprostol must never be used in a scarred uterus with a live fetus.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old para 1 is found to have an intrauterine fetal death at 34 weeks. She is well, with normal clotting. The cervix is closed and firm. She has no uterine scar.
questions.q: Which agent is most appropriate to induce labour?
questions.why: Misoprostol is used for the dead fetus with an unripe cervix (dose by weeks); dinoprostone is kept for the live fetus. Artificial rupture of membranes is avoided in intrauterine fetal death because of infection risk.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida at 41+4 weeks had a dinoprostone 3 mg tablet 2 hours ago. She now has mild irregular tightenings and the cervix is 3 cm dilated. The registrar wants to start oxytocin.
questions.q: When is the earliest that oxytocin should be started?
options: At least 6 hours after the prostaglandin
questions.why: Oxytocin is started at least 6 hours after the last prostaglandin, to avoid hyperstimulation. It can be used once that gap has passed.

questions.stem: A midwife prepares oxytocin for induction: 5 IU in 500 mL normal saline, run through a 20-drop/mL giving set. There is no infusion pump.
questions.q: How many drops per minute give the starting dose of 2 mU/min?
questions.why: 5 IU in 500 mL = 10 mU/mL; with 20 drops/mL each drop/min gives 0.5 mU/min, so 2 mU/min = 4 drops/min. 32 is the maximum in mU/min, not drops.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old is on an oxytocin infusion at 8 mU/min after artificial rupture of membranes. Over the last 30 minutes she has had 4 contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting 50 seconds. CTG is normal and the cervix is progressing.
questions.q: What should be done with the infusion?
options: Increase to the maximum of 32 mU/min
questions.why: Once 3–4 good contractions of 40–60 s come in 10 min, the rate is kept, not increased. Raising it risks tachysystole.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old on oxytocin at 12 mU/min has 6 contractions in 10 minutes. The CTG shows a baseline of 140/min, normal variability and no decelerations.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate action?
options: Increase the rate to complete the first stage
questions.why: Tachysystole (> 5 in 10 min) with a normal fetal heart rate is managed by reducing oxytocin. Terbutaline is added if the fetal heart rate becomes abnormal.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old on oxytocin has 6 contractions in 10 minutes. The fetal heart rate has dropped to 80/min for 5 minutes. The oxytocin has been stopped, she is in the left lateral position and IV fluids are running, but the fetal heart rate is still 80/min.
questions.q: Which drug should be given now?
questions.why: Hyperstimulation with persistent fetal bradycardia is treated with terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously to relax the uterus. If the bradycardia persists, caesarean follows.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old primigravida has had oxytocin running for 18 hours in 3 L of 5% dextrose. She becomes confused and then has a generalised convulsion. Blood pressure is 120/75 mmHg and urine protein is negative.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Long oxytocin (which has antidiuretic action) in large volumes of dextrose causes hyponatraemia and convulsions; saline should be used. Normal blood pressure and no proteinuria make eclampsia unlikely.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old para 4 at 39 weeks is booked for induction for diabetes. The scan shows an AFI of 30 cm and the head is 5/5 palpable and freely mobile above the brim. The registrar plans artificial rupture of membranes as the first step.
questions.q: What is the main risk of artificial rupture of membranes in this woman?
questions.why: With polyhydramnios and a high free head, artificial rupture of membranes carries a high risk of cord prolapse (and abruption). Artificial rupture of membranes should be done only with the head fixed.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old with one previous caesarean is on oxytocin after a Foley balloon induction at 41 weeks. At 7 cm the fetal heart rate suddenly drops to 70/min. She complains of pain over the scar, there is fresh vaginal bleeding, contractions have stopped and the head, which was 2/5, is now 4/5 palpable.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Fetal bradycardia, scar pain, bleeding, loss of contractions and a rising head mean scar rupture: stop oxytocin and do a laparotomy. Abruption does not stop contractions or make the head rise.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old primigravida is seen at 32 weeks. On palpation there is a hard, round, ballotable mass in the fundus and the fetal heart is heard above the umbilicus. She is well with no complications.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure and re-examine with a scan at 36 weeks
questions.why: Breech is common before 36 weeks and most turn by themselves; plan at 36 weeks with a scan. ECV is done at 36 weeks in a primigravida.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks has a scan confirming a frank breech, estimated fetal weight 2.7 kg, normal liquor, fundal posterior placenta and a flexed head. She has no medical problems and the membranes are intact.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Wait for spontaneous labour and allow vaginal breech
questions.why: ECV is offered at 36 weeks in a primigravida with no contraindication; about 40% succeed in primigravidae. Postural methods do not work.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old para 2 at 37 weeks has a breech presentation. The scan shows the placenta covering the internal os. She has had no bleeding.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: Placenta praevia is an absolute contraindication to ECV and needs caesarean anyway. Vaginal delivery is impossible with praevia.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old para 1 at 37 weeks is in the labour ward for external cephalic version. Scan confirms breech with normal liquor and CTG is normal.
questions.q: Which drug should be given before the procedure to improve success?
questions.why: A tocolytic, terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously, relaxes the uterus and raises ECV success. Oxytocin would make the uterus contract.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old RhD-negative woman, not sensitised, has a successful ECV at 37 weeks. The CTG is normal for 30 minutes afterwards.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: No further action as the version succeeded
Anti-D 500 IU IM and a Kleihauer test
questions.why: ECV can cause feto-maternal bleeding, so an RhD-negative woman gets anti-D 500 IU within 72 hours with a Kleihauer. Success of the version does not remove the risk.

questions.stem: Immediately after an ECV at 37 weeks, a 28-year-old has vaginal bleeding of about 100 mL and lower abdominal pain. The fetal heart rate is 80/min and has not recovered after 6 minutes in the left lateral position.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Turn the baby back to breech
questions.why: Bleeding with persistent bradycardia after ECV suggests abruption and needs emergency caesarean. Transient fetal heart rate slowing (about 8%) usually recovers within minutes, but this has not.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks has a frank breech after a failed ECV. Scan shows a flexed head and estimated fetal weight 4.1 kg. Her pelvis seems adequate and she wants to try a vaginal birth.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Assisted vaginal breech delivery, as the breech is frank
Induction of labour now with prostaglandin
Await spontaneous labour and use oxytocin if slow
questions.why: Vaginal breech needs estimated fetal weight 2.5–3.8 kg; a baby over 3.8 kg is delivered by elective caesarean at 39 weeks. A frank breech alone does not make vaginal delivery safe.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old para 2 arrives in labour at 39 weeks. The cervix is 8 cm and a frank breech is felt low in the pelvis. Bedside scan shows estimated fetal weight 3.2 kg and a flexed head. A senior obstetrician skilled in breech delivery and a paediatrician are present.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: Advanced labour with criteria met (frank, 2.5–3.8 kg, flexed head) and skilled staff allows assisted vaginal breech. Total breech extraction is only for the second twin or acute distress at full dilatation.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks presents in early labour, cervix 3 cm. On examination a foot is felt below the buttocks. She has no other problems.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: A footling breech in early labour is delivered by caesarean: high risk of cord prolapse and of the body slipping through a part-dilated cervix. ECV needs a non-labouring woman with intact membranes.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old at 37 weeks with a breech presentation has spontaneous rupture of membranes at home. On arrival the fetal heart rate is 70/min. Vaginal examination finds a foot in the vagina and the cervix 4 cm dilated.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the fetal bradycardia?
questions.why: Footling breech carries the highest risk of cord prolapse (about 15%), and bradycardia straight after rupture of membranes fits it: caesarean now. Head compression gives early decelerations, not a fixed bradycardia.

questions.stem: During an assisted vaginal breech delivery, the body has been born to the umbilicus and the scapulae are visible, but neither arm can be felt in front of the chest; both are extended above the head.
questions.q: Which manoeuvre should be used?
questions.why: Extended arms are delivered by Løvset: rotate the body 180° to bring the posterior arm under the pubis, then reverse. Pinard is for extended legs.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old primigravida at 39 weeks with a frank breech chose a vaginal birth. She has been 5 cm dilated for 4 hours with 2 weak contractions in 10 minutes. CTG is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Artificial rupture of membranes and oxytocin
questions.why: Slow progress in breech labour is managed by caesarean, not oxytocin, because forcing the body through may trap the head. Augmentation is used for slow cephalic labour.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old para 1 in the second stage of a breech labour at 39 weeks has thick fresh meconium draining. The fetal heart rate is 140/min with normal variability and accelerations, and the buttocks are distending the perineum.
questions.q: What is the best interpretation and management?
options: Often normal in breech from compression of the fetal abdomen; continue
questions.why: Fresh meconium in a breech second stage is usually from compression of the fetal abdomen and, with a normal CTG, is not fetal distress. In a cephalic labour thick meconium is distress until proved otherwise.

questions.stem: A girl is born by assisted vaginal breech at 39 weeks. She is well, with good tone, and weighs 3.3 kg.
questions.q: Which screening is most important for this baby because of the presentation?
options: Hip examination at birth and hip ultrasound at 6 weeks
questions.why: Breech is a risk factor for developmental dysplasia of the hip: Ortolani and Barlow at birth and hip ultrasound at 6 weeks. The other tests are not indicated by breech alone.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old para 3 at 36 weeks has a breech presentation for the third pregnancy in a row. Each previous baby was a normal size at term and had no anomaly.
questions.q: What is the most likely underlying cause?
options: A uterine anomaly such as a septate or bicornuate uterus
questions.why: Recurrent breech in pregnancy after pregnancy points to a uterine shape problem. Prematurity is the commonest association overall but does not explain repeated term breech babies.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks is 6 cm dilated and complains mainly of severe backache. She wants to push although the cervix is not fully dilated. The lower abdomen looks flat, limbs are felt in front and the fetal heart rate is heard in the flank. On vaginal examination the anterior fontanelle is easily felt near the front of the pelvis.
questions.q: What is the most likely fetal position?
options: Direct occipito-anterior with deflexion of the head
questions.why: Backache, early urge to push, a flat lower abdomen and an anterior fontanelle felt in front are the picture of occipito-posterior position. In occipito-anterior the posterior fontanelle is felt in front.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida without epidural has been fully dilated for 2.5 hours with good contractions. The head is 0/5 palpable, at the level of the ischial spines with the sagittal suture in the transverse diameter, and has not descended for 1 hour. There is no gross moulding and the fetal heart rate is normal. An experienced obstetrician is present.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Non-rotational forceps in the labour room
Oxytocin and continue pushing for 1 more hour
Rotational delivery in theatre (manual rotation, Kielland forceps or ventouse)
questions.why: This is deep transverse arrest: the head needs rotation by a skilled operator, with caesarean if it fails. Non-rotational forceps cannot be applied correctly to a transverse head.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old para 1 has been pushing for 1 hour. The head is crowning, and the posterior fontanelle is felt at the back, near the sacrum. The fetal heart rate is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Deliver the head by flexion with a generous episiotomy
questions.why: With the occiput at the sacrum (face to pubis) and the head crowning, delivery is by flexion with a generous episiotomy. Rotation is not needed once the head is this low.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old para 2 at 40 weeks is 7 cm dilated. On vaginal examination the doctor feels a mouth with hard gums, the nose and malar bones; the chin is felt behind the symphysis pubis. Contractions are good and the cervix has dilated 2 cm in the last 2 hours. CTG is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Apply a fetal scalp electrode to the face
questions.why: A mento-anterior face with good progress can deliver vaginally (born by flexion under the pubis). Scalp electrodes and ventouse must never be used on the face.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old para 3 has been fully dilated for 2 hours with good contractions. Vaginal examination shows the mouth, nose and malar bones, with the chin felt toward the sacrum. There has been no descent in the last hour.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: A persistent mento-posterior face cannot deliver because the neck is already fully extended, so caesarean is needed. Forceps are allowed only for mento-anterior.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old para 2 has a face presentation with the chin under the symphysis at +2 station. She has been fully dilated for 1.5 hours and is exhausted with poor pushing. CTG is normal.
questions.q: Which method of delivery is most appropriate?
questions.why: Low forceps may be used for a mento-anterior face at a low station; ventouse is never used on the face. Caesarean is not needed with a low mento-anterior face.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old at 36 weeks has an ultrasound for a large uterus. It shows a fully extended fetal head with the face presenting and polyhydramnios.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Detailed anomaly scan of the fetal head and neck
questions.why: Face presentation with polyhydramnios needs a look for a cause: anencephaly or a neck mass (goitre, cystic hygroma). Face is not an indication for caesarean by itself.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old para 1 at 40 weeks is fully dilated. Abdominally the head is 3/5 palpable. On vaginal examination the anterior fontanelle, the orbital ridges and the root of the nose are felt; no mouth or chin can be felt. The estimated fetal weight is 3.4 kg.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: This is brow presentation (mento-vertical 13.5 cm) at term: if it persists the labour obstructs, so caesarean. Forceps, ventouse and oxytocin are all contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old para 3 is in early labour at 35 weeks with the cervix 3 cm. On vaginal examination the anterior fontanelle and orbital ridges are felt but no chin. Scan shows estimated fetal weight 2.1 kg. Contractions are good and the CTG is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Observe for a short time, as the head may flex or extend
Artificial rupture of membranes and forceps
questions.why: In early labour a brow, especially with a small fetus, may convert to vertex or face, so watch for a short time. Caesarean is for a brow that persists.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old para 5 at 37 weeks has a wide uterus with a fundal height less than her dates, an empty pelvis on palpation and the fetal head in her right flank. She is not in labour, membranes are intact and the placenta is fundal on scan.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Admit and attempt external cephalic version
questions.why: This is a transverse lie at 37 weeks in a multipara: admit (so caesarean is ready if membranes rupture) and try ECV. Induction or artificial rupture of membranes with a transverse lie is contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old para 6 arrives after 24 hours of labour at home. The fetal arm is hanging out of the vagina, the uterus is tightly moulded around the fetus, there is a ridge across the lower abdomen and no fetal heart is heard on scan.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Internal podalic version and breech extraction
Destructive operation by the junior on duty
questions.why: A neglected shoulder presentation is delivered by caesarean even with a dead fetus; manipulation or traction ruptures the thin lower segment. IPV is only for a second twin with intact membranes.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old para 2 delivers the first twin, cephalic, at 37 weeks. On examination the second twin lies transverse with intact membranes and a normal heart rate. The cervix stays fully dilated and an experienced obstetrician is present.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management of the second twin?
options: Oxytocin and wait for spontaneous delivery
Internal podalic version and breech extraction
Give the third-stage oxytocin and wait
questions.why: A transverse second twin with intact membranes can be turned by ECV or internal podalic version and delivered by breech extraction. Giving a third-stage uterotonic before the second twin is born would trap it.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old para 3 is 7 cm dilated with good contractions. On vaginal examination a small hand is felt beside the head. The head is descending well and the CTG is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Push the hand up above the head
Leave the hand and continue labour
questions.why: A compound presentation with good progress is left alone: the hand usually slips back as the head descends. Pulling the hand is wrong; caesarean is only for arrest or cord prolapse.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old para 5 at 38 weeks has a lie that has changed between cephalic, oblique and transverse at each visit since 36 weeks. She is admitted to the antenatal ward.
questions.q: What is the main danger if her membranes rupture?
questions.why: An unstable lie leaves the pelvis empty, so rupture of membranes can sweep the cord down: cord prolapse. That is why she is admitted from 37 weeks.

questions.theme: Fetal heart rate patterns in labour
questions.lead: For each CTG description choose the most likely pattern. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: A 29-year-old with pre-eclampsia and a small baby at 38 weeks is in labour at 5 cm. With every contraction the fetal heart rate falls by 20 bpm, the lowest point coming 30 seconds after the peak of the contraction, slowly returning after it ends.
items.why: A dip that lags behind the peak of each contraction reflects placental insufficiency.

items.stem: A 25-year-old at 40 weeks has had ruptured membranes for 12 hours and the scan before labour showed reduced liquor. The fetal heart rate shows sudden V-shaped drops of 40–60 bpm that vary in shape and timing with the contractions and recover quickly.
items.why: Abrupt dips of changing shape and timing are cord compression, the commonest deceleration in labour.

items.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 9 cm has a baseline of 130/min with good variability. Each contraction is matched by a smooth fall of 20 bpm that starts with the contraction, is lowest at its peak and recovers as it ends.
items.why: Dips that mirror the contraction are from head compression and are normal.

items.stem: A 30-year-old at 39 weeks, after a dose of pethidine 2 hours ago, has a baseline of 168/min that has stayed the same for 40 minutes, with normal variability and no decelerations. Her temperature is 38.4 °C.
items.why: A baseline above 160/min with maternal fever points to infection; pethidine reduces variability rather than raising the baseline.

questions.theme: Abdominal pain and fluid loss before 37 weeks
questions.lead: For each patient choose the most likely diagnosis. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: A 23-year-old at 28 weeks has lower abdominal tightenings, a temperature of 38.9 °C, rigors, burning on passing urine and right loin tenderness. The cervix is closed and long.
items.why: Fever, dysuria and loin tenderness with a closed cervix point to pyelonephritis, a known trigger of preterm labour.

items.stem: A 30-year-old at 20 weeks with a known 7 cm intramural fibroid has severe pain localised over the mass, which is tender, with a temperature of 37.8 °C. The cervix is closed and the fetus is well.
items.why: Localised pain and tenderness over a known fibroid with low fever in mid-pregnancy is red degeneration.

items.stem: A 26-year-old at 31 weeks has painful contractions every 4 minutes. The cervix was 1 cm on admission and is now 3 cm and fully effaced, with intact membranes.
items.why: Regular contractions with progressive dilatation between 24 and 37 weeks is established preterm labour.

items.stem: A 28-year-old at 34 weeks has had watery loss for 2 days with no contractions. Speculum shows a pool of clear fluid in the posterior fornix, and dried fluid on a slide shows a fern pattern.
items.why: Pooling and ferning confirm ruptured membranes; with no contractions before 37 weeks this is preterm prelabour rupture of membranes.

questions.theme: Management of women at or after term
options: Artificial rupture of membranes and oxytocin
questions.lead: For each patient choose the most appropriate next step. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 40+3 weeks with a low-risk pregnancy asks if anything can be done to reduce her chance of needing a formal induction. The placenta is fundal and the membranes are intact.
items.why: A sweep at 40–41 weeks releases local prostaglandins and about 30% labour within 7 days.

items.stem: A 33-year-old para 3 at 41+3 weeks is admitted for induction. The cervix is 3 cm, 1 cm long, soft and anterior, and the head is fixed at station −1. CTG is normal.
items.why: The Bishop score is favourable (≥ 8) and the head is fixed, so artificial rupture of membranes followed by oxytocin is used.

items.stem: A 30-year-old at 41+2 weeks had a classical caesarean section at 28 weeks for severe pre-eclampsia. She asks about induction.
items.why: A classical scar is a contraindication to induction because of rupture risk; she needs an elective caesarean.

questions.theme: Manoeuvres in assisted vaginal breech delivery
questions.lead: For each situation choose the most appropriate manoeuvre. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: A frank breech is being delivered. The buttocks and trunk are born but the legs remain extended alongside the body, splinting it.
items.why: Pressing the popliteal fossa flexes the knee and lets the foot be delivered.

items.stem: The body and arms are born and the baby hangs until the nape of the neck is seen under the symphysis. The head now needs delivery.
items.why: The Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit manoeuvre, with jaw flexion and shoulder traction, is the first choice for the aftercoming head.

items.stem: The aftercoming head is in the pelvis but does not deliver after a correct Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit attempt. The body is held up in a towel.
items.why: Forceps on the aftercoming head are used when the Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit manoeuvre fails.

items.stem: A 28-week breech delivers rapidly; the body and arms are out but the head is trapped by a cervix that is only 7 cm dilated.
items.why: Incisions at 2 and 10 o'clock release a head trapped in an incompletely dilated cervix, then the Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit manoeuvre.

questions.theme: Presenting diameters of the fetal head
questions.lead: For each vaginal examination finding choose the presenting diameter. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: Primigravida in normal labour: the small Y-shaped posterior fontanelle is felt in the centre of the cervix toward the front, and the anterior fontanelle cannot be reached.
items.why: A well-flexed vertex in occipito-anterior presents the smallest diameter.

items.stem: Multipara at 7 cm: mouth with gums, nose and both malar bones are felt, the head fully extended, chin behind the pubis.
items.why: A fully extended face presents the submento-bregmatic diameter, which allows vaginal birth when mento-anterior.

items.stem: Primigravida with severe backache at 6 cm: the diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle is felt easily at the front of the pelvis; the head is deflexed.
items.why: A deflexed occipito-posterior head presents the occipito-frontal diameter, so labour is slow.

items.stem: Multipara fully dilated, head high: anterior fontanelle, orbital ridges and root of the nose are felt, with no chin.
items.why: Brow presents the largest diameter, which cannot pass a normal pelvis at term.

questions.stem: A para 4 woman at 40 weeks with known polyhydramnios is in labour at 6 cm. The membranes rupture with a large gush, and within a minute the fetal heart rate falls to 70 bpm and remains there. She has no pain other than her contractions, there is no bleeding and the liquor is clear.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Rupture of the membranes followed by sudden bradycardia, in a well mother with clear liquor, is the classic picture of cord prolapse. Vasa praevia also follows rupture of membranes, but with fresh bleeding.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman at 39 weeks is 5 cm dilated. Artificial rupture of membranes is performed for slow progress; two minutes later the fetal heart rate is 80 bpm. On vaginal examination a pulsating loop of cord lies in the vagina below the head.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Call for help and push the head up with two fingers, keeping it up
Try to push the cord back into the uterus above the head
Start oxytocin to speed up full dilatation
Get an ultrasound scan to confirm the fetal heart
Transfer her to theatre lying on her back
questions.why: Calling for help and elevating the presenting part relieve the pressure on the cord and gain time for delivery. Replacing the cord causes spasm and is never attempted.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman at 38 weeks is in early labour at 4 cm with intact membranes. On vaginal examination a soft, pulsating cord is felt through the membranes in front of the head. The CTG is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Allow labour to continue with continuous CTG
Knee-chest position and await full dilatation
questions.why: Cord presentation in labour is managed by caesarean section, because the cord prolapses as soon as the membranes rupture. Artificial rupture of membranes is contraindicated.

questions.stem: A primigravida at 40 weeks has been fully dilated for 50 minutes, with the vertex occipito-anterior at station +2. The membranes rupture and the fetal heart rate falls to 90 bpm. A pulsating loop of cord is felt beside the head.
questions.q: What is the best mode of delivery?
options: Forceps or ventouse delivery in the room
Push the head up and wait for spontaneous delivery
Fill the bladder and transfer to theatre
Terbutaline and repeat CTG in 20 minutes
questions.why: At full dilatation with a low head, instrumental delivery is quicker than caesarean section. Caesarean section is chosen when the head is high or the lie is not cephalic.

questions.stem: A para 5 woman at 39 weeks is fully dilated. The head is 4/5 palpable above the pelvic brim. After spontaneous rupture of membranes a pulsating cord is seen at the vulva and the fetal heart rate is 85 bpm.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate mode of delivery?
options: Ventouse delivery in the labour room
Forceps delivery in the labour room
Encourage pushing and await spontaneous birth
Internal podalic version and breech extraction
Caesarean section while the part is held up
questions.why: Even at full dilatation, a high, unengaged head cannot be delivered safely vaginally, so caesarean section is required. Ventouse delivery requires an engaged head.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman at 37 weeks arrives from a village 3 hours after her membranes ruptured. A loop of cord is hanging out of the vulva; it is cold and not pulsating. Bedside ultrasound shows no fetal heart activity.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan for delivery?
options: Vaginal delivery, awaiting labour or inducing
Elevate the head and fill the bladder
questions.why: Once fetal death is confirmed there is no fetal indication for caesarean section, so she delivers vaginally. Caesarean section would only add maternal risk.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman at 38 weeks is 3 cm dilated. Cord prolapse is found after spontaneous rupture of membranes. The cord is limp and no pulsation is felt, but bedside ultrasound shows a fetal heart rate of 90 bpm.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Vaginal delivery, as the cord is not pulsating
Category 1 caesarean section, keeping the part elevated
questions.why: A cord without pulsation may be in spasm; fetal heart activity on ultrasound shows that the fetus is alive. A live fetus with a cervix that is not fully dilated requires a category 1 caesarean section.

questions.stem: A para 4 woman at 38 weeks is in a rural health centre. Cord prolapse is found at 4 cm with a pulsating cord. The nearest operating theatre is 90 minutes away by ambulance, and the midwife cannot keep her hand in the vagina for the whole journey.
questions.q: Which measure is best for the journey?
options: Fill the bladder with 500 mL warm saline, clamp the catheter, and transfer in exaggerated left Sims position
Knee-chest position on the ambulance floor for the whole journey
Push the cord back into the uterus and transfer supine
Oxytocin infusion to speed up labour during transfer
Wrap the cord in a dry towel and transfer sitting up
questions.why: A full bladder lifts the presenting part off the cord, and the left Sims position is safe in a moving vehicle. The knee–chest position is unsafe in an ambulance.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman at 39 weeks has cord prolapse at 5 cm. A Foley catheter was used to fill her bladder before transfer. She is now on the operating table under general anaesthesia and the surgeon has opened the abdomen.
questions.q: What must be done before the uterine incision?
options: Unclamp the catheter and empty the bladder
Turn her to the knee-chest position
Push the presenting part down into the pelvis
questions.why: The full bladder lies in front of the lower uterine segment and is at risk of injury, so it is emptied before the uterus is opened.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman at 39 weeks is 4 cm dilated. A pulsating loop of cord is in the vagina and the presenting part is being held up. The theatre will be ready in 15 minutes. She is contracting strongly every 2 minutes, and the fetal heart rate falls to 80 bpm with each contraction.
questions.q: Which drug is most appropriate now?
questions.why: Subcutaneous terbutaline acts within minutes and stops the contractions pressing the head onto the cord. Oral nifedipine acts too slowly for an emergency.

questions.stem: Five women with intact membranes are reviewed in the antenatal clinic.
questions.q: Which woman has the highest risk of cord prolapse if her membranes rupture?
questions.why: Footling breech carries a risk of about 15%, compared with about 5% for complete breech and 0.5% for frank breech. An engaged head fills the pelvis and protects the cord.

questions.stem: A para 6 woman at 38 weeks has polyhydramnios. The lie was transverse, then oblique, then cephalic at three successive visits. Today it is cephalic with a high head, and induction of labour is planned.
questions.q: What is the safest method of rupturing her membranes?
options: Routine ARM in the labour room once the cervix is 2 cm
ARM after starting a high-dose oxytocin infusion
Controlled ARM in theatre with the head held at the brim and liquor let out slowly
ARM with the patient sitting upright to bring the head down
No ARM; wait for spontaneous rupture at home
questions.why: With polyhydramnios and a high head, controlled artificial rupture of membranes in theatre releases the liquor slowly and allows immediate caesarean section if the cord prolapses.

questions.stem: A para 5 woman is 37 weeks pregnant. At the last three visits the fetus was transverse, breech and then cephalic. She lives two hours from the hospital.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice now?
options: Return in 2 weeks for another scan
Book an elective caesarean section at 42 weeks
Perform ARM today to fix the lie
Deliver at home with a trained midwife
questions.why: A woman with an unstable lie is admitted from 37 weeks, because cord prolapse after rupture of membranes at home would be fatal for the baby. Artificial rupture of membranes with a high, changing lie causes cord prolapse.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 24 weeks is now in labour at 6 cm, and a pulsating loop of cord is felt in the vagina. The fetal heart rate is 140 bpm on Doppler.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Fill the bladder and give terbutaline to delay delivery
Push the cord back and give steroids
Manage as a miscarriage: vaginal delivery, no caesarean
questions.why: Before 26 weeks, cord prolapse is managed as a miscarriage and delivery is vaginal. Caesarean section adds maternal risk when the baby has very little chance of survival.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman delivered 10 minutes ago; the intern pulled hard on the cord before any sign of placental separation. She now has severe lower abdominal pain and feels faint. Her pulse is 54/min, blood pressure 75/40 mmHg and blood loss about 400 mL. The fundus cannot be felt on abdominal palpation.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Pain in the third stage with shock out of proportion to the blood loss, bradycardia and an absent fundus are the classic signs of uterine inversion. Atony gives a soft fundus that is easily palpable.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is in shock a few minutes after delivery. There is a dark-red, rounded mass at the introitus with the placenta still attached to it, and no fundus is palpable abdominally. Help has been called and two cannulae are in place.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Peel the placenta off the mass first, then push it back
Start an oxytocin infusion before any replacement
Push the fundus back up through the cervix with the placenta left on
Get an ultrasound to confirm the findings
Take her to theatre for laparotomy
questions.why: The uterus is replaced immediately with the placenta left in place. Removing the placenta first exposes the placental bed and causes very heavy bleeding.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after delivery, the uterus of a para 4 woman is inverted into the vagina. Two attempts at manual replacement have failed because a tight cervical ring does not allow the fundus through. There is no sign of a tear.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ergometrine 0.5 mg IM to stop the bleeding
Terbutaline 0.25 mg SC (or volatile GA) to relax the ring, then try manual replacement again
Oxytocin 40 IU infusion and try again
Pack the vagina and wait 6 hours
questions.why: A tight ring is relaxed with a tocolytic or a volatile anaesthetic before replacement is attempted again. Oxytocic drugs tighten the ring and are withheld until after replacement.

questions.stem: In a para 2 woman, an inverted uterus has been replaced manually after terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously. The placenta is still attached and the doctor's fist is inside the fundus.
questions.q: Which drug should be started now?
options: Oxytocin 40 IU in 500 mL over 4 hours, stopping the tocolytic
A second dose of terbutaline 0.25 mg SC
Magnesium sulphate 4 g IV over 15 minutes
questions.why: Once the uterus has been replaced, the tocolytic is stopped and oxytocin is given to contract the uterus, hold it in place and control bleeding.

questions.stem: In a para 3 woman the inverted uterus reaches the vulva. Manual replacement has failed despite terbutaline. The team plans to run warm saline rapidly into the vagina while sealing the labia with a silicone ventouse cup.
questions.q: What must be excluded before this method is used?
questions.why: Hydrostatic (O'Sullivan) replacement requires an intact genital tract; if there is a rupture the saline escapes into the peritoneal cavity and the method fails.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes after delivery a para 2 woman has heavy bleeding and pain. The fundus is not palpable abdominally. On vaginal examination a soft, purple mass has passed through the cervix and lies in the vagina, but it does not reach the vulva.
questions.q: Which degree of inversion is this?
questions.why: In second-degree inversion the fundus has passed through the cervix but remains in the vagina. In third-degree inversion it reaches or passes the vulva.

questions.stem: Six weeks after a home delivery, a para 4 woman has irregular bleeding, an offensive discharge and a haemoglobin of 7 g/dL. Speculum examination shows a red mass in the vagina; no stalk can be felt around it. On bimanual examination there is no fundus, only a cup-shaped depression at the top.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: An absent fundus with a cup-shaped depression and a mass in the vagina indicate chronic inversion. A fibroid polyp has a stalk, and a normal fundus is palpable above it.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman has just delivered. She has severe pain and a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg. No fundus is palpable abdominally and a purple mass lies at the introitus. The house officer wishes to arrange an ultrasound scan before any treatment.
questions.q: What is the best advice?
options: No scan: replace the uterus now and send bloods at the same time
MRI pelvis to confirm the degree
questions.why: Acute inversion is a clinical diagnosis, and with every minute the cervical ring tightens. Four to six units of blood are cross-matched at the same time. Ultrasound is reserved for unclear subacute or chronic cases.

questions.stem: Five minutes after delivery a para 3 woman suddenly becomes pale and clammy. Her pulse is 50/min and blood pressure 70/40 mmHg, with a blood loss of only 300 mL. No fundus is palpable and a red mass is seen in the vagina.
questions.q: What best explains her bradycardia?
options: Side effect of oxytocin given in the third stage
Vagal stimulation from traction on the tubes, ovaries and peritoneum
Complete heart block from pre-existing disease
questions.why: Traction on the structures drawn into the ring triggers neurogenic shock with bradycardia. Blood loss alone causes tachycardia.

questions.stem: Midwives are being taught how to manage the third stage of labour after oxytocin 10 IU IM.
questions.q: Which practice best prevents uterine inversion?
options: Firm cord traction straight after the baby is born
Controlled cord traction only after signs of separation, with suprapubic counter-pressure
Fundal pressure (Credé) to expel the placenta
Early manual removal while the uterus is still soft
Waiting with the mother upright and pulling on the cord
questions.why: Waiting for the signs of separation and applying suprapubic counter-pressure prevent the fundus from being pulled down. Traction before separation is the commonest cause of inversion.

questions.stem: A para 4 woman books at 10 weeks. At her last delivery at home, the uterus inverted after the cord was pulled and was replaced in hospital.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan for this delivery?
options: Home birth with a physiological third stage
Hospital delivery with a skilled attendant, active third stage, IV line and cross-matched blood ready
questions.why: Inversion can recur, so she should deliver in hospital with active management of the third stage and resuscitation facilities ready. Caesarean section is not indicated for this reason.

questions.stem: Five days after a home delivery, a para 3 woman is brought with a fever of 38.7 °C, offensive discharge and a haemoglobin of 8 g/dL. A swollen red mass fills the vagina; the fundus is not palpable and the cervical ring is tight and oedematous.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate Johnson manoeuvre in the ward without anaesthesia
Fluids, blood and antibiotics, then replacement under GA, usually at laparotomy
O'Sullivan hydrostatic method in the ward
Discharge on oral antibiotics and review in 4 weeks
questions.why: In subacute inversion the ring is fixed and the uterus is oedematous and infected, so manual replacement rarely succeeds. Shock and infection are treated first, and the uterus is then replaced under general anaesthesia, often by the Huntington or Haultain procedure.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman delivers in a village with a trained midwife. Immediately after forceful cord traction she collapses, and a red mass appears at the vulva with the placenta attached. One immediate attempt at replacement has failed. The hospital is 2 hours away.
questions.q: What should the midwife do next?
options: Remove the placenta and transfer sitting up
Keep pushing for 30 minutes before calling for transport
Cover the uterus with a warm wet towel, start IV fluids and transfer lying flat with the placenta left on
Pack the vagina tightly with dry gauze and wait
questions.why: In the community one early attempt at replacement is made; if it fails, the uterus is protected, the woman is resuscitated and she is transferred lying flat with the placenta attached. Removing the placenta causes massive bleeding.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old para 5 woman at 39 weeks is on an oxytocin infusion for induction of labour. Ten minutes after artificial rupture of membranes at 6 cm she says that something is wrong, becomes breathless and cyanosed, and has a convulsion. Her oxygen saturation is 78% and blood pressure 70/30 mmHg. An hour later blood continues to ooze from her cannula sites.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Sudden hypoxia and collapse around rupture of the membranes, followed by DIC, is the classic picture of amniotic fluid embolism. Pulmonary embolism rarely causes early DIC and usually occurs after delivery.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman in labour at 7 cm suddenly becomes breathless and agitated. She is cyanosed, with an oxygen saturation of 80%, pulse 130/min and blood pressure 75/40 mmHg. She is still breathing and has a pulse. Help has been called.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Move her to theatre for immediate caesarean section
Give 3 L of crystalloid as fast as possible
Oxygen 15 L/min, airway support and left uterine displacement
Send a clotting screen and wait for the results
questions.why: Oxygen and displacement of the uterus off the inferior vena cava maintain life in the first minutes. Large volumes of fluid cause pulmonary oedema when the right heart is failing.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman at 36 weeks collapses in labour after sudden breathlessness and is now in cardiac arrest. CPR at 30:2 with left uterine displacement has continued for 4 minutes with no cardiac output.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Transfer her to theatre for caesarean section
Continue CPR for another 20 minutes before any delivery
Wait for consent from her husband
Ventouse delivery through the partly dilated cervix
Perimortem caesarean section where she lies, with CPR continuing
questions.why: From 20 weeks, perimortem caesarean section is started at 4 minutes and the baby should be delivered by 5 minutes. Transfer wastes time and interrupts CPR.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman at 16 weeks has a cardiac arrest during surgical evacuation for a missed miscarriage. CPR has been in progress for 4 minutes.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Continue CPR; a perimortem uterine evacuation is not indicated
Immediate hysterotomy to empty the uterus
Turn her into a full left lateral position and stop compressions
Stop CPR as the outcome is hopeless
questions.why: Before 20 weeks the uterus is too small to compress the inferior vena cava, so emptying it does not improve CPR. The 4-minute rule applies only from 20 weeks.

questions.stem: A consultant teaches the team why the baby must be delivered within 5 minutes during a maternal cardiac arrest at 34 weeks.
questions.q: What is the main reason for this delivery?
options: The baby has the best chance if delivered at 5 minutes
It removes the source of the amniotic fluid
Emptying the uterus relieves IVC and aortic compression so that CPR works
It stops bleeding from the placental bed
It allows a hysterectomy to be done at the same time
questions.why: Perimortem caesarean section is performed mainly for the mother: venous return increases and chest compressions become effective. Fetal survival is a secondary benefit.

questions.stem: A para 4 woman survived a sudden collapse in labour and was delivered by caesarean section. She is now bleeding from the wound and cannula sites. Her platelet count is 90 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen 1.2 g/L and prothrombin time prolonged. FFP 15 mL/kg is being given.
questions.q: Which product should be added?
questions.why: A fibrinogen level below 2 g/L is the indication for cryoprecipitate. Platelets are given when the count is below 50 × 10⁹/L.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman collapsed with cyanosis during labour in a rural hospital that has no laboratory. She has now delivered and is bleeding from the uterus and puncture sites.
questions.q: Which bedside test best demonstrates a clotting failure?
options: Bedside clot test: blood in a plain tube does not clot in 7–10 minutes
questions.why: The bedside clotting test is quick and reliable: failure to form a clot within 7–10 minutes indicates DIC. Blood products are given without waiting for laboratory results.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman is intubated and receiving oxygen after a sudden collapse in labour. After a careful 1 L fluid bolus her blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg, the JVP is raised and echocardiography shows a dilated right ventricle.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give another 2 L of crystalloid quickly
Start a vasopressor such as noradrenaline or phenylephrine
questions.why: Hypotension after fluids with a failing right heart requires a vasopressor, with or without an inotrope. Further fluid worsens right heart failure and pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman in labour at 5 cm, with membranes ruptured for 20 hours, is given ampicillin 2 g IV. Ten minutes later she is breathless, with wheeze, urticaria and swollen lips. Her blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate drug?
questions.why: Collapse with a rash and wheeze immediately after a drug is anaphylaxis, and intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line treatment. Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts only.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman is in labour with an epidural. Two minutes after a top-up she reports tingling around the mouth and ringing in the ears, and then has a convulsion. Her blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg.
questions.q: Besides airway support and stopping the injection, what specific treatment is needed?
questions.why: Perioral tingling and tinnitus after an epidural top-up suggest local anaesthetic toxicity, which is treated with 20% lipid emulsion. Magnesium sulphate is used for an eclamptic convulsion.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman died 1 hour after a sudden collapse with cyanosis and bleeding during labour. The family agrees to a post-mortem.
questions.q: Which finding gives the definitive diagnosis?
options: Fetal squames and debris in the pulmonary vessels at post-mortem
Fetal squames in blood taken from a pulmonary artery catheter before death
A very high D-dimer before death
Bilateral shadows on the last chest X-ray
A dilated right ventricle on echo before death
questions.why: Only fetal squames in the pulmonary vessels at post-mortem examination are diagnostic. Squames in blood from a pulmonary artery catheter in a living woman are supportive only, because they are also found in normal women.

questions.stem: On day 5 after an emergency caesarean section, a para 2 woman has sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Her left calf is swollen. Her oxygen saturation is 90%, pulse 115/min and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. There is no bleeding and the clotting screen is normal.
questions.q: Which investigation is most appropriate?
questions.why: Postnatal pleuritic pain with a swollen calf and no early DIC suggests pulmonary embolism, which is confirmed by CT pulmonary angiography and treated with heparin.

questions.stem: A para 4 woman had a sudden collapse at delivery and is now stable with intensive care support; FFP and cryoprecipitate have been given. The uterus is soft and bleeding continues despite an oxytocin infusion of 40 IU in 500 mL. She does not have asthma.
questions.q: Which drug is most appropriate next?
questions.why: For atony that persists after oxytocin, carboprost 250 µg IM is the next uterotonic. Terbutaline relaxes the uterus and would increase the bleeding.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is in a rural hospital that has no blood components. After a sudden collapse with cyanosis in labour she is delivered, but she bleeds from multiple sites and her blood does not clot.
questions.q: Which is the best practical replacement in this setting?
options: Fresh whole blood from relatives donated as early as possible
Wait for transfer before giving any blood
questions.why: Fresh whole blood provides red cells, clotting factors and platelets when components are not available. Large volumes of crystalloid dilute the clotting factors and cause pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman survived a sudden collapse with cyanosis and DIC in labour. Before discharge she asks about her next pregnancy.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Recurrence is rare; deliver in a hospital with an ICU
Recurrence is about 50%; avoid any further pregnancy
Elective caesarean at 37 weeks prevents it
Low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks prevents it
Avoid ARM and oxytocin and she is fully protected
questions.why: Recurrence is rare, so a further pregnancy is not contraindicated, but she should deliver where intensive care support is available. Amniotic fluid embolism cannot be prevented by caesarean section or drugs.

questions.stem: A primigravida at 41 weeks has gestational diabetes treated with insulin. After a 3-hour second stage the head delivers slowly and then retracts tightly against the perineum. Restitution does not occur, and gentle downward traction with the next contraction fails.
questions.q: After calling for help, what is the first manoeuvre?
questions.why: The McRoberts manoeuvre (hips hyperflexed onto the abdomen) is the first manoeuvre; with suprapubic pressure it is successful in about 80% of cases. Episiotomy only provides room for the hands and does not release the shoulder.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman at 40 weeks has an estimated fetal weight of 4.2 kg. The head has delivered but the shoulders are impacted. Help has arrived, she is lying flat with her thighs flexed onto her abdomen, and routine traction has failed.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Suprapubic pressure from the side of the fetal back
Stronger downward traction on the head
questions.why: The McRoberts manoeuvre is followed by suprapubic pressure (Rubin I) on the back of the anterior shoulder. Fundal pressure impacts the shoulder further against the symphysis pubis.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is 41 weeks pregnant. The shoulders are impacted after delivery of the head. The McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure have each been tried for 60 seconds without success. The baby is alive and the theatre is not yet ready.
questions.q: Which manoeuvre is the best next choice?
questions.why: After the McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure, the internal manoeuvres follow; delivery of the posterior arm reduces the width of the shoulders. The Zavanelli manoeuvre and symphysiotomy are last resorts.

questions.stem: In a para 2 woman the shoulders do not follow after delivery of the head. One midwife flexes the woman's hips, a doctor applies suprapubic pressure, a student pushes on the fundus and another doctor performs an episiotomy.
questions.q: Which action is most likely to cause harm?
options: Flexing the hips onto the abdomen
