questions.why: Fundal pressure impacts the shoulder further and can cause uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury, so it is never used.

questions.stem: A midwife asks why flexing the mother's thighs onto her abdomen helps when the shoulders are stuck after the head.
questions.q: What is the main mechanism?
options: It widens the pelvic inlet by 3 cm
It turns the shoulders into the transverse diameter
It increases the force of uterine contractions
It flattens the sacrum and rotates the symphysis upward
It relaxes the pelvic floor muscles
questions.why: The McRoberts manoeuvre straightens the lumbosacral angle and rotates the symphysis pubis upwards over the anterior shoulder; it does not change the bony diameters of the pelvis.

questions.stem: The head has delivered and the shoulders are impacted; the McRoberts position has been adopted. The fetal back is on the mother's left (left occipito-anterior). The assistant is about to apply suprapubic pressure.
questions.q: Where should the pressure be applied?
options: Down and sideways from the fetal back side, on the back of the anterior shoulder
Straight down on the uterine fundus
On the front of the anterior shoulder, pushing it toward the fetal back
On the mother's right flank toward the umbilicus
On the perineum to push it backward
questions.why: Pressure on the back of the anterior shoulder, applied from the side of the fetal back, adducts the shoulder into the oblique diameter. Fundal pressure is contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 4.6 kg baby was born after a difficult delivery with strong traction on the head. The right arm lies limp and internally rotated, with the elbow extended and the wrist flexed. The grasp reflex is present but the Moro reflex is absent on the right.
questions.q: Which nerve roots are injured?
questions.why: The waiter's tip position with a preserved grasp reflex indicates Erb's palsy, caused by stretching of C5–C6. Injury to C8–T1 gives a claw hand with an absent grasp reflex.

questions.stem: A 4.4 kg baby is born after shoulder dystocia. The left hand is clawed with no grasp reflex. The left eyelid droops and the left pupil is small.
questions.q: What is the most likely injury?
questions.why: A claw hand with ptosis and a small pupil indicates a lower brachial plexus injury that involves the sympathetic chain. In Erb's palsy the grasp reflex is preserved.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman at 41 weeks delivers a 4.3 kg baby after a long induced labour; the McRoberts manoeuvre, suprapubic pressure and delivery of the posterior arm were needed. The placenta has been delivered complete.
questions.q: Which maternal complication is most important to anticipate in the next hour?
questions.why: Postpartum haemorrhage is the commonest maternal complication of shoulder dystocia and results from atony and tears. An oxytocin infusion is started and the whole genital tract is examined.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman with pre-existing type 2 diabetes treated with insulin is 38 weeks pregnant. The estimated fetal weight on ultrasound is 4.7 kg. Her previous baby weighed 3.6 kg and was born by normal delivery.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Planned ventouse in the second stage
questions.why: In a diabetic woman an estimated fetal weight above 4.5 kg is an indication for elective caesarean section to avoid shoulder dystocia. In a non-diabetic woman the threshold is 5 kg.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman with gestational diabetes well controlled on metformin is 37 weeks pregnant. The estimated fetal weight is 4.2 kg. She has no other problems.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Planned birth at 38–39 weeks in hospital with an experienced team
Home birth with a trained midwife
questions.why: With good control and an estimated fetal weight below 4.5 kg, caesarean section is not automatically indicated; she delivers at 38–39 weeks in hospital. Waiting beyond term increases fetal size and risk.

questions.stem: A para 4 woman is 42 weeks pregnant. The head was delivered 5 minutes ago. The McRoberts manoeuvre, suprapubic pressure, internal rotation, delivery of the posterior arm and the all-fours position have all failed. The baby is still alive and the theatre next door is ready.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Wait for the next contraction and pull harder
Push the head back with terbutaline 0.25 mg SC, then caesarean section
questions.why: When all the HELPERR steps have failed and a theatre is ready, the Zavanelli manoeuvre (cephalic replacement) under tocolysis followed by caesarean section is chosen.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is in a peripheral hospital far from any operating theatre. The baby's head delivered 6 minutes ago, and every manoeuvre, including delivery of the posterior arm and the all-fours position, has failed. The fetal heart is still heard.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate last-resort procedure?
options: Zavanelli manoeuvre and transfer for caesarean
Symphysiotomy under local anaesthesia, with a catheter displacing the urethra
questions.why: Where caesarean section is not available nearby, symphysiotomy is a life-saving last resort for a live baby. Cleidotomy is reserved for a dead baby.

questions.stem: A para 5 woman has shoulder dystocia. All manoeuvres have failed, and no fetal heart has been detected on Doppler for the last 5 minutes.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate procedure to deliver the body?
questions.why: When the baby is dead, the aim is to protect the mother, so the clavicles are divided (cleidotomy). Symphysiotomy and caesarean section expose her to risk without fetal benefit.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman had shoulder dystocia at her first delivery; the baby had an Erb's palsy that recovered. She is now 30 weeks pregnant and asks whether it can happen again.
questions.q: What is the best estimate of recurrence?
questions.why: The recurrence rate after a previous shoulder dystocia is about 1 in 10, so the mode of delivery is discussed with an experienced team. The background rate is 1 in 200.

questions.theme: Collapse around delivery
questions.lead: For each patient choose the most likely cause of her collapse. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: Thirty minutes after a normal delivery a para 6 woman is in shock, with a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg and a pulse of 128/min. The fundus is soft, at the level of the umbilicus, and clots are expelled when it is rubbed.
items.why: A soft fundus that becomes firm when rubbed indicates atony; the shock corresponds to the blood loss and there is tachycardia.

items.stem: A para 3 woman with a previous caesarean section is induced with oxytocin. At 8 cm she has sudden severe pain, the contractions stop, the head recedes out of the pelvis and fetal parts are palpable under the abdominal wall. Her pulse is 140/min.
items.why: A uterine scar, sudden pain, cessation of contractions and recession of the head indicate uterine rupture.

items.stem: Two hours after delivery with repair of a second-degree tear, a para 2 woman has severe perineal pain and cannot pass urine. Her pulse is 120/min and the fundus is firm. A tense, tender swelling bulges from the right vaginal wall.
items.why: A firm uterus with a tense, painful swelling of the vaginal wall and shock indicates a haematoma, often beneath the repair.

items.stem: A para 1 woman at 39 weeks is in labour at 7 cm with clear liquor. Minutes after artificial rupture of membranes she becomes agitated, cyanosed and hypotensive, and then has a convulsion. Her blood pressure had been 110/70 mmHg and there was no proteinuria. Later she oozes continuously from the cannula sites.
items.why: Hypoxia and collapse around rupture of the membranes, followed by DIC, with a previously normal blood pressure, indicate amniotic fluid embolism and not eclampsia.

questions.theme: Delivery when the shoulders are stuck
questions.lead: For each situation choose the most appropriate next action. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: The head of a 4.3 kg baby delivered 20 seconds ago and has retracted against the perineum. Help has just arrived and the woman is lying on her back with her legs in stirrups.
items.why: After calling for help, the first step is to lay the woman flat and hyperflex her hips (McRoberts manoeuvre).

items.stem: A theatre next door is ready. Every manoeuvre, including the all-fours position, has failed; the baby is alive and the head was delivered 5 minutes ago.
items.why: When a theatre is ready, the head is replaced under terbutaline and caesarean section is performed (Zavanelli manoeuvre).

items.stem: In a peripheral unit with no operating theatre within 3 hours, all manoeuvres have failed and the fetal heart is still heard.
items.why: Where caesarean section is not available nearby, symphysiotomy under local anaesthesia can save a live baby.

items.stem: All manoeuvres have failed and the fetal heart has been absent for several minutes.
items.why: When the baby is dead, division of the clavicles (cleidotomy) protects the mother from further trauma.

questions.theme: Management in cord and third-stage emergencies
options: Forceps or ventouse in the room
Vaginal delivery, awaiting labour or inducing
Fill the bladder and transfer in exaggerated left Sims
Conservative management in hospital, no ARM
questions.lead: For each patient choose the most appropriate management. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: A para 1 woman at 32 weeks is not in labour and has intact membranes. Ultrasound and vaginal examination show a loop of cord lying below the breech. The CTG is normal.
items.why: Preterm cord presentation with intact membranes is managed conservatively, and artificial rupture of membranes is avoided.

items.stem: A para 4 woman in a rural health centre is 3 cm dilated with a pulsating cord in the vagina; the referral hospital is 2 hours away by road.
items.why: A full bladder keeps the presenting part elevated during a long transfer; the knee–chest position is unsafe in a vehicle.

items.stem: In a para 3 woman the uterus is inverted to the vulva after the third stage. Manual replacement failed even after terbutaline; examination shows no tear in the vagina or uterus.
items.why: When manual replacement has failed and rupture has been excluded, hydrostatic pressure with warm saline can replace the fundus.

items.stem: A para 5 woman is undergoing laparotomy for uterine inversion. Clamps on the round ligaments cannot pull the fundus up through a very tight ring.
items.why: When the ring is too tight, a posterior incision through it (Haultain procedure) allows replacement, followed by repair.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman is seen on day 7 after a normal vaginal delivery. She is well and breastfeeding, and her lochia is pink-brown and not offensive.
questions.q: Where is the fundus expected to be felt?
options: At the level of the umbilicus
About midway between the umbilicus and the symphysis pubis
questions.why: The fundus is at the umbilicus after delivery and falls by about 1 cm a day, so by day 7 it is about halfway down. It is not palpable by day 10–14.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is seen on day 16 after a home delivery. Her lochia has become bright red again and the uterus is still palpable three finger breadths above the symphysis. Her temperature is 37.2 °C.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.why: A uterus that is still palpable after day 14 with a return of red lochia suggests retained tissue and subinvolution; ultrasound is used to look for it.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman is seen on day 2 after a normal delivery. She feels well; her temperature is 37.1 °C and her pulse 82/min. A routine blood count shows a white cell count of 19 × 10⁹/L with a normal haemoglobin.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Take blood cultures and repeat the count in 6 hours
Reassure: this is normal after delivery
questions.why: A white cell count of up to 20–25 × 10⁹/L is normal in the first days after delivery. In a well, afebrile woman it does not indicate infection.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman with moderate mitral stenosis is in labour at 38 weeks. She has been stable throughout pregnancy.
questions.q: When is she at the greatest risk of pulmonary oedema?
options: In the latent phase of labour
Immediately after delivery of the placenta
questions.why: Contraction of the uterus after delivery returns blood to the circulation (autotransfusion), which raises cardiac output at the time when the heart is least able to cope.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman is reviewed 8 hours after a ventouse delivery under epidural analgesia. She has not passed urine. A tender suprapubic swelling is palpable and the fundus is displaced upwards and to the right.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Encourage oral fluids and wait 6 hours
Request a pelvic ultrasound for haematoma
questions.why: A woman should pass urine within 6 hours of delivery. A full bladder after epidural analgesia and instrumental delivery indicates urinary retention, which requires catheterisation; it also prevents the uterus from contracting well.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman with blood group O RhD-negative delivered a healthy baby today. The baby is O RhD-positive and the direct Coombs test is negative. She had no antibodies at booking.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Anti-D 500 IU IM within 72 hours, with a Kleihauer test
No anti-D, as the Coombs test is negative
Anti-D 1500 IU only if she plans another pregnancy
questions.why: A non-sensitised RhD-negative mother of an RhD-positive baby receives 500 IU of anti-D within 72 hours. The Kleihauer test shows whether a larger fetomaternal haemorrhage requires a larger dose.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman is breastfeeding on day 1 after a normal delivery. Her booking rubella IgG was negative.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Delay MMR until she stops breastfeeding
Give rubella immunoglobulin to the baby
No vaccine; she will be immune after this pregnancy
Give MMR before discharge and avoid pregnancy for 1 month
Give MMR at the start of her next pregnancy
questions.why: Non-immune mothers are vaccinated before discharge, and breastfeeding is not a contraindication. Because a live vaccine is avoided in pregnancy, she should avoid pregnancy for 1 month.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman had gestational diabetes controlled by diet. She delivered a 3.8 kg baby at 39 weeks, and her capillary glucose is normal after delivery.
questions.q: What follow-up is most appropriate?
options: Fasting glucose or OGTT at 6 weeks
No follow-up, as GDM always resolves
questions.why: Testing at 6 weeks detects diabetes that has persisted after pregnancy. HbA1c soon after delivery is unreliable.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is HBsAg-positive. Her baby is born at term and is well. She wishes to breastfeed.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Express milk and heat it before feeding
Breastfeed; the baby gets hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG at birth
Breastfeed only after the baby's third vaccine dose
Breastfeed only if her viral load is undetectable
questions.why: Hepatitis B is not a contraindication to breastfeeding once the baby has received the vaccine and HBIG.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman on day 3 after delivery has had a cough for 6 weeks, and her sputum smear is positive for acid-fast bacilli. She has not yet started treatment.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan for feeding the baby?
options: Stop breastfeeding permanently and use formula
Breastfeed directly from today without any precautions
Separate mother and baby for 6 months
Give the baby BCG only and continue direct feeding
Start her treatment; she expresses milk while the baby gets isoniazid and BCG, then breastfeeds directly after about 2 weeks
questions.why: A mother with untreated smear-positive tuberculosis starts treatment, wears a mask and expresses her milk; the baby receives isoniazid prophylaxis and BCG. Direct breastfeeding resumes once she is smear-negative.

questions.stem: A breastfed baby, 6 days old, has vomiting, poor feeding, rising jaundice and an enlarged liver. Slit-lamp examination shows bilateral cataracts.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate feeding advice?
options: Stop breastfeeding and use a lactose-free formula
Breastfeed but give extra water feeds
Switch to standard cow's milk formula
Express breast milk and feed it by cup
questions.why: Vomiting, jaundice and cataracts in a breastfed baby suggest galactosaemia, which is an absolute contraindication to breast milk.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman delivered a stillborn baby at 38 weeks. She is normotensive and has no other illness. She asks for medication to suppress lactation.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate drug?
options: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily for 14 days
Cabergoline 1 mg orally as a single dose within 24 hours
questions.why: A single dose of cabergoline is the drug of choice. Bromocriptine and high-dose oestrogen are no longer used because of the risks of stroke, myocardial infarction and VTE.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman is seen on day 4 after delivery. Both breasts are hard, full and tender, and the baby has difficulty latching on. Her temperature is 37.9 °C and there is no area of redness.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Frequent feeds, express to soften, warm packs before and cold after, paracetamol
questions.why: Hardness of both breasts on days 3–5 with a low-grade fever is breast engorgement, which is relieved by emptying the breasts. Antibiotics are indicated for a red, wedge-shaped area with high fever.

questions.stem: Three weeks after delivery, a para 2 woman has a painful, red, wedge-shaped area on the right breast, a temperature of 38.6 °C and generalised aches. No fluctuant lump is palpable.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop feeding from the right breast until it settles
Flucloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly for 10–14 days and continue feeding from both breasts
questions.why: Infective mastitis is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus; flucloxacillin is given and continued breastfeeding helps to empty the breast. Tetracycline is avoided during breastfeeding.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman has taken flucloxacillin for 5 days for a red, tender breast. She still has a fever of 38.8 °C and now has a tense, fluctuant, very tender lump in the upper outer quadrant.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and continue the same antibiotic for 10 more days
Ultrasound and needle aspiration or incision and drainage
questions.why: A fluctuant mass with persistent fever is a breast abscess, and the pus must be drained. She may continue to feed from the other breast.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is exclusively breastfeeding 6 weeks after delivery. She asks for a contraceptive pill to start today.
questions.q: Which method is most suitable?
options: No method is needed while breastfeeding
questions.why: Progestogen-only methods do not reduce milk production and are the first choice during breastfeeding. The combined pill is avoided until 6 months.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman has a single temperature of 38.2 °C on day 12 after a vaginal delivery. All earlier observations were normal.
questions.q: Which term best describes this?
questions.why: Puerperal pyrexia is a temperature of 38 °C or more at any time in the first 14 days. Puerperal morbidity requires 38 °C or more on 2 of the first 10 days, excluding the first 24 hours.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman is seen on day 3 after a caesarean section for prolonged labour with membranes ruptured for 30 hours. Her temperature is 38.6 °C and pulse 110/min. The lochia is offensive and the uterus is bulky and tender. The wound is clean and the breasts are soft.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Fever with offensive lochia and a tender, bulky uterus indicates endometritis, the commonest cause of puerperal fever.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is seen on day 4 after a long labour with many vaginal examinations. She has fever and offensive lochia, and the uterus is tender. A high vaginal swab is sent.
questions.q: Which organism is classically the commonest cause of this infection?
questions.why: Anaerobic streptococci, together with Bacteroides, are the classic commonest organisms in endometritis and cause the offensive odour. Staphylococcus aureus causes mastitis and wound infection.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman is seen on day 2 after a normal delivery. She has diarrhoea, vomiting and lower abdominal pain severe enough to require morphine, although the uterus is only mildly tender. Her temperature is 38.9 °C and pulse 132/min. Her son had a sore throat last week.
questions.q: Which organism is most likely?
questions.why: Pain out of proportion to the signs, diarrhoea and vomiting, and a family member with a sore throat suggest group A streptococcus, which is spread by the hands from the throat and causes rapidly fatal sepsis.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman is seen on day 3; her daughter has tonsillitis. She has severe abdominal pain requiring morphine, a red rash, a temperature of 39.2 °C and a blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg after fluids. IV piperacillin–tazobactam has been started.
questions.q: Which antibiotic should be added, and why?
options: Clindamycin, because it blocks toxin production
Vancomycin, because GAS is usually resistant to penicillin
Doxycycline, because it penetrates the uterus well
questions.why: Clindamycin suppresses streptococcal toxin production, so it is added in severe group A streptococcal sepsis. Gentamicin has no anaerobic cover.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is confused on day 4 after a caesarean section. Her temperature is 35.4 °C, pulse 128/min, respiratory rate 26/min and blood pressure 95/60 mmHg.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start the Sepsis Six within 1 hour
Observe for 4 hours, as she has no fever
Send cultures and wait for results before antibiotics
CT head to look for a stroke first
questions.why: A low temperature, tachycardia and tachypnoea with confusion indicate high-risk sepsis (obstetric qSOFA ≥ 2). A normal or low temperature does not exclude sepsis.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman has a fever of 38.7 °C, offensive lochia and a tender uterus on day 2 after an emergency caesarean section. She is breastfeeding. Cultures have been sent.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate first-line antibiotic regimen?
options: Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV daily plus metronidazole 500 mg IV 8-hourly
questions.why: Endometritis is polymicrobial and requires IV broad-spectrum antibiotics that include anaerobic cover. Tetracycline and chloramphenicol are avoided during breastfeeding.

questions.stem: A para 4 woman on day 6 has received IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole for 3 days for postnatal uterine infection. She is still febrile. The uterus is bulky, the os admits one finger and the lochia is heavy.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Change to meropenem and wait 3 more days
Pelvic ultrasound for retained products, then gentle evacuation
Stop antibiotics, as this is drug fever
questions.why: Failure to respond within 48–72 hours requires a search for the cause; a bulky uterus with an open os suggests retained tissue, which is removed after antibiotics have been started.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman is seen on day 7 after a caesarean section. She has spiking fevers up to 39 °C despite 5 days of IV antibiotics, but between the spikes she appears well and eats. Pelvic ultrasound shows no collection or retained tissue. The malaria film and urine are negative.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Change antibiotics to a carbapenem only
CT of the pelvis and add therapeutic heparin
questions.why: A spiking fever despite antibiotics, with no collection, in a woman who appears well suggests pelvic (ovarian) vein thrombophlebitis, which responds to heparin.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman is seen on day 9 after a caesarean section. She has a swinging fever, diarrhoea and painful straining at stool. On rectal examination a tender, fluctuant mass is felt in front of the rectum.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Drain the collection and continue IV antibiotics
questions.why: A swinging fever, diarrhoea, tenesmus and a mass in the pouch of Douglas indicate a pelvic abscess. The pus must be drained under ultrasound guidance, by colpotomy or by laparotomy.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is seen on day 4 after a caesarean section. She has severe wound pain that is far greater than the redness suggests. The skin around the wound is dusky and crepitus is felt. Her pulse is 125/min and blood pressure 90/55 mmHg.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Remove alternate sutures and review in 24 hours
Urgent surgical debridement with IV antibiotics
Wound swab and wait for the result
questions.why: Pain out of proportion to the signs, dusky skin and crepitus indicate necrotising fasciitis; early surgical debridement is life-saving.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman is about to have an emergency caesarean section. She has a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin.
questions.q: What is the best antibiotic prophylaxis?
options: Clindamycin 900 mg IV before the skin incision
Cefuroxime 1.5 g IV after cord clamping
Co-amoxiclav 1.2 g IV before the skin incision
Ampicillin 2 g IV before the skin incision
No prophylaxis, as it is an emergency
questions.why: Prophylaxis is given before the skin incision; in a woman with penicillin anaphylaxis, clindamycin replaces the cephalosporin. Co-amoxiclav is avoided before delivery because of necrotising enterocolitis.

questions.stem: A para 4 woman in Shendi is seen on day 5 after a normal delivery. She has rigors and a fever of 39.5 °C. The uterus is involuting and not tender, the lochia is normal, the breasts are soft, the chest is clear and the urine dipstick is normal.
questions.q: Besides blood cultures, which investigation is most important now?
options: Malaria blood film or rapid diagnostic test
questions.why: In Sudan every postnatal fever requires a malaria film or rapid diagnostic test, especially when no pelvic source is found. The Widal test is unreliable; blood culture is used for typhoid.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman is seen on day 3 after a long labour during which she was catheterised. She has rigors, a temperature of 39 °C, right loin pain and dysuria. The uterus is not tender and the lochia is normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment after sending an MSU?
options: IV clindamycin plus gentamicin for endometritis
questions.why: Loin pain and rigors after catheterisation suggest pyelonephritis, which requires IV treatment. Oral cefalexin is used for simple cystitis.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman was admitted on day 3 with fever, offensive lochia and a tender uterus, and was started on IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole. She has been afebrile for 48 hours, the uterus is no longer tender and she is eating well.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop antibiotics; no oral course is needed
Switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for 14 days
Switch to oral doxycycline for 7 days
questions.why: IV antibiotics are continued until the woman has been afebrile for 48 hours; after uncomplicated endometritis an oral course gives no additional benefit.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman presents to a rural health centre on day 3 after a home delivery. Her temperature is 39 °C and pulse 124/min; she has offensive lochia and a tender uterus. The nearest hospital is 2 hours away.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate action before referral?
options: Give oral amoxicillin and send her home
Transfer without any treatment to avoid masking signs
Give the first dose of IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, start IV fluids, then transfer
Paracetamol only and review in 24 hours
questions.why: Each hour of delay in giving antibiotics increases the risk of death. A septic mother receives IV antibiotics and fluids before transfer, and is never sent home on oral drugs alone.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman is seen on day 4 after a normal delivery. She cries easily, feels irritable and anxious, and is not sleeping well. She is feeding and caring for her baby well and has no thoughts of harm.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure, explain it is common and passes, and arrange family support
questions.why: Tearfulness in the first days in a mother who is coping fully is the baby blues, which affects up to 80% of mothers and resolves within 2 weeks. Antidepressants are not needed.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman is seen 7 weeks after delivery. For the last month she has felt low for most of the day, takes no pleasure in anything, cannot sleep even when the baby sleeps, and says she is a bad mother. She has no delusions and knows that she is unwell. Her temperature and blood pressure are normal.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Low mood and anhedonia for more than 2 weeks, with guilt and poor bonding, indicate postnatal depression. The baby blues lasts less than 2 weeks; psychosis is characterised by delusions and loss of insight.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is breastfeeding 8 weeks after delivery. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 16, with a score of 0 on the self-harm question. Haemoglobin and TSH are normal. She has moderate depression.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily and stop breastfeeding
Reassurance only and repeat the score in 6 months
Sertraline 50 mg once daily plus CBT, continuing breastfeeding
questions.why: Sertraline passes into breast milk in very small amounts and is the SSRI of choice; breastfeeding continues. Fluoxetine accumulates in the baby.

questions.stem: At her 6-week postnatal visit a para 1 woman has an Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score of 8. She scored 2 on the last question, stating that the thought of harming herself has occurred "sometimes".
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure, as the total score is below 13
Repeat the score at the next visit in 3 months
Assess her mental state and risk the same day
Start sertraline and review in 4 weeks
Refer for CBT on the routine waiting list
questions.why: Any score on the self-harm item requires assessment on the same day, whatever the total score.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman is seen on day 6 after delivery. She has not slept for 3 nights, is restless and perplexed, and says that voices are telling her the baby is the devil. Her temperature is 37 °C, blood pressure 115/75 mmHg and urinalysis normal.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and review at the 6-week visit
Do not leave her alone with the baby, and arrange same-day psychiatric admission
Start sertraline and send her home
Send her home with her mother to help with sleep
questions.why: Delusions about the baby with loss of insight in the first 2 weeks constitute a psychiatric emergency, with a risk of suicide and infanticide. Organic causes have been excluded.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman is seen on day 5 after a long labour with manual removal of the placenta. She is confused, agitated and disorientated in place. Her temperature is 39 °C, pulse 124/min and blood pressure 120/80 mmHg; the lochia is offensive.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause of her confusion?
questions.why: Confusion with fever and offensive lochia is organic until proved otherwise; a septic screen and a malaria film are done first.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman on day 8 after delivery has had a severe headache for 2 days and had a convulsion this morning. Her blood pressure is 120/75 mmHg, there is no proteinuria and her temperature is normal.
questions.q: Which investigation is most appropriate?
questions.why: Headache and convulsions in the first or second week with a normal blood pressure suggest cerebral venous thrombosis, which is best demonstrated by MR venography.

questions.stem: Five months after delivery a para 1 woman is tired, low in mood, intolerant of cold and has gained weight. In the second month she had palpitations and lost weight. She is not anaemic.
questions.q: Which investigation is most appropriate?
questions.why: A hyperthyroid phase followed by a hypothyroid phase at 4–8 months indicates postpartum thyroiditis, which mimics depression.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman with bipolar disorder became elated, sleepless and deluded on day 5 after delivery. The psychiatrist has started lithium. She wishes to breastfeed.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate feeding advice?
options: Breastfeed and check the baby's lithium level weekly
Breastfeed only from the left breast
Breastfeed if she takes lithium after the feeds
Breastfeed and give the baby vitamin K
questions.why: Lithium reaches high levels in breast milk and can be toxic to the baby, so breastfeeding is avoided. Antipsychotic drugs usually allow breastfeeding.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman with bipolar disorder is 34 weeks pregnant. After her first delivery she had a psychotic episode on day 4. She is currently well and not taking medication.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Shared psychiatry plan, hospital birth and prophylaxis with an antipsychotic or lithium right after delivery
Elective caesarean at 37 weeks to reduce stress
questions.why: With bipolar disorder and a previous puerperal psychosis, her risk is about 60%; prophylaxis starts immediately after delivery, with daily review for the first 2 weeks.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman had postnatal depression after her first delivery, treated with sertraline. She is now 12 weeks pregnant and asks about the chance of recurrence after this delivery.
questions.q: What is the best estimate?
questions.why: Postnatal depression recurs in about 1 in 4 women after the next delivery. About 50% is the figure for puerperal psychosis.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman began hearing voices and became agitated on day 7 after delivery and was admitted. Despite olanzapine she has refused all food and drink for 3 days and is not speaking.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.why: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) acts rapidly and is safe in the puerperium; it is used when the illness is life-threatening, as in refusal of food and drink.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman is breastfeeding 2 weeks after delivery. She has moderate depression and needs an antidepressant.
questions.q: Which drug is least suitable?
questions.why: Fluoxetine has a long half-life and accumulates in the newborn. Sertraline and paroxetine reach very low levels in breast milk.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, well controlled on sodium valproate, wishes to conceive.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Continue valproate and add folic acid 400 µg
Switch from valproate to another drug before conception, under psychiatric care
Stop all mood stabilisers once pregnant
Continue valproate and have a detailed scan at 20 weeks
questions.why: Valproate causes neural tube defects and reduced IQ, so it is changed before pregnancy. Stopping all treatment carries a risk of relapse.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman became tearful from day 4 after delivery. She is now 4 weeks postpartum, still cries on most days and has lost interest in her baby.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure: baby blues can last up to 3 months
Screen with the Edinburgh scale and assess for depression
questions.why: Symptoms that last longer than 2 weeks are no longer the baby blues; prolonged or severe blues is a risk factor for depression and requires screening.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis develops pulmonary oedema at 30 weeks and dies despite treatment.
questions.q: How is this death classified?
questions.why: Death from a pre-existing disease that is made worse by pregnancy is an indirect maternal death.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman develops peripartum cardiomyopathy and dies of heart failure 4 months after delivery.
questions.q: How is this death classified?
questions.why: A death from a direct or indirect cause between 42 days and 1 year after the end of pregnancy is a late maternal death.

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks dies in a road traffic accident on her way to the market.
questions.q: How is this death handled when calculating the maternal mortality ratio?
options: Counted as a direct maternal death
Counted as an indirect maternal death
Counted as a late maternal death
Counted as a maternal near miss
Excluded: it is a coincidental death
questions.why: Accidental and incidental deaths are not maternal deaths and are not counted in the maternal mortality ratio, although they are pregnancy-related deaths.

questions.stem: A para 1 woman dies of pulmonary embolism on day 10 after an emergency caesarean section.
questions.q: How is this death classified?
options: Not a maternal death, as it occurred after delivery
questions.why: Venous thromboembolism is an obstetric complication of the puerperium, so the death is direct; any death within 42 days from such a cause is counted.

questions.stem: In one year a state records 40 maternal deaths. There were 16 000 live births and 16 300 total births, and 120 000 women aged 15–49.
questions.q: What is the maternal mortality ratio?
questions.why: Maternal mortality ratio = maternal deaths ÷ live births × 100 000 = 40 ÷ 16 000 × 100 000 = 250. Deaths per number of women aged 15–49 is the maternal mortality rate.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman had eclampsia at 36 weeks, followed by a massive PPH that required an emergency hysterectomy and intensive care. She went home well on day 12.
questions.q: Which term best describes her case?
questions.why: A woman who nearly died from a life-threatening complication but survived is a maternal near miss; such cases are reviewed to improve care.

questions.stem: The maternal death review committee of a Sudanese state hospital is listing the causes of last year's deaths.
questions.q: Which cause is most likely to top the list?
questions.why: Sepsis is the leading cause of maternal death in Sudan, ahead of haemorrhage. Worldwide, haemorrhage is the leading cause.

questions.stem: A para 5 woman in a village bled heavily after a home delivery. Her mother-in-law considered the bleeding normal, and the family waited for her husband to return from the farm before leaving. She died on arrival at the hospital.
questions.q: Which delay mainly caused her death?
options: Delay in booking for antenatal care
Delay in diagnosis at the hospital
Delay in deciding to seek care
questions.why: Failure to recognise danger and waiting for permission constitute the first delay: the decision to seek care.

questions.stem: A para 4 woman lives 80 km from the nearest hospital, and the road is cut off in the rainy season. In her last pregnancy she nearly died of haemorrhage on the way.
questions.q: Which intervention best addresses her main delay?
options: Training more obstetricians at the hospital
A maternity waiting home near the hospital before term
A blood bank at the hospital
questions.why: Maternity waiting homes address the second delay, reaching care, by bringing the woman close to the hospital before labour.

questions.stem: A para 2 woman reaches a referral hospital 1 hour after a PPH. She waits 3 hours for blood because the blood bank has none, and dies.
questions.q: Which delay is this?
options: Delay in deciding to seek care
No delay; this is an unavoidable death
questions.why: Once the woman has reached the facility, a lack of blood, staff or an operating theatre is the third delay: receiving adequate care.

questions.stem: A public health lecturer compares how quickly untreated obstetric complications kill.
questions.q: Which complication, if untreated, causes death in the shortest time?
questions.why: Untreated PPH causes death in about 2 hours, compared with about 1 day for uterine rupture, 2 days for eclampsia, 3 days for obstructed labour and 6 days for sepsis.

questions.stem: A rural hospital gives parenteral antibiotics, oxytocics and MgSO4, and performs manual removal of the placenta, MVA, assisted vaginal birth and newborn resuscitation.
questions.q: What must be added to make it a comprehensive emergency obstetric care facility?
questions.why: These are the seven signal functions of basic EmONC; comprehensive care adds caesarean section and blood transfusion.

questions.stem: A survey team in a district without vital registration asks adults how many of their sisters reached adult life and how many of them died during pregnancy, childbirth or within 6 weeks after.
questions.q: Which method of measuring maternal mortality is this?
questions.why: The sisterhood method asks adults about deaths among their sisters; it is useful where vital registration is poor.

questions.stem: A medical officer compares the leading causes of maternal death in different settings for a lecture.
questions.q: Which statement is correct?
options: Worldwide, sepsis is the leading cause
In Sudan, haemorrhage is the leading cause, ahead of sepsis
In the UK, VTE is the leading direct cause and cardiac disease the leading cause overall
Worldwide, VTE causes about a quarter of deaths
In the UK, haemorrhage is the leading direct cause
questions.why: In the United Kingdom VTE is the leading direct cause and cardiac disease the leading cause overall. Worldwide haemorrhage leads (about 27%); in Sudan sepsis leads.

questions.stem: A para 3 woman delivered a healthy baby in a health centre 6 hours ago and is ready to return to her village.
questions.q: Which postnatal follow-up best reduces her risk of dying?
options: Checks at 24 hours, day 3, week 1–2 and 6 weeks
A single check at 6 weeks only
A check at 3 months with the baby's vaccines
Only return if she feels unwell
A check at 6 months for contraception
questions.why: Most maternal deaths occur in the first days after delivery, so the early checks (day 3 and week 1–2) are the most important, with the final check at 6 weeks.

questions.theme: Fever after birth: think by day
questions.lead: For each woman choose the most likely cause of her fever. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: Day 1 after a caesarean under general anaesthesia. Temperature 38.1 °C, RR 24/min, SpO2 93%. Crackles at both lung bases; the uterus and wound are normal.
items.why: Fever on days 0–2 after general anaesthesia with chest signs arises from the lungs.

items.stem: Day 3 after a normal birth. Temperature 37.9 °C. Both breasts are hard, full and tender; no red area. Uterus and lochia are normal.
items.why: Hardness of both breasts on days 3–5 with a low-grade fever is engorgement, not infection.

items.stem: Day 12 after a caesarean. Low-grade fever 37.8 °C and a painful swollen left calf, 3 cm bigger than the right.
items.why: A low-grade fever with a tender, swollen calf in weeks 1–3 indicates deep vein thrombosis, which is confirmed by Doppler ultrasound.

items.stem: Day 6 after a caesarean. Temperature 38.4 °C. The lower part of the wound is red, hot and opened, with pus coming out. The uterus is not tender.
items.why: A red, hot, discharging wound on days 4–8 is a wound infection; it is opened and the pus is drained.

questions.theme: Altered mood or behaviour after birth
questions.lead: For each woman choose the most likely diagnosis. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: Para 4, 3 months after a massive PPH with 8 units transfused. She is tired and low, her milk never came in, she has no periods and her BP is 90/60 mmHg. Hb 12 g/dL.
items.why: Failure of lactation, amenorrhoea and a low blood pressure after a massive PPH indicate pituitary necrosis.

items.stem: Para 1, day 5. Afebrile, BP normal. She is elated, talks fast, has not slept for 3 nights and says the baby was swapped at birth. Her sister has bipolar disorder.
items.why: Mania with delusions and a family history of bipolar disorder in the first 2 weeks indicates puerperal psychosis.

items.stem: Para 2, day 3 after birth, is confused and has a fit. BP 170/110 mmHg, urine protein 3+.
items.why: Convulsions with a high blood pressure and proteinuria after delivery indicate eclampsia; pre-eclampsia can begin up to 6 weeks postpartum.

items.stem: Para 3, 6 weeks after a PPH. She is tired, breathless on walking and tearful. She is pale; Hb 6.8 g/dL. She enjoys her baby and has no guilt.
items.why: Tiredness and low mood with a haemoglobin below 7 g/dL after a PPH indicate anaemia, which is treated before depression is diagnosed.

questions.theme: Contraception after birth
options: Wait until 4 weeks for an IUD
questions.lead: For each woman choose the most appropriate advice. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: Para 2, 3 months after birth, fully breastfeeding day and night. She has had no period and wants a method without drugs.
items.why: No menstruation, full breastfeeding and a baby under 6 months give 98% protection.

items.stem: Para 1 is bottle-feeding because of a breast problem. She is 3 weeks after birth, has no VTE risk factors and wants the combined pill.
items.why: In a woman who is not breastfeeding and has no risk of VTE, the combined pill can be started from day 21.

items.stem: Para 3, day 10 after a vaginal birth, asks for a copper IUD to be fitted today.
items.why: Between 48 hours and 4 weeks the soft uterus carries a high risk of expulsion and perforation.

items.stem: Para 6, day 2 after a normal birth. She and her husband have completed their family and want a permanent method before she goes home.
items.why: Puerperal mini-laparotomy within 7 days is convenient; otherwise interval sterilisation is performed after 6 weeks.

questions.stem: In a history station, a 31-year-old G3 P2 at 34 weeks says she had bright red bleeding this morning. You have taken the history and the examiner asks about your examination plan.
questions.q: Which step must you avoid until a scan is done?
options: Sterile speculum examination after the scan
questions.why: A finger in the cervix can tear a praevia and cause very heavy bleeding. Speculum is safe once the placenta is located.

questions.stem: A male student enters an abdominal examination station. The patient, 24 weeks pregnant, looks uneasy and glances at the door. No nurse is in the room.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start palpation quickly to save time
Offer a female chaperone before examining
Skip the examination and take a history
questions.why: Intimate or abdominal examination by a male student needs consent and a female chaperone. Examining over clothes gives wrong findings.

questions.stem: At the 4-minute bell you have finished palpation but not auscultation. The patient is lying uncovered.
questions.q: What should you do now?
options: Continue until the examiner stops you
Cover her, summarise briefly, thank her, then present
Start auscultation and skip the closing
questions.why: Closing steps carry marks and protect dignity; an unfinished but safe closing beats running over time.

questions.stem: You must tell a 29-year-old woman that her 20-week scan shows no fetal heart. She is standing alone outside the clinic and asks, "Is my baby fine?"
questions.q: What is the best first action?
options: Tell her the result at once, standing outside the clinic
Say the doctor will tell her later
Move to a quiet room and ask whom she wants with her
questions.why: SPIKES starts with the setting: private room, seated, support person. Bad news is never given standing in a public place.

questions.stem: A woman agrees to caesarean section for breech. You have explained the operation and the common and serious risks.
questions.q: Which element of consent is still missing?
options: Alternatives, including vaginal breech or ECV, and doing nothing
The name of the anaesthetic drug
questions.why: BRAN needs alternatives and the option of doing nothing. An adult woman consents for herself; the husband's signature is not required.

questions.stem: During a counselling station the patient's mother keeps answering every question for her daughter, a 23-year-old primigravida.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate response?
options: Address all questions to the mother
Ask the mother to leave immediately
Thank the mother, then direct questions back to the patient
questions.why: Respect the family but keep the patient at the centre; she is the one who decides.

questions.stem: At the end of a history station the examiner asks you to present. You took a full history of a woman with headache at 35 weeks.
questions.q: Which presentation order is best?
options: Name and age, gestation, complaint, positives, relevant negatives, impression, plan
Every question you asked, in order
questions.why: A structured presentation of under a minute: who, why, positives, relevant negatives, impression and plan.

questions.stem: In a counselling station a 26-year-old says, "I'm not sure I understood all of that."
questions.q: Which technique best confirms understanding?
options: Give her a leaflet and finish
Ask her to explain the plan in her own words
questions.why: Teach-back shows what she actually understood; "Do you understand?" usually gets a polite yes.

questions.stem: An obese woman at 30 weeks has an arm circumference of 38 cm. With the standard adult cuff her blood pressure is 156/98 mmHg. She has no symptoms and her urine is clear.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step in this station?
options: Repeat with a large cuff after rest
Repeat in 4 hours with the same cuff
questions.why: A cuff too small for the arm over-reads. Confirm the reading with the right cuff before diagnosing hypertension.

questions.stem: While measuring blood pressure at 32 weeks you hear clear tapping at 138 mmHg. The sounds become muffled at 84 mmHg and are still heard down to 0 mmHg.
questions.q: How should you record this blood pressure?
questions.why: When sounds persist to zero (K5 absent), K4 (muffling) is used for the diastolic.

questions.stem: A woman in left lateral position in labour has a blood pressure of 112/64 mmHg taken with the cuff on her uppermost right arm. Half an hour ago, sitting, it was 146/94.
questions.q: What explains the difference?
options: Cuff arm above heart level gives a falsely low reading
questions.why: In left lateral the upper arm is above the heart, so the reading is falsely low. Measure seated or on the lower arm.

questions.stem: A primigravida at 35 weeks has blood pressure 152/10 mmHg0 mmHg twice, 4 hours apart. Urine dipstick shows protein 2+. She has no headache or visual symptoms.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next test?
questions.why: Dipstick ≥ 1+ with new hypertension needs quantification: PCR (≥ 30 mg/mmol significant) or 24-hour urine.

questions.stem: A woman at 28 weeks has no symptoms. Dipstick: protein 1+, nitrite positive, leucocytes 2+, glucose negative. Blood pressure 118/7 mmHg2 mmHg.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Send MSU for culture, then treat
questions.why: Nitrite and leucocytes point to infection; culture before the antibiotic. Bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated.

questions.stem: In a urine station the student dips the strip, lays it on a tissue and reads all the pads together after 3 minutes.
questions.q: Which pads are most likely to give a wrong result?
options: None: all can be read at 3 min
questions.why: Each pad has its own time; glucose (about 30 s) and ketones (about 40 s) read late give false values. Leucocytes are read at about 2 min.

questions.stem: A woman at 26 weeks has glycosuria 1+ on one visit. She has no risk factors, blood pressure is normal and the fundus fits the dates.
questions.q: What is the best interpretation?
options: Likely low renal threshold; recheck and screen per protocol
questions.why: Glycosuria is common in pregnancy (renal threshold falls) and is a poor test; repeated or ≥ 2+ needs an OGTT.

questions.stem: Blood pressure is 164/112 mmHg on a single reading at 36 weeks in a woman with headache and protein 3+.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: ≥ 160/110 is severe: one reading is enough; repeat within 15 min and start IV/oral antihypertensive with magnesium sulphate for severe PE.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old G2 P1 at 34 weeks has an intrauterine fetal death confirmed on real-time scan. She is well, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg, temperature normal, membranes intact, and clotting is normal. She asks which way is best.
questions.q: Which option do most women and doctors prefer?
questions.why: Induction shortens grief and avoids DIC from a retained fetus; caesarean section adds risk without benefit; artificial rupture of membranes risks infection.

questions.stem: Five days after an intrauterine fetal death delivery, a woman's breasts are painful and engorged. Her blood pressure during pregnancy was 160/105 and she is still on labetalol.
questions.q: What is the best advice?
options: Supportive bra, cold packs and analgesia
questions.why: Cabergoline is avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia (vasoconstriction); bromocriptine and oestrogen are no longer used.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old with a mechanical mitral valve on warfarin has a positive pregnancy test 5 weeks after her last period.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Switch to weight-based LMWH twice daily now
questions.why: Warfarin embryopathy occurs at 6–12 weeks; switch to low-molecular-weight heparin before 6 weeks. Stopping anticoagulation risks valve thrombosis.

questions.stem: A woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis, NYHA II, delivers vaginally. Ten minutes later bleeding is heavy and the uterus is soft.
questions.q: Which drug should be avoided?
questions.why: Ergometrine constricts veins and pushes blood into the heart, precipitating pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with epilepsy, fit-free for 2 years on sodium valproate, has just married and wants a baby.
questions.q: What is the best advice?
options: Switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam with the neurologist before conceiving, and start folic acid 5 mg
questions.why: Valproate carries the highest anomaly risk; switch before conception, never stop suddenly, and give folic acid 5 mg.

questions.stem: Day 2 after a normal birth, a 22-year-old exclusively breastfeeding mother wants reliable contraception starting before she leaves hospital tomorrow.
questions.q: Which method is most suitable now?
questions.why: Progestogen-only methods are safe from birth and do not reduce milk; IUD only ≤ 48 hours or from 4 weeks; combined methods wait 6 months.

questions.stem: A woman with gestational diabetes on insulin calls at 3 am: she is sweaty and shaky. Her glucometer reads 3.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: What should she do first?
options: Drink 15–20 g of sugar in water and recheck in 15 minutes
questions.why: Treat a hypo at once with fast sugar, recheck after 15 min, repeat if needed, then a snack; review the bedtime dose.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old had one lower-segment caesarean for fetal distress. She is now 36 weeks, cephalic, with no other problems, and asks about her options.
questions.q: What is the approximate rupture risk if she labours spontaneously?
questions.why: About 0.5% after one lower-segment scar in spontaneous labour; higher (2–3×) with induction. VBAC succeeds in 72–75%.

questions.theme: Counselling: the key advice
options: Oral glucose and recheck in 15 minutes
questions.lead: For each patient choose the single most appropriate advice.

items.stem: Woman with two previous caesarean sections, now 36 weeks, asks about labour.
items.why: Two or more previous caesarean section: VBAC not advised; elective caesarean section at 39 weeks.

items.stem: Mechanical valve, pregnancy test positive at 5 weeks.
items.why: Avoid warfarin embryopathy at 6–12 weeks.

items.stem: Woman on carbamazepine planning pregnancy next year.
items.why: Antiepileptics: high-dose folic acid from 3 months before conception.

items.stem: Intrauterine fetal death at 34 weeks, mother well, wants it over soon.
items.why: Induction is preferred; caesarean section only for usual indications.

questions.stem: In an abdominal examination station, a G2P1 at 34 weeks lies flat on the couch. Two minutes into palpation she says she feels dizzy and sweaty. Her pulse is 112/min and blood pressure 86/52 mmHg.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step in this station?
options: Raise her legs on two pillows
Measure the SFH quickly and finish
Tilt her to the left with a wedge under the right hip
questions.why: Supine hypotension from aortocaval compression settles with left lateral tilt. Leg raising does not relieve caval compression.

questions.stem: A primigravida at 32 weeks by a sure LMP and an early scan is examined. The symphysis–fundal height is 37 cm. The uterus is tense and shiny, fetal parts are hard to feel and a fluid thrill is present.
questions.q: What does this finding most likely mean?
questions.why: Tense uterus with fluid thrill and parts hard to feel is polyhydramnios. Twins give many parts and extra poles, not a fluid thrill.

questions.stem: At 37 weeks you feel a hard, round, ballotable mass in the fundus. A soft, broad mass lies above the symphysis. The back is on the mother's right.
questions.q: Where should you place the Pinard to hear the fetal heart?
options: Above the umbilicus on the left
Above the umbilicus on the right
Below the umbilicus on the left
Midway between umbilicus and right ASIS
questions.why: This is a breech with the back on the right: the heart is heard above the umbilicus on the back side.

questions.stem: A woman at 35 weeks has a broad uterus with a low fundus. The fundus and the pelvis feel empty, and a hard round mass lies in the left flank.
questions.q: What is the lie and presentation?
questions.why: Empty fundus and pelvis with the head in a flank = transverse lie, shoulder presenting.

questions.stem: A primigravida at 39 weeks has a cephalic presentation. With the pelvic grip, your fingers converge below the head and you count 5 finger breadths of head above the brim.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ultrasound for placental site and pelvis assessment
Reassure: normal at term in a primigravida
questions.why: A free head (5/5) at term in a primigravida suggests praevia, cephalopelvic disproportion or wrong dates: scan first. In a multipara it can be normal.

questions.stem: During an OSCE you measure the symphysis–fundal height at 30 cm in a woman at 34 weeks. She had a normal symphysis–fundal height at 30 weeks. Blood pressure 130/8 mmHg0 mmHg, urine clear.
questions.q: What is the best next step?
options: Growth scan with liquor and umbilical Doppler
questions.why: Symphysis–fundal height more than 2 cm below dates or static growth needs an ultrasound for fetal growth restriction and liquor.

questions.stem: You count a 'fetal heart' of 92/min with the Pinard at 30 weeks. The mother's radial pulse, felt at the same time, is 92/min.
questions.q: What does this finding mean?
options: Fetal distress: start CTG and oxygen
You are hearing the maternal pulse
questions.why: Matching rates mean you are hearing the mother. Move the Pinard to the fetal back, or use a Doppler.

questions.stem: In the pelvic grip at 38 weeks, the cephalic prominence is felt on the same side as the fetal back. The head is 3/5 palpable.
questions.q: What is the most likely attitude of the fetal head?
questions.why: A cephalic prominence on the same side as the back means the occiput is prominent: the head is extended (face). Opposite the back = flexed.

questions.stem: In a PPH drill station, a para 5 is bleeding 20 minutes after a normal birth. You have called for help; she has oxygen by mask and two large cannulae with warm saline running. Her pulse is 124/min and blood pressure 88/56 mmHg. The fundus is soft and 3 cm above the umbilicus.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step in this station?
options: Rub up the uterus and give oxytocin 10 IU slow IV
questions.why: A soft, high fundus is atony: massage plus oxytocin comes first. Ergometrine is the next rung, not the first drug.

questions.stem: A primigravida at 36 weeks has PPH after delivery. She had blood pressure 158/10 mmHg4 mmHg in labour and received magnesium sulphate. The uterus stays soft despite massage and an oxytocin infusion.
questions.q: Which drug should be avoided next?
options: Oxytocin 40 IU in 500 mL over 4 h
questions.why: Ergometrine raises blood pressure and is avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia. Carboprost is avoided in asthma, which she does not have.

questions.stem: In an eclampsia drill the examiner hands you 10 mL ampoules of 50% magnesium sulphate, saline and a 20 mL syringe, and asks you to prepare the loading dose for IV use.
questions.q: Which preparation is correct?
options: 8 mL of 50% + 12 mL saline over 5–15 min
8 mL of 50% undiluted as a fast bolus
10 mL of 50% + 10 mL saline over 1 min
questions.why: 50% magnesium sulphate holds 1 g per 2 mL, so 4 g is 8 mL, diluted to 20 mL and given over 5–15 min. A fast undiluted bolus risks arrest.

questions.stem: A woman 8 hours after an eclamptic convulsion is on magnesium sulphate 1 g/h. On your hourly check her knee jerks are absent, respiratory rate 9/min, oxygen saturation 91% on air, urine 20 mL in the last hour.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop MgSO₄, give calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV slowly and oxygen
questions.why: Lost reflexes with RR below 12 is toxicity with respiratory depression: stop and give the antidote. Reducing the rate is not enough at this stage.

questions.stem: On a birthing mannequin, the head of a 4.4 kg baby of a diabetic mother has delivered but retracts against the perineum. Gentle axial traction fails. Help has been called and the time noted. The mother is lying flat with her legs in stirrups.
questions.q: What is the next step in this station?
options: Fundal pressure with the next contraction
questions.why: After help, McRoberts is the first manoeuvre; with suprapubic pressure it frees most cases. Internal manoeuvres and the posterior arm come later.

questions.stem: Para 3 at 38 weeks, 5 cm dilated, has spontaneous rupture of membranes. A loop of cord is felt in the vagina and the fetal heart rate is 80 bpm. Help has been called and theatre informed.
questions.q: What should your hand do while she is moved to theatre?
options: Push the cord back above the head
Hold the cord to feel its pulse continuously
Push the presenting part up and keep it there
Leave the vagina to avoid infection
Apply fundal pressure to deliver quickly
questions.why: Elevating the presenting part keeps pressure off the cord until delivery. Handling or replacing the cord causes spasm.

questions.stem: A term baby is born floppy and not breathing after a long second stage. He has been dried, wrapped and placed with the head in the neutral position. Heart rate is 70/min.
questions.q: What is the next step?
options: Give five inflation breaths with a bag and mask
Deep suction of the oropharynx and trachea
Give adrenaline through the umbilical vein
Assign the 1-minute Apgar score and wait
questions.why: Lung inflation is the key step in an apnoeic newborn. Compressions start only if HR stays below 60 after 30 s of effective ventilation.

questions.stem: At 5 minutes a newborn has a pink body with blue hands and feet, heart rate 110/min, grimaces on suction, has some flexion of the limbs and a weak, irregular cry.
questions.q: What is the Apgar score?
questions.why: Colour 1, pulse ≥ 100 = 2, grimace 1, some flexion 1, weak irregular cry 1: total 6. A 7 would need a good cry or active movement.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman's last menstrual period began on 1 March 2026. Her cycles are regular, every 28 days, and she was not on hormonal contraception.
questions.q: What is her expected date of delivery?
questions.why: Naegele: add 7 days (8 March), subtract 3 months (8 December 2025), add 1 year: 8 December 2026.

questions.stem: A woman is pregnant now. She had a caesarean at term, twins delivered vaginally at 35 weeks, and a miscarriage at 9 weeks.
questions.q: How is her obstetric history written?
questions.why: Four pregnancies including this one; two births ≥ 24 weeks (twins count as one birth); one loss < 24 weeks.

questions.stem: In a history station, a 22-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks has blood pressure 150/100 mmHg. She reports a headache since morning not relieved by paracetamol and flashing lights. No fits.
questions.q: What does this history point to?
questions.why: Severe headache and visual disturbance are severe features of pre-eclampsia, whatever the blood pressure level.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old at 7 weeks of amenorrhoea had right iliac fossa pain yesterday, then light dark spotting. Today she fainted at home and has pain at the tip of her right shoulder. She had an IUCD removed last year after pelvic infection.
questions.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Pain before bleeding, syncope and shoulder-tip pain (diaphragm irritation by blood) with PID history point to ruptured ectopic.

questions.stem: A G5 P4 at 33 weeks woke at night lying in blood: bright red, painless. She had two small bleeds at 30 weeks. She had two previous caesarean sections.
questions.q: What is the most important thing to avoid at this stage?
questions.why: The history points to placenta praevia; digital vaginal examination may cause very heavy bleeding. Previous caesarean section also raises accreta risk.

questions.stem: A G6 P5 at 28 weeks has Hb 7.5 g/dL. She drinks tea after every meal, eats clay, and her last baby was born 13 months ago. She stopped her iron tablets due to nausea.
questions.q: What is the most likely type of anaemia?
questions.why: Pica, tea with meals, short birth interval and poor adherence all point to iron deficiency; confirm with MCV and ferritin.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old primigravida from Gezira at 24 weeks has had fever with rigors for 3 days. She is alert, can swallow tablets, has no jaundice or dark urine, and sleeps without a net.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate first test?
options: Blood film or RDT for malaria
questions.why: In an endemic area, fever in pregnancy is malaria until proven otherwise; test first, then grade severity.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida at 32 weeks reports wet underwear since morning. On questioning she leaks only when she coughs or laughs, the fluid smells of urine, and there was no gush.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Leak only on coughing, smell of urine and no gush suggest stress incontinence; speculum shows no pool.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old G2 P1 at 36 weeks says the baby has moved less since yesterday. Her blood pressure was 145/95 last week and the last scan said the baby was small.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Advise kick counting at home for 2 days
Listen to the fetal heart now, then CTG
Book a scan for next week
questions.why: Reduced movements need same-day assessment: fetal heart, CTG, then growth and Doppler scan given her fetal growth restriction risk.

questions.stem: A primigravida has been fully dilated for 2.5 hours without epidural. The head is 0/5 palpable, station +2, position direct occipito-anterior, membranes ruptured, CTG normal. She is exhausted.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: Delay in the second stage with all prerequisites met is an indication for low instrumental delivery. Rotation is not needed in occipito-anterior.

questions.stem: A woman is fully dilated with fetal bradycardia. On abdominal palpation 2/5 of the head is palpable; on vaginal examination there is caput and moulding +3, station −1.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate delivery?
questions.why: Head above the spines and more than 1/5 palpable is a contraindication to instruments; deliver by caesarean.

questions.stem: You are applying a ventouse cup on a model. The examiner asks where the centre of the cup should lie.
questions.q: Where is the correct position?
options: On the occipital bone behind the posterior fontanelle
On the sagittal suture 3 cm in front of the posterior fontanelle
questions.why: The flexion point keeps the head flexed. An anterior cup deflexes the head and fails.

questions.stem: During a ventouse delivery, the cup has come off twice and the head has not descended with the last pull.
questions.q: What is the next step?
questions.why: Two detachments or no descent are stop rules. Sequential instruments without descent increase fetal injury.

questions.stem: A woman at 32 weeks is fully dilated with fetal distress; the head is 0/5, occipito-anterior, station +2.
questions.q: Which instrument is most suitable?
questions.why: Ventouse is avoided before 34 weeks; forceps can be used at any gestation.

questions.stem: At 6 cm, the midwife feels a loop of pulsating cord in the vagina. Fetal heart rate is 90 bpm.
questions.q: Which category of caesarean section is this?
questions.why: Cord prolapse with bradycardia is an immediate threat to fetal life: within 30 min of decision.

questions.stem: A healthy woman, BMI 27, has an emergency caesarean in labour for failure to progress.
questions.q: Which thromboprophylaxis is most appropriate?
options: Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily for 10 days
questions.why: Emergency caesarean is a strong risk factor; low-molecular-weight heparin for 10 days, plus mobilisation and stockings.

questions.stem: Before an elective caesarean, the intern plans to give cefuroxime after the cord is clamped.
questions.q: What is the correct timing of the prophylactic antibiotic?
options: At the end of the operation
questions.why: Giving it before incision lowers wound and uterine infection more, without harm to the baby.

questions.stem: A woman had a caesarean 3 years ago through a vertical incision in the upper uterus at 26 weeks. She is now 36 weeks pregnant and asks about a vaginal birth.
questions.q: What is the best advice?
options: Vaginal birth after caesarean is safe
questions.why: A classical scar ruptures in 2–9%, often before labour; plan elective caesarean.

questions.stem: A primigravida has just delivered a baby. Before you give oxytocin, the midwife says the uterus still feels large.
questions.q: What must you do first?
options: Palpate the abdomen to exclude a second twin
questions.why: A uterotonic before a second twin is delivered can trap it. Palpation (or scan) comes first.

questions.stem: During a normal birth on a model, the head has delivered and you feel a loop of cord round the neck that is very tight and cannot be slipped over the head.
questions.q: What is the next step?
options: Clamp the cord twice and cut between
questions.why: A tight cord that cannot be slipped is clamped and cut before the shoulders are delivered.

questions.stem: After restitution, the next contraction comes. The head faces the mother's right thigh.
questions.q: How should the anterior shoulder be delivered?
options: Strong lateral traction toward the side
Gentle traction downward on the parietal bones
questions.why: Gentle downward traction delivers the anterior shoulder; upward traction then delivers the posterior shoulder.

questions.stem: Forty minutes after a vaginal birth with oxytocin 10 IU IM and controlled cord traction, the placenta has not delivered. Bleeding is minimal and the uterus is contracted.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Strong cord traction without a contraction
Empty the bladder, then manual removal of the placenta
questions.why: Retained placenta is diagnosed at 30 min with active management. Pulling without a contraction risks inversion.

questions.stem: A primigravida needs a ventouse for delay in the second stage. You decide on an episiotomy.
questions.q: Which description is correct?
options: Midline cut toward the anus, 6 cm long
Mediolateral cut from the fourchette, 60° from the midline, at crowning
Mediolateral cut before the head reaches the perineum
Lateral cut from the labia minora
J-shaped cut through the anal sphincter
questions.why: Mediolateral at 60° at crowning protects the sphincter. Cutting too early causes bleeding without benefit.

questions.stem: After a forceps delivery, a tear is examined. The perineal muscles are torn and on rectal examination about two thirds of the external anal sphincter thickness is torn; the internal sphincter is intact.
questions.q: How is this tear classified?
questions.why: More than 50% of the EAS is 3b. 3c means the internal sphincter is also torn.

questions.stem: You have repaired a mediolateral episiotomy in three layers.
questions.q: Which step must follow before you finish?
options: Rectal examination and counting swabs and needle
questions.why: PR excludes stitches in the rectum and the count prevents a retained swab.

questions.stem: A woman attends 6 weeks after a long labour ended by forceps. She cannot control flatus and soils her underwear. The perineum looks healed.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Anal incontinence after an instrumental birth suggests a sphincter injury not recognised by PR at delivery.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks is admitted at 08:00 with regular contractions. The cervix is 6 cm dilated, 3/5 of the head is palpable, membranes intact. You are asked to start her partogram.
questions.q: Where should the first X be plotted?
options: At hour 0 on the 4 cm line
On the action line at the 6 cm point
At hour 0 on the 6 cm line, left of the alert line
On the alert line at the 6 cm point
questions.why: A woman admitted in the active phase is plotted on the alert line at her dilatation. Plotting at hour 0 left of the line falsely suggests faster progress.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old primigravida has been in active labour for 4 hours. Cervix went from 4 to 5 cm. The partogram shows 2 contractions in 10 minutes in dotted boxes. Fetal heart rate 140, liquor intact, no moulding, head 4/5.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Amniotomy and oxytocin infusion, reassess in 2 hours
questions.why: Slow progress with weak, short contractions and no obstruction is treated by augmentation. Caesarean is for obstruction or fetal compromise.

questions.stem: A para 5 at 41 weeks has had strong contractions, 5 in 10 minutes lasting over 40 s, for 4 hours. Cervix remains 7 cm, head 3/5 palpable, moulding +3, urine is scanty and blood-stained, pulse 124/min.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Resuscitate and perform emergency caesarean section
questions.why: Good contractions with no descent, severe moulding and haematuria mean obstructed labour. Oxytocin risks uterine rupture in a grand multipara.

questions.stem: A partogram shows the liquor letter changing from C to M at 03:00. The fetal heart remains 140–150.
questions.q: What does this change mean?
questions.why: I intact, C clear, M meconium, B blood, A absent. Meconium calls for closer fetal monitoring.

questions.stem: A woman at 38 weeks with pre-eclampsia is on CTG at 6 cm. Baseline 155, variability 3 bpm for 60 minutes, no accelerations. Each contraction is followed by a smooth fall of 30 bpm whose lowest point comes 30 s after the contraction peak.
questions.q: How do you classify this CTG?
questions.why: Repeated late decelerations and variability < 5 for > 50 min are pathological features. Fetal sleep does not cause late decelerations.

questions.stem: At 8 cm, shortly after amniotomy, the fetal heart rate falls from 140 to 80 bpm and stays there for 4 minutes. Contractions are 3 in 10 minutes and the mother's blood pressure is normal.
questions.q: What is the most important immediate step after calling for help?
options: Vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse
questions.why: A sudden bradycardia just after artificial rupture of membranes suggests cord prolapse, found by vaginal examination. Scalp sampling is not done in a prolonged bradycardia.

questions.stem: A CTG in labour shows a baseline of 140 with a bandwidth of 15 bpm, three rises of 20 bpm lasting 20 s in 10 minutes, no dips, and 3 contractions in 10 minutes.
questions.q: What is the best interpretation?
questions.why: All features are normal and accelerations are reassuring.

questions.theme: CTG patterns in labour
questions.lead: For each trace choose the most likely pattern.

items.stem: At 9 cm, U-shaped dips begin and end with each contraction, variability normal.
items.why: Mirror image of the contraction: head compression.

items.stem: After rupture of membranes with scanty liquor, abrupt V-shaped dips of 50 bpm, quick recovery, not at a fixed point of the contraction.
items.why: Abrupt V shape at varying times: cord compression.

items.stem: A smooth regular wave of 10 bpm amplitude, 3 cycles per minute, no variability, in a Rh-isoimmunised woman.
items.why: Sinusoidal pattern suggests severe fetal anaemia.

items.stem: A trace reading 88 bpm that rises when the mother's pulse rises; abdominal palpation finds the fetal back away from the probe.
items.why: Probe is picking up the maternal pulse: compare with her pulse and reposition.

questions.stem: At a spotter station you are shown long obstetric forceps with almost no pelvic curve and a lock that lets one blade slide along the other.
questions.q: What is the main use of this instrument?
options: Outlet delivery with the head on the perineum
Rotation of an occipito-transverse or occipito-posterior head
Delivery of the head at caesarean section
Delivery of the aftercoming head of the breech only
questions.why: These are Kielland forceps: the sliding lock corrects asynclitism and they are used to rotate. Wrigley forceps are the outlet and caesarean forceps.

questions.stem: A spotter shows an amber ampoule kept in a dark box in the labour ward fridge. The examiner says it is given 0.5 mg IM for postpartum haemorrhage.
questions.q: In which patient is this drug contraindicated?
options: Woman after a vaginal twin delivery
questions.why: Ergometrine raises blood pressure and is avoided in hypertension, pre-eclampsia and heart disease. Asthma is the contraindication to carboprost.

questions.stem: A spotter shows a 60 mL plastic syringe with a valve and a lock, beside flexible plastic cannulas of 4 to 12 mm. The patient is at 9 weeks with an incomplete miscarriage, stable.
questions.q: Which cannula size is usually chosen?
options: Any size, as long as the vacuum is strong
questions.why: For manual vacuum aspiration the cannula size in mm is about the weeks of gestation. Too small blocks; too big needs more dilatation.

questions.stem: A breastfeeding mother, 3 weeks after a normal birth, sees a copper T device at the family planning spotter and asks if it can be fitted today.
questions.q: What is the best answer?
options: Yes, today is the best time
Wait until 4 weeks after the birth
