questions.why: A copper IUCD is fitted within 48 hours of birth or after 4 weeks; between them expulsion and perforation are more likely. Breastfeeding is not a problem.

questions.stem: In a PPH station the examiner shows a plain glass tube with 3 mL of the patient's blood. After 12 minutes of gentle tilting every 30 seconds the blood is still liquid.
questions.q: What does this finding mean?
questions.why: No clot in 7–10 minutes means low fibrinogen: coagulopathy. Blood products are needed alongside treating the cause.

questions.stem: A spotter shows a transvaginal scan of a woman with 10 weeks of amenorrhoea, vomiting and bleeding. The uterus is filled with many small cystic spaces in a bright pattern; no fetus is seen.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.why: The 'snowstorm' picture is a complete mole: suction evacuation, then follow β-hCG to normal. Medical evacuation is avoided because of trophoblast spread.

questions.theme: Spotter: name the item
questions.lead: For each description choose the item. Each option may be used once, more than once or not at all.

items.stem: Used with the woman in the left lateral position to inspect the anterior vaginal wall for a vesicovaginal fistula; an assistant must hold it.
items.why: Sims speculum retracts the posterior wall and is not self-retaining.

items.stem: Inserted through the cervix with 30–50 mL saline in its balloon and kept on traction for 12–24 hours in a woman with a previous caesarean.
items.why: Mechanical induction with a Foley is safer than prostaglandin after a scar.

items.stem: Filled with 300–500 mL saline inside the uterus when atony persists after oxytocin, ergometrine and misoprostol.
items.why: Bakri balloon tamponade for atonic PPH.

items.stem: Two of them are 'walked' around the cervix after a forceps delivery when a firm uterus is still bleeding.
items.why: Sponge-holding forceps expose the whole cervix to find a tear.

questions.stem: A woman at 31 weeks reports a gush of clear fluid 2 hours ago. No contractions. Fundus fits dates, cephalic, fetal heart rate 144/min.
questions.q: What is the next step in this station?
options: Digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix
questions.why: Suspected preterm prelabour rupture of membranes without labour: sterile speculum to look for pooling. Digital vaginal examination raises infection risk.

questions.stem: At 34 weeks a woman has painless bright red bleeding. The placental site is not yet known. She is stable.
questions.q: What should be avoided until the placental site is known?
questions.why: No digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia is excluded by scan; it can provoke very heavy bleeding.

questions.stem: On sterile speculum examination at 33 weeks you see a pool of fluid in the posterior fornix. Nitrazine paper turns blue. There is also fresh blood in the vagina.
questions.q: What does the nitrazine result mean?
options: Blood can make nitrazine falsely positive; confirm with fern or scan
questions.why: Blood, semen and BV raise vaginal pH and can make nitrazine falsely positive; fern test or liquor volume helps.

questions.stem: During a speculum station the student cannot see the cervix after opening the Cusco speculum; only vaginal walls bulge between the blades.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Remove and do a digital VE
Close the blades, withdraw slightly, angle down and reopen
Open the blades fully and wider
questions.why: The cervix is usually posterior; partly withdraw, re-angle backwards and down, and reopen.

questions.stem: A primigravida in labour: cervix 6 cm, thin, well applied; vertex at station 0. The small Y-shaped fontanelle is felt anteriorly to the mother's left.
questions.q: What is the position?
questions.why: The posterior fontanelle marks the occiput: anterior and to her left = LOA.

questions.stem: At full dilatation after 2 hours of pushing, the head is 3/5 palpable abdominally. On vaginal examination the skull bones overlap and cannot be pushed back, with a large caput at the introitus.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.why: Moulding +3, big caput and a head 3/5 above the brim = obstruction; the caput makes station look low. Caesarean, not instruments.

questions.stem: A woman at 41+3 weeks is booked for induction. Vaginal examination: cervix 1 cm, 3 cm long, firm, posterior, station −3.
questions.q: What is the most appropriate method to start induction?
questions.why: Bishop score = 1 (unfavourable, ≤ 6): ripen the cervix first; artificial rupture of membranes needs a favourable cervix.

questions.theme: Findings at speculum and vaginal examination
questions.lead: For each finding choose the most likely interpretation.

items.stem: A pool of clear fluid in the posterior fornix that increases when she coughs.
items.why: Pooling plus leak on coughing confirms ruptured membranes.

items.stem: Post-coital spotting; a red velvety ring around the os that bleeds on touch; placenta fundal on scan.
items.why: Ectropion: columnar epithelium on the ectocervix, common in pregnancy.

items.stem: On vaginal examination in labour the large diamond-shaped fontanelle is felt easily in the centre.
items.why: An easily felt anterior fontanelle means a deflexed head, usually occipito-posterior.

items.stem: On vaginal examination no cervix can be felt around the head.
items.why: No cervical rim = 10 cm, full dilatation.

questions.stem: Currently pregnant. Previous: term vaginal birth, miscarriage at 10 weeks, stillbirth at 30 weeks.
questions.q: How is her parity written?
questions.why: Stillbirth ≥ 24 weeks counts as para; the miscarriage is '+'; the current pregnancy adds to G.

questions.stem: Currently pregnant. Previous twin delivery at 35 weeks; no other pregnancies.
questions.q: How is she described?
questions.why: Twins are one pregnancy and one birth event.

questions.stem: A woman at 30 weeks gives a history of painless, bright red, recurrent vaginal bleeding after intercourse and at rest.
questions.q: Which examination must be avoided until a scan is done?
questions.why: Painless bright red bleeding suggests praevia; digital examination can cause very heavy bleeding.

questions.stem: A woman with two previous caesarean sections attends for booking.
questions.q: Which piece of past history most changes your plan for this birth?
questions.why: A classical (upper segment) incision means elective caesarean section with no labour; lower segment scars guide VBAC decisions.

questions.stem: Booking at 10 weeks. Her previous baby weighed 4.6 kg; she has no known illness.
questions.q: Which test should be arranged?
questions.why: A previous baby ≥ 4.5 kg is a risk factor for gestational diabetes; screen with OGTT.

questions.stem: A woman at 8 weeks says she had a 'grape-like' tissue passed with bleeding.
questions.q: What does this history suggest?
questions.why: Passage of vesicles is characteristic of a hydatidiform mole.

questions.stem: Booking history: three previous losses at 18, 20 and 21 weeks, each with painless sudden rupture of membranes and rapid delivery.
questions.q: What is the most likely cause?
questions.why: Painless mid-trimester losses with rapid delivery suggest cervical weakness.

questions.stem: At 6 weeks' amenorrhoea a woman reports sudden lower abdominal pain and pain at the tip of her right shoulder.
questions.q: What does the shoulder pain indicate?
questions.why: Shoulder-tip pain is referred from diaphragmatic irritation by intraperitoneal blood: ruptured ectopic.

questions.stem: A woman who had a blood transfusion after a road accident is now pregnant.
questions.q: Why is this history important?
questions.why: Transfusion can sensitise her to red-cell antigens, causing haemolytic disease of the fetus.

questions.stem: A Sudanese primigravida at 36 weeks has a history of type III female genital cutting.
questions.q: What should be planned?
questions.why: Type III FGC needs deinfibulation for examination and delivery; re-infibulation is not done.

questions.stem: A woman at 33 weeks presents with vaginal bleeding.
questions.q: Which feature in her history most suggests placental abruption?
options: Constant abdominal pain with a hard tender uterus
questions.why: Abruption causes constant pain with a woody tender uterus; praevia is painless.

questions.stem: A student presents a long case and stops after the drug history.
questions.q: What is missing from the presentation?
options: A summary and diagnosis or differential
questions.why: A history presentation ends with a summary and a diagnosis.

questions.stem: Primigravida at 38 weeks: head 5/5 palpable and freely ballotable.
questions.q: Which cause must be excluded first by ultrasound?
questions.why: In a primigravida the head usually engages by 36–38 weeks; a high head suggests praevia, cephalopelvic disproportion or wrong dates, and praevia must be excluded.

questions.stem: Symphysis–fundal height 28 cm at 33 weeks by a sure LMP confirmed at 12 weeks.
questions.q: What is the next step?
options: Ultrasound for fetal growth and liquor
questions.why: Symphysis–fundal height more than 2 cm below weeks needs a growth and liquor scan.

questions.stem: On the fundal grip you feel a hard, round, ballotable mass.
questions.q: What is the presentation?
questions.why: A head in the fundus means the breech is presenting.

questions.stem: The abdomen is broad, the fundus is empty and the pelvis feels empty at 34 weeks.
questions.q: What is the most likely lie?
questions.why: Empty fundus and pelvis with a broad uterus = transverse lie.

questions.stem: During the 4th Leopold grip your fingers diverge as they slide into the pelvis.
questions.q: What does this mean?
questions.why: Diverging fingers indicate that the widest diameter has entered the pelvis: engaged.

questions.stem: Only two fifths of the fetal head are palpable above the brim.
questions.q: How do you describe the head?
questions.why: ≤ 2/5 palpable = engaged.

questions.stem: Using a Pinard stethoscope you count 84 beats per minute at 36 weeks.
questions.q: What is the first thing to do?
options: Feel the mother's radial pulse at the same time
questions.why: You may be counting the maternal pulse; compare with her radial pulse first.

questions.stem: Breech presentation at 36 weeks.
questions.q: Where will you best hear the fetal heart?
options: In the flank below the costal margin only
questions.why: With breech the fetal back and shoulder are higher, so the heart is heard at or above the umbilicus.

questions.stem: A tense, shiny abdomen at 32 weeks; fetal parts are hard to feel and a fluid thrill is present.
questions.q: What is the most likely finding on scan?
questions.why: These are classic signs of excess liquor.

questions.stem: Leaking clear fluid at 31 weeks without contractions.
questions.q: Which examination is appropriate?
questions.why: In suspected preterm prelabour rupture of membranes use a sterile speculum; avoid digital examination (infection).

questions.stem: Abdominal inspection shows a low transverse scar just above the pubic hairline.
questions.q: What operation does this usually indicate?
questions.why: A Pfannenstiel incision is used for lower segment caesarean section (and some gynaecological surgery).

questions.stem: A primigravida of height 146 cm has a high head at 39 weeks.
questions.q: What does her height suggest?
questions.why: Short stature (< 150 cm) suggests a small pelvis and cephalopelvic disproportion.

questions.theme: Findings on abdominal examination
questions.lead: For each finding choose the most likely explanation.

items.stem: Hard round ballotable mass in the fundus; fetal heart above the umbilicus.
items.why: Head in the fundus, breech presenting.

items.stem: Fetal parts felt very easily, uterus moulded round the fetus, symphysis–fundal height 4 cm below dates.
items.why: Little liquor: parts easy to feel.

items.stem: Hard, tender, woody uterus with dark vaginal bleeding.
items.why: Classic abruption.

items.stem: Two fetal heart rates 20 bpm apart.
items.why: Two hearts at different rates = twins.
